Predicting Arabica and Robusta Coffee Futures Prices: An Econometric and Machine Learning Approach with Macroeconomic, Climatic, and Speculative Determinants

  • Show All Code
  • Hide All Code
  • View Source

Master’s Thesis in Management — Business Analytics Orientation

Author

Mohamed Hussein

Published

August 30, 2026

Abstract

This thesis compares six forecasting models, Linear Regression, ARIMAX, Random Forest, XGBoost, Support Vector Machine, and Artificial Neural Network, in predicting monthly ICE Arabica and ICE Futures Europe Robusta coffee futures prices. Arabica is estimated over 211 monthly observations (June 2006-December 2023) and Robusta over 192 (January 2008-December 2023), the periods for which all fourteen predictors are simultaneously available. These predictors span four macroeconomic and financial variables (CPI, WTI, the Federal Funds Rate, DXY), sugar and cocoa futures prices as market-spillover variables, four USDA supply-and-demand fundamentals, temperature and precipitation indices for the leading producer countries, the Oceanic Niño Index, and CFTC net Managed Money positioning. All models are evaluated under an identical walk-forward expanding-window protocol with an 80/20 train-test split, ensuring genuine out-of-sample comparability across econometric and machine learning approaches. ARIMAX, the only model to combine an explicit autoregressive structure with the fourteen exogenous determinants, achieves the strongest out-of-sample performance for both varieties (R² = 0.955 for Arabica, 0.926 for Robusta), outperforming every machine learning model tested; among the four machine learning models, XGBoost performs best (R² = 0.812 and 0.797, respectively). Linear Regression proves highly sensitive to multicollinearity, collapsing to an R² of 0.276 for Robusta despite a respectable 0.784 for Arabica. Permutation importance shows that Ending stocks, COT net Managed Money, and WTI matter most for Arabica, while WTI and the Federal Funds Rate matter most for Robusta, a divide not anticipated by the existing literature.

1 Introduction

Coffee futures prices respond to a wide array of forces: macroeconomic conditions, climate in producing regions, and the positioning of speculative traders in derivatives markets. Forecasting them accurately, and knowing which of these forces actually drive them, matters to a broad set of actors. Producers and cooperatives carry the price risk directly. Roasters and traders manage procurement costs around it. Policymakers watch it for what it implies about the welfare of coffee-dependent economies. Yet the empirical literature on coffee price forecasting remains comparatively thin. As the next section documents, it has rarely combined a rich set of exogenous predictors with a systematic comparison of econometric and machine learning approaches, and rarer still has it done so on the specific futures contracts that anchor global coffee pricing.

Section 2 reviews this literature in detail and identifies four gaps that motivate the present thesis. Coffee-specific forecasting studies rely almost exclusively on univariate or lightly specified models, with no macroeconomic, climatic, or financial variables built in. Most also work from spot prices or generic commodity indices rather than the ICE Arabica and LIFFE Robusta contracts that actually set the global benchmark. To the best of current knowledge, no study has modelled both varieties within a shared multivariate framework using a common set of predictors. And despite mounting evidence of the financialization of commodity futures markets, CFTC speculative positioning data has yet to be evaluated as a predictor in an out-of-sample coffee price forecasting framework, as opposed to explaining price movements that have already occurred.

These gaps translate into the following four research questions:

RQ1. How accurately can Arabica and Robusta coffee futures prices be forecast out-of-sample when a shared set of macroeconomic, climatic, fundamental, and speculative determinants is incorporated into a multivariate forecasting framework?

RQ2. How do the four machine learning models considered (Random Forest, XGBoost, Support Vector Machine, and Artificial Neural Network) perform, in terms of out-of-sample forecasting accuracy, relative to the two econometric benchmarks (linear regression and ARIMAX), when both are estimated under a common predictor set and an identical walk-forward validation protocol?

RQ3. Which of the macroeconomic, climatic, fundamental, and speculative determinants considered contribute most to forecasting accuracy for each coffee variety, and do Arabica and Robusta differ systematically in the determinants that matter most, reflecting their distinct market structures and producing geographies?

RQ4. Does speculative positioning by Managed Money traders, as captured by the CFTC Disaggregated Commitments of Traders report, contribute meaningfully to the forecasting accuracy and to the explanatory structure of Arabica and Robusta futures prices?

To address these questions, the present thesis compares six forecasting models: two econometric benchmarks, linear regression (MLR) and ARIMAX, and four machine learning algorithms, Random Forest, XGBoost, Support Vector Machine (SVM), and Artificial Neural Network (ANN). All six draw on a common monthly dataset spanning January 2000 to December 2023, built from fourteen macroeconomic, climatic, fundamental, and speculative predictors, and are evaluated using an identical walk-forward validation protocol for both varieties. The complete data processing pipeline, model code, and rendered analysis are made publicly available online.2

The remainder of this thesis is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews the relevant literature on coffee market dynamics, the financialization of commodity futures markets, the climatic determinants of coffee production, and the forecasting models applied to agricultural commodity prices. Section 3 describes the data sources, the construction of the two dependent variables and fourteen exogenous predictors, and the estimation strategy underlying the six forecasting models. Section 4 presents the out-of-sample forecasting results, including comparative model performance and forecast trajectories, before turning to interpretation through the coefficient-based readings available for the econometric models and the variable importance and partial dependence analysis computed for the machine learning models. Section 5 discusses the results in light of the research questions stated above. Section 6 concludes with a summary of findings, limitations, and directions for future research.

2 Literature Review

2.1 Coffee Futures Markets as an Object of Forecasting

Coffee is one of the most widely traded agricultural commodities in the world, yet forecasting its price remains a distinctly complex undertaking. This complexity reflects the structural heterogeneity of its two principal varieties, treated in the literature as fundamentally distinct markets rather than a single unified coffee market (Milas et al., 2004). Arabica futures are traded on the Intercontinental Exchange (ICE) in New York under the Coffee ‘C’ contract, the world benchmark for Arabica coffee pricing, under which physical delivery of exchange-grade green beans from up to twenty countries of origin is settled (ICE Futures U.S., n.d.). Robusta futures are listed on ICE Futures Europe in London, the former LIFFE exchange, where contracts are priced in U.S. dollars per metric tonne and serve as the global benchmark for Robusta coffee pricing (ICE Futures Europe, n.d.). Beyond their geographic separation, the two contracts differ in their pricing conventions: the Coffee ‘C’ contract is quoted in U.S. cents per pound for a lot of 37,500 pounds (ICE Futures U.S., n.d.), while the Robusta contract is priced in U.S. dollars per metric tonne for a lot of ten tonnes (ICE Futures Europe, n.d.), a distinction that requires unit harmonization prior to any comparative analysis. Together, these markets serve not only as price benchmarks for the global coffee trade but also as instruments through which producers, exporters, roasters, and financial investors manage price risk. This benchmark role reflects an informational function: because futures contracts are standardized and traded on centralized exchanges, they aggregate the dispersed information of market participants more effectively than spot markets, which remain fragmented by quality, location, and delivery terms (Cheng & Xiong, 2014).

The economic significance of these markets is difficult to overstate. While coffee is consumed predominantly in high-income countries, its production is almost exclusively concentrated in developing nations, with over fifty countries across Latin America, Africa, and Asia engaged in its cultivation and export (Lewin et al., 2004). This asymmetry generates a trade flow that typically moves from developing to developed regions (Ge et al., 2025), exposing producers to substantial price risks that futures markets are designed, at least in part, to mitigate (Lewin et al., 2004). Yet these same markets have proven highly volatile. The International Coffee Organization (ICO, 2020) documents the considerable price swings of the 2019-2020 period, attributing them to a combination of supply shocks, declining global inventories, and demand disruptions stemming from the COVID-19 pandemic. More recently, the USDA Foreign Agricultural Service (2025a) projected that global ending stocks would decline for a fifth consecutive year to just 20.1 million bags in 2025/26, even as world production was forecast to reach a record 178.8 million bags. This apparent contradiction reflects five consecutive years of consumption growth outpacing available supplies.

What makes these markets particularly challenging to model is not volatility alone, but the diversity of forces driving it. Unlike equity markets, agricultural commodity markets are shaped by a heterogeneous set of determinants spanning the supply side, including production, stocks, and climate, the demand side, encompassing consumption and economic growth, and the financial side, covering exchange rates, energy prices, and speculative positioning (Maurice & Davis, 2012). The influence of financial actors has grown substantially in recent decades, as commodity index investment has made prices increasingly sensitive to the risk appetite of institutional investors rather than to supply and demand conditions alone (Tang & Xiong, 2012). An additional layer of complexity arises from the interconnectedness of the two coffee markets themselves. Ge et al. (2025) document measurable and time-varying cross-market connectedness between ICE Arabica and LIFFE Robusta futures, with a two-way volatility spillover averaging 16 to 19 percent between the two markets, indicating that shocks originating in one propagate to the other.

2.2 Financialization of Futures Markets and the Role of Speculative Positioning

Over the past two decades, financial investors, including commodity index traders and hedge funds, have become substantial participants in commodity futures markets (Cheng & Xiong, 2014; Irwin & Sanders, 2011). This process, commonly referred to as financialization, has generated a broader debate: rather than resolving it directly, Cheng and Xiong (2014) argue that both the view that financialization caused a price bubble and the view that speculation is inconsequential are too simplistic, and that the more productive question concerns how financial investors have altered the underlying functioning of these markets. Its empirical consequences for the structure of commodity price co-movement are nonetheless well documented and carry direct implications for forecasting.

Tang and Xiong (2012) document a sharp increase in the correlation between non-energy commodities and crude oil prices beginning around 2004, coinciding with the large-scale entry of commodity index investors into futures markets, interpreting this as evidence that index investment introduced a new source of systematic risk linking otherwise heterogeneous commodities. For coffee futures, this implies that macro-financial variables such as oil prices and speculative positioning may carry predictive content beyond what supply and demand fundamentals alone provide.

Complementary evidence at the level of soft commodities reinforces this picture. Maurice and Davis (2012), whose analysis of market efficiency was discussed in the preceding section, also examine the long-run causal structure of price determination across coffee and cocoa, finding that oil price movements exert a causal influence on both Arabica and Robusta prices with transmission lags of approximately four years. Their analysis further suggests that growing speculative activity contributed to the price surges of the late 2000s, pushing prices above levels that fundamentals alone would justify, a result consistent with the financialization narrative of Tang and Xiong (2012) and one that strengthens the case for treating speculative positioning as a distinct predictor rather than subsuming it within broader macro-financial controls. Ederer et al. (2016), using a different multivariate time series framework than the one applied in this thesis, find that net long positions of Managed Money account for approximately 50% of the variation in Arabica coffee futures prices between 2006 and 2012, the largest share among the five commodities for which they find a statistically significant effect.

Taken together, this body of evidence indicates that speculative positioning is an empirically supported channel through which financialization influences coffee futures prices, rather than a peripheral consideration. The net positioning of managed money traders, derived from the Commodity Futures Trading Commission’s Disaggregated Commitments of Traders reports, is therefore included as a predictor in the present thesis on grounds that are both theoretically grounded and empirically supported across multiple methodological frameworks.

2.3 Climatic Determinants of Coffee Production and Price Volatility

Coffee cultivation is among the most climatically sensitive of all major agricultural commodities, and this sensitivity has direct consequences for price dynamics on futures markets. The two principal varieties occupy distinct agronomic niches: Arabica is concentrated in the higher-altitude zones of South America, while Robusta is predominantly grown in the lower-altitude regions of Southeast Asia and Africa, a divide reflected in the variety-specific country groupings used for the climate indices (Section 3.3.5). This geographic divergence means that climate shocks do not affect the two markets symmetrically, and that any forecasting framework treating them as interchangeable would misrepresent the structure of supply-side risk to which each is exposed.

The degree to which temperature constrains coffee production is well documented at the agronomic level. Läderach et al. (2017) show that even modest temperature increases are sufficient to compromise the viability of entire production zones, projecting that areas between 500 and 800 meters above sea level in Nicaragua will lose their agronomic suitability for Arabica by 2050 as growing conditions shift upward along the altitudinal gradient. While this projection operates on a longer horizon than the forecasting exercise of the present thesis, it establishes that temperature is a first-order constraint on coffee production at the agronomic level, which motivates its inclusion as a predictor alongside the shorter-term variation captured in the monthly series used here.

The El Niño-Southern Oscillation phenomenon has received the most sustained empirical attention as a systematic driver of coffee supply shocks. ENSO describes the interaction between ocean and atmosphere in the tropical Pacific, producing two alternating phases: El Niño, characterized by unusually warm sea surface temperatures in the central and eastern Pacific, and La Niña, associated with colder-than-normal conditions and intensified trade winds (Ubilava, 2012). These phases recur every two to seven years and generate geographically differentiated weather anomalies with direct consequences for coffee-growing regions. Because Arabica and Robusta are cultivated in climatically distinct geographies, ENSO shocks affect the two markets through structurally asymmetric supply channels. El Niño tends to create favorable conditions for Arabica production in Central America while simultaneously depressing Robusta output in Southeast Asia, generating opposing price pressures across the two futures markets (Ubilava, 2012). La Niña produces the reverse pattern, though its effects on coffee prices tend to be more persistent due to the asymmetric dynamics of the ENSO cycle itself (Ubilava, 2012). Overall, Ubilava (2012) finds that ENSO shocks exert a statistically significant influence on world coffee price dynamics, with effects detectable for up to one year following the initial shock.

Bastianin et al. (2018) offer an important qualification to this picture. While confirming that ENSO anomalies exert a statistically significant influence on Colombian Arabica production, exports, and price, they find that the overall explanatory power of ENSO remains modest in variance decomposition terms: in the short run, ENSO shocks account for only 2.2% of the variation in Colombian coffee production and 0.2% of the variability in its real price, rising to 8.3% and 5.8% respectively in the long run. By contrast, shocks arising in the world coffee market explain 97% of the variation in the real price of Colombian coffee on impact. This result does not undermine the case for including climate variables, but it does clarify their role: rather than standalone predictors capable of driving forecast accuracy on their own, they are best understood as one component of a broader multivariate framework in which macroeconomic and financial forces carry the greater share of explanatory weight.

Taken together, the evidence reviewed in this section points to a consistent conclusion: climate variables, and ENSO indices in particular, carry genuine but bounded explanatory content for coffee futures prices. Their inclusion alongside macroeconomic and financial predictors is empirically warranted, but their relative contribution to forecast accuracy is likely to be modest compared to demand-side and global market forces. This bounded role is precisely what motivates their integration into a broader multivariate framework rather than their treatment as primary drivers, a distinction that shapes both the variable selection and the interpretive expectations of the present thesis.

2.4 Forecasting Models Applied to Agricultural Commodity Prices

Two broad families of models are commonly applied to agricultural commodity price forecasting: time series econometric models such as ARIMA and its multivariate extension ARIMAX, valued for their parsimony and interpretability, and machine learning methods, increasingly used as an alternative for capturing non-linear dynamics. Understanding where each family succeeds and where it fails is a necessary starting point for motivating the comparative framework adopted in this thesis.

Applied to coffee price series, the limitations of purely autoregressive specifications become apparent early. Maurice and Davis (2012), whose account of the heterogeneous supply, demand, and financial determinants of coffee prices already informs the discussion of market complexity in Section 2.1, provide one of the most comprehensive empirical analyses of price volatility across coffee and related soft commodities, finding that coffee futures markets are broadly efficient in the weak-form sense: if past prices alone contain no exploitable predictive content, meaningful forecasts require the integration of fundamental and financial determinants alongside the price series itself.

Ahumada and Cornejo (2016) forecast quarterly prices of corn, soybeans, and wheat using a multivariate framework estimated on USDA production and inventory data, GDP growth for China, India, and the OECD, the US real exchange rate, and monetary aggregates. They find that models incorporating price interdependence and macroeconomic fundamentals generally outperform single-equation specifications and beat the random walk over a large part of the 2008-2014 out-of-sample period.

Milas et al. (2004) provide an early benchmark, applying linear and non-linear time series models to the spot prices of four coffee types using quarterly data spanning 1962 to 2001. Their out-of-sample evaluation reveals that non-linear specifications improve forecast accuracy over the random walk primarily for Colombian Milds (a washed Arabica origin), while neither class of model consistently outperforms the random walk for the remaining varieties, a result the authors attribute partly to the absence of detectable non-linearity in the forecast period. Their models rely exclusively on the price history of the four series, incorporating no macroeconomic, climatic, or financial determinants. This limitation is illustrated by the 2019-2020 price swings documented in Section 2.1, where the ICO (2020) attributes the disruption to a combination of supply shocks, declining global inventories, and pandemic-driven demand shifts, none of which is represented in a model constrained to its own lagged values.

Deina et al. (2022) show that this limitation persists even in more recent work. Applying a comparative forecasting framework to monthly Arabica and Robusta price series, benchmarking linear time series models against neural network specifications across horizons of one to twelve steps ahead, they find that non-linear methods outperform linear benchmarks on all standard error metrics, consistently across varieties and horizons. Yet, like Milas et al., their models rely exclusively on price history, without macroeconomic, climatic, or financial determinants.

Evidence beyond coffee presents a more mixed picture. Kohzadi et al. (1996) demonstrated, on monthly cash prices of wheat and live cattle over 1950-1990, that a feedforward neural network with a single hidden layer outperformed an ARIMA benchmark on all standard error metrics while also capturing a statistically significant number of price turning points that the linear model failed to detect. Like Kohzadi et al., the present thesis relies on walk-forward validation, evaluating each model sequentially out of sample, applied at the same monthly frequency to Arabica futures prices from 2006 to 2023 and Robusta futures prices from 2008 to 2023. However, Masini et al. (2023), in a comprehensive survey of supervised machine learning methods for time-series forecasting, find that nonlinear methods do not systematically outperform linear ones: in their own empirical illustration, a penalized linear regression is the best-performing model and random forest underperforms.

Oktoviany et al. (2021) develop a machine learning framework for agricultural commodity futures that incorporates meteorological variables and USDA supply-and-demand fundamentals as predictors. Although their application focuses on maize rather than coffee, the logic of integrating weather, stocks, and production into a machine learning architecture is directly transposable to the present setting, and their use of Refinitiv as the primary data source provides bibliographic precedent for the same choice made in this thesis.

Fang et al. (2020), decomposing six categories of Chinese agricultural futures prices into fast-moving and slow-moving components and testing SVM, neural network, and ARIMA specifications on each, find that SVM and neural networks dominate on the volatile, high-frequency component while no method holds a systematic advantage on the underlying trend, a result suggesting that the relative performance of ML models over econometric benchmarks depends on the structure of price variation being modelled.

Nayak et al. (2024) provide a particularly close methodological parallel, evaluating ARIMAX and MLR alongside ANN, SVR, Random Forest, and XGBoost, together with several deep learning architectures outside the scope of the present thesis, for the prediction of vegetable prices in India using weather variables as exogenous inputs. Their results reveal a more nuanced hierarchy than a simple split between linear and non-linear methods: the deep learning architectures introduced in the same study clearly dominate, but among the remaining six models, nearly identical to the model set used in the present thesis, the linear econometric benchmarks, ARIMAX and MLR, are frequently competitive with or superior to Random Forest and Support Vector Regression, while the artificial neural network posts the weakest results throughout.

Taken together, the literature surveyed in this section points to four interconnected gaps that the present thesis aims to address. Coffee-specific forecasting studies have relied almost exclusively on univariate or lightly specified models that incorporate no macroeconomic, climatic, or financial determinants, leaving a substantial share of price variance unexplained. Existing studies operate predominantly on spot price series or generic commodity indices rather than on the ICE Arabica and LIFFE Robusta futures contracts that serve as the global benchmarks for coffee pricing. No study has, to the best of current knowledge, modelled both varieties within a shared multivariate forecasting framework incorporating a common set of exogenous predictors, a gap made more consequential by the cross-market connectedness between Arabica and Robusta documented in Section 2.1, and one that separates the present thesis from studies such as Deina et al. (2022), which analyse both varieties but without exogenous determinants. Finally, despite empirical evidence that financialization constitutes a structurally significant influence on coffee futures markets, speculative positioning data derived from the CFTC Disaggregated Commitments of Traders reports has not been evaluated as a predictor in an out-of-sample coffee price forecasting framework, as opposed to explaining price movements that have already occurred. The present thesis addresses each of these gaps by applying a structured comparison of econometric and machine learning models to monthly ICE Arabica and LIFFE Robusta futures prices drawn from a dataset spanning 2000-2023, under a common set of macroeconomic, climatic, fundamental, and speculative predictors.

3 Data and Methodology

This section documents the construction of the monthly dataset used throughout the analysis, from the raw source files through to the assembled dataset passed to the six forecasting models. Eight data sources are combined: futures prices, macroeconomic indicators, USDA supply-and-demand fundamentals, ERA5 climate reanalysis data, the ENSO index, and CFTC speculative positioning data. Each subsection below covers one data source, its transformation into a monthly series, and, where relevant, the reasoning behind specific processing choices.

Setup

This chunk initialises the working environment for the entire pipeline. All raw input data file paths and global constants are defined here and referenced in every subsequent chunk. Output files produced later in the pipeline, including the climate indices and the final assembled datasets, are written to the shared PATH_OUTPUT directory defined here, although their individual filenames are set locally in the chunk that creates each file rather than centralised here. Constructing all paths relative to BASE_PATH means that relocating the data folder requires editing a single line.

Show code 
# Force reticulate to use the r-tensorflow virtual environment
# (Python 3.11) instead of the default system Python (3.13,
# which TensorFlow does not yet support). Must be set before
# any package below (e.g. keras3) triggers Python initialisation.

Sys.setenv(RETICULATE_PYTHON = "C:/Users/Mohamed/Documents/.virtualenvs/r-tensorflow/Scripts/python.exe")

packages_requis <- c(
  "readxl", "dplyr", "tidyr", "lubridate", "zoo", "readr",
  "ggplot2", "corrplot", "tseries", "urca", "forecast",
  "scales", "gridExtra", "knitr", "kableExtra", "moments",
  "ggrepel", "randomForest", "xgboost", "e1071", "nnet",
  "Metrics", "tibble", "ggh4x", "car", "broom", "tidytext", "neuralnet", "RSNNS", "glmnet", "rpart", "reticulate", "keras3"
)
for (pkg in packages_requis) {
  if (!requireNamespace(pkg, quietly = TRUE)) {
    install.packages(pkg, dependencies = TRUE)
  }
}
invisible(lapply(packages_requis, library, character.only = TRUE))

# Create output folders if they do not already exist
if (!dir.exists(PATH_OUTPUT)) dir.create(PATH_OUTPUT)
dir.create(file.path(PATH_OUTPUT, "tables"), showWarnings = FALSE)

3.1 Sample Period and Data Overview

The empirical analysis covers the period from January 2000 to December 2023, yielding 288 monthly observations in the assembled monthly dataset. The choice of this starting point reflects three converging considerations. First, the suspension of the International Coffee Organization’s export quota system in 1989, and its definitive abandonment following the failure of successive revival attempts over the subsequent four years, produced a decade of institutional transition that fundamentally restructured the price formation environment prevailing over the analysis period (Lewin et al., 2004). Price data prior to 2000 reflect a structurally distinct market environment whose inclusion would introduce regime-change discontinuities that complicate time series modelling without adding comparably informative variation. Second, the ERA5 reanalysis dataset used for climate variables reaches its highest spatial and temporal reliability from 2000 onward, corresponding to the transition to the modern satellite era documented by (Hersbach et al., 2020). Third, the CFTC Disaggregated Commitments of Traders report provides historical data only from June 2006 onward, and Robusta futures prices from Refinitiv are unavailable before January 2008. The analysis period ends in December 2023, the last month for which all data sources were simultaneously available at the time of data collection.

The dataset integrates eight distinct data sources spanning six variable categories: dependent variables, market spillover variables, macroeconomic and financial variables, supply-and-demand fundamentals, speculative positioning variables, and climate variables. Two structural data gaps deserve explicit acknowledgement. Robusta futures prices are available from Refinitiv only from January 2008 onward, so all Robusta model specifications are estimated on the 2008-2023 sub-period. The Managed Money net position is missing for the 77 months preceding June 2006. Since this variable enters all six model specifications as one of the fourteen exogenous predictors, this constraint also applies to Arabica, whose estimation sample accordingly begins in June 2006 rather than January 2000, yielding 211 monthly observations against Robusta’s 192. No imputation is applied to either series; missing values are handled in the modelling phase by restricting each specification to the sub-period for which all required variables are simultaneously available. The two final datasets used throughout the modelling phase are constructed by joining all variable series onto a complete monthly date spine covering January 2000 to December 2023, yielding a base monthly dataset of 288 observations across 16 analytical variables before the sample restrictions described above are applied.

3.2 Overview of the Dataset

This study draws on eight distinct data sources covering January 2000 to December 2023, yielding 288 monthly observations for the main analysis. Three considerations shape this choice of starting point. The International Coffee Organization suspended its export quota system in 1989, and the institutional transition that followed over the next decade reshaped how coffee prices were formed throughout the period (Lewin et al., 2004). Data from before 2000 would therefore reflect a structurally different market, and including it would introduce regime-change breaks that complicate time series modelling rather than clarify it. The timing also lines up well with the climate data: the ERA5 reanalysis dataset used for the climate variables reaches its highest spatial and temporal reliability from 2000 onward, coinciding with the transition to the modern satellite era (Hersbach et al., 2020). A third, more practical constraint comes from two variables that simply aren’t available earlier: the CFTC Disaggregated COT report only begins in June 2006, and Refinitiv’s Robusta futures prices only start in January 2008. The analysis runs through December 2023, the last month for which every data source could be aligned at the time of collection.

Two data availability constraints are worth flagging explicitly here. Robusta futures prices from Refinitiv only go back to 2008, so the 96 months from 2000 to 2007 are missing for this variable, and Robusta models are accordingly estimated on the 2008–2023 sub-period. The CFTC Disaggregated COT report follows a similar pattern: it was not introduced until June 2006, since this is the report that separates Managed Money from commercial hedgers, so the net speculative position variable is missing for the 77 months preceding that date. Both gaps are addressed directly in the modelling phase.

3.3 Dependent Variables

The two dependent variables are the monthly average closing prices of Arabica coffee futures traded on ICE Futures U.S. (contract symbol KC) and Robusta coffee futures traded on ICE Futures Europe, formerly the London International Financial Futures and Options Exchange (contract symbol RC). Both series come from Refinitiv via the CEDIF data facility at the University of Lausanne, the primary source for price data throughout this study, which offers institutional-grade quality since prices reflect actual transaction records from the ICE exchanges rather than aggregated or estimated values from secondary sources.

Arabica and Robusta are treated as two distinct dependent variables and modelled separately throughout the analysis, reflecting their different market structures, consumer bases and price determinants. A combined coffee price index is not constructed, since aggregating the two would obscure the variety-specific dynamics this study sets out to capture.

This chunk reads the four Refinitiv price series, Arabica, Robusta, Cocoa and Sugar, from their raw Excel files and aggregates them from daily to monthly frequency. A single reusable function handles the parsing logic for all four files, which share the same Refinitiv export format. The chunk then builds the time series plots for the two dependent variables.

Show code 
# ----------------------------------------------------------
# READING FUNCTION — REFINITIV EXCEL FORMAT
# Refinitiv exports contain metadata rows above the actual
# data. The function locates the header row by searching for
# the string "Exchange Date" in the first column, discards
# everything above it, converts the raw Excel date serial
# numbers to proper R Date objects, and aggregates daily
# closing prices to monthly averages.
#
# Arguments:
#   fichier       : path to the .xlsx file
#   nom_variable  : name to assign to the price column
#                   in the returned data frame
# Returns:
#   A two-column data frame: date (YYYY-MM) and the named
#   monthly average price variable.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

lire_refinitiv <- function(fichier, nom_variable) {

  # Read the raw file without column names (metadata rows present)
  df_raw <- read_excel(fichier, col_names = FALSE)

  # Locate the header row containing "Exchange Date"
  idx_hdr <- which(sapply(df_raw[[1]], function(x)
    identical(as.character(x), "Exchange Date")))
  if (length(idx_hdr) == 0) stop("Header not found in: ", fichier)

  # Retain only the two relevant columns (date and close price)
  # starting from the row immediately after the header
  df_data <- df_raw[(idx_hdr + 1):nrow(df_raw), 1:2]
  colnames(df_data) <- c("date_raw", "close")

  df_data %>%
    mutate(
      # Refinitiv stores dates as Excel serial numbers (days since
      # 1899-12-30). Multiply by 86400 to convert to POSIX seconds.
      date_raw = as.Date(as.POSIXct(as.numeric(date_raw) * 86400,
                                     origin = "1899-12-30", tz = "UTC")),
      close = as.numeric(close)
    ) %>%
    filter(!is.na(date_raw), !is.na(close)) %>%
    arrange(date_raw) %>%
    # Aggregate to monthly frequency: compute the arithmetic mean
    # of all trading days within each calendar month.
    # This is preferred over end-of-month prices as it is less
    # sensitive to contract rollover volatility.
    mutate(date = format(date_raw, "%Y-%m")) %>%
    group_by(date) %>%
    summarise(!!nom_variable := mean(close, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")
}

# Apply the function to all four Refinitiv price series
arabica  <- lire_refinitiv(FICHIER_ARABICA,  "prix_arabica")
robusta  <- lire_refinitiv(FICHIER_ROBUSTA,  "prix_robusta")
cacao_ny <- lire_refinitiv(FICHIER_CACAO_NY, "prix_cacao")
sucre_11 <- lire_refinitiv(FICHIER_SUCRE_11, "prix_sucre")


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# PLOT DATA — DEPENDENT VARIABLES
# Build a complete monthly date spine covering the full
# analysis period, then left-join the two coffee price
# series. Left-joining preserves all months in the spine,
# so months with no Robusta data (2000-2007) appear as NA
# rather than being silently dropped.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

df_prix <- data.frame(
  date = format(seq(as.Date("2000-01-01"),
                    as.Date("2023-12-01"), by = "month"), "%Y-%m")
) %>%
  left_join(arabica, by = "date") %>%
  left_join(robusta, by = "date") %>%
  mutate(date_fmt = as.Date(paste0(date, "-01")))

# ----------------------------------------------------------

The Arabica price series covers the full 2000–2023 period and displays the volatility typical of agricultural commodity markets. Robusta, available from 2008 onward, shares the same broad phases of decline and recovery over the period they overlap, though the timing of individual peaks and troughs differs somewhat between the two.

3.4 Explanatory Variables

3.4.1 Market Spillover Variables

Sugar and cocoa prices are included as potential spillover variables. Coffee, sugar and cocoa are all tropical agricultural commodities exposed to similar climate shocks and traded on overlapping futures markets (Maurice & Davis, 2012), and in Brazil specifically, the world’s largest producer of both coffee and sugar, land substitution between the two crops creates a direct supply-side link (Gilio & Moraes, 2016). Sugar is captured via the Sugar No.11 contract (raw cane sugar, ICE Futures U.S.) and cocoa via the ICE New York contract, both sourced from Refinitiv via CEDIF (Refinitiv, 2026) and aggregated to monthly frequency using the same procedure as the coffee price series.

3.4.2 Macroeconomic and Financial Variables

Four macroeconomic variables are included to capture the broader financial and monetary environment that influences commodity prices, all available at monthly frequency.

The WTI crude oil price, sourced from the Federal Reserve Economic Data (FRED) database maintained by the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis (Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis, 2026a), captures the energy cost dimension of coffee production and transportation, as well as the broader commodity price cycle that tends to move raw materials together. The US Dollar Index (DXY), sourced from Investing.com (Investing.com, 2026), measures the value of the dollar against a basket of major currencies, and since coffee futures are priced in dollars, a stronger dollar tends to depress prices for non-dollar buyers by reducing global demand. The Federal Funds Rate, also sourced from FRED (Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis, 2026b), proxies the Federal Reserve’s monetary policy stance, which shapes global capital flows, risk appetite and commodity price dynamics more broadly. The Consumer Price Index (CPI), also sourced from FRED (Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis, 2026c), captures the general US inflation environment, controlling for the upward drift in nominal commodity prices that comes with overall price-level changes rather than coffee-specific supply and demand conditions. OECD quarterly real GDP growth, sourced from the OECD Data Explorer (OECD, 2026), is used in a robustness check reported in the Appendix, where the frequency conversion this requires is detailed.

This chunk reads the four macroeconomic variables from their respective source files and produces a four-panel time series plot. Three series, CPI, WTI and the Federal Funds Rate, are downloaded from FRED and share an identical CSV structure, handled by a single reusable function. The Dollar Index (DXY) requires separate parsing because its Investing.com export uses a different date format and embeds numeric commas in price values.

Show code 
# ----------------------------------------------------------
# READING FUNCTION — FRED CSV FORMAT
# FRED exports are two-column CSVs with a date column and
# a value column. The function renames both columns, converts
# the date to YYYY-MM format, and returns a two-column frame
# ready for joining against the monthly date spine.
#
# Arguments:
#   fichier      : path to the .csv file
#   nom_variable : name to assign to the value column
# ----------------------------------------------------------

lire_fred <- function(fichier, nom_variable) {
  df <- read_csv(fichier, show_col_types = FALSE)
  colnames(df) <- c("date_raw", nom_variable)
  df %>%
    mutate(date = format(as.Date(date_raw), "%Y-%m")) %>%
    select(date, all_of(nom_variable))
}

# Apply to the three FRED series
cpi <- lire_fred(FICHIER_CPI, "cpi")
wti <- lire_fred(FICHIER_WTI, "wti")
fed <- lire_fred(FICHIER_FED, "fed_funds_rate")


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# DXY — INVESTING.COM FORMAT (REQUIRES SEPARATE PARSING)
# The Investing.com CSV uses a non-standard date format
# (MM/DD/YYYY), wraps all fields in double quotes, and
# formats numeric values with comma thousands separators
# (e.g. "1,234.56"). Standard read_csv() fails on this
# structure, so the file is read line by line, quotes are
# stripped manually, and commas inside numbers are removed
# before coercing to numeric.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

dxy_lines <- readLines(FICHIER_DXY)

# Remove all double-quote characters from every line
dxy_clean <- gsub('"', '', dxy_lines)

# Re-parse the cleaned text as a standard CSV
dxy_df <- read.csv(text = paste(dxy_clean, collapse = "\n"),
                   stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

dxy <- dxy_df %>%
  select(date_raw = 1, dxy = 2) %>%
  mutate(
    # Remove thousands separator commas before coercing to numeric
    dxy  = as.numeric(gsub(",", "", as.character(dxy))),
    # Convert MM/DD/YYYY date strings to YYYY-MM format
    date = format(as.Date(date_raw, format = "%m/%d/%Y"), "%Y-%m")
  ) %>%
  filter(!is.na(date), !is.na(dxy)) %>%
  arrange(date) %>%
  select(date, dxy)


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# PLOT DATA — MACROECONOMIC VARIABLES
# A complete monthly date spine is built for 2000-2023, then
# all four series are left-joined onto it. Left-joining
# ensures that any months missing from individual series
# appear as NA rather than collapsing the spine.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

df_macro <- data.frame(
  date = format(seq(as.Date("2000-01-01"),
                    as.Date("2023-12-01"), by = "month"), "%Y-%m")
) %>%
  left_join(wti, by = "date") %>%
  left_join(dxy, by = "date") %>%
  left_join(fed, by = "date") %>%
  left_join(cpi, by = "date") %>%
  mutate(date_fmt = as.Date(paste0(date, "-01")))


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# FOUR-PANEL TIME SERIES PLOT
# Each panel uses a distinct color to differentiate the
# series at a glance. No y-axis label is added since the
# panel title already carries the unit information.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

gridExtra::grid.arrange(

  ggplot(df_macro, aes(date_fmt, wti)) +
    geom_line(color = "black", linewidth = 0.6) +
    labs(title = "WTI crude oil (USD/barrel)", x = NULL, y = NULL) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 9) +
    scale_x_date(date_breaks = "4 years", date_labels = "%Y"),

  ggplot(df_macro, aes(date_fmt, dxy)) +
    geom_line(color = "#1f78b4", linewidth = 0.6) +
    labs(title = "US Dollar Index (DXY)", x = NULL, y = NULL) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 9) +
    scale_x_date(date_breaks = "4 years", date_labels = "%Y"),

  ggplot(df_macro, aes(date_fmt, fed_funds_rate)) +
    geom_line(color = "#e31a1c", linewidth = 0.6) +
    labs(title = "Federal Funds Rate (%)", x = NULL, y = NULL) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 9) +
    scale_x_date(date_breaks = "4 years", date_labels = "%Y"),

  ggplot(df_macro, aes(date_fmt, cpi)) +
    geom_line(color = "#33a02c", linewidth = 0.6) +
    labs(title = "US CPI (index)", x = NULL, y = NULL) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 9) +
    scale_x_date(date_breaks = "4 years", date_labels = "%Y"),

  ncol = 2,
  top  = "Macroeconomic variables, 2000–2023"
)
Show code 
write.csv(cpi, file.path(PATH_OUTPUT, "cpi.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(wti, file.path(PATH_OUTPUT, "wti.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(fed, file.path(PATH_OUTPUT, "fed.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(dxy, file.path(PATH_OUTPUT, "dxy.csv"), row.names = FALSE)

The four macroeconomic series trace markedly different paths over the analysis period. WTI crude oil is by far the most volatile of the four: it spikes above 130 USD per barrel in 2008 before collapsing sharply, declines again in 2014–2016, drops to a deep trough in 2020 as the pandemic collapsed oil demand, and climbs back above 100 USD per barrel in 2022. The US Dollar Index moves through a broader multi-year cycle instead, declining from a peak near 120 in the early 2000s to a low near 72 by 2008, recovering gradually through the 2010s, then rising sharply from 2021 onward. The Federal Funds Rate follows the well-documented arc of US monetary policy over the period: near zero after the 2008 financial crisis, staying there for an extended stretch, then climbing sharply again from 2022 as the Fed responded to elevated inflation. CPI stands apart from the other three, tracing a smooth and persistent upward trend throughout, with a visible acceleration in slope from 2021 onward.

3.4.3 Supply-and-Demand Fundamentals

Supply-and-demand fundamentals are sourced from the USDA Foreign Agricultural Service Production, Supply and Distribution (PSD) Online database (USDA Foreign Agricultural Service, 2025b), which publishes annual crop-year estimates for the United States and key producing and consuming countries across all major agricultural commodities. Four variables are retained here: world coffee production, world domestic consumption, world exports and world ending stocks, each aggregated to a world total by summing across all countries for the corresponding crop year.

This chunk reads the USDA FAS PSD export file, aggregates country-level data to world totals for the four supply-and-demand variables, and expands the resulting annual series to monthly frequency by repeating each crop-year value across the twelve months of that year. The raw file uses an unusual structure, a single-column CSV embedded inside an Excel file, which requires a two-step parsing approach before standard tidyverse operations can be applied.

Show code 
# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 1 — PARSE THE RAW USDA FILE
# The USDA FAS PSD export is structured as an Excel file
# whose first column contains a single long CSV string, with
# the header in row 1 and one data record per subsequent row.
# The file is first read as a raw Excel object, then the
# embedded CSV is reconstructed and parsed properly.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

df_usda_raw <- read_excel(FICHIER_USDA, col_names = FALSE)

# Extract the header string from cell [1,1]
col_name <- as.character(df_usda_raw[1, 1])

# Extract all non-empty data rows from column 1
lignes <- df_usda_raw[-1, 1] %>%
  pull() %>%
  na.omit() %>%
  as.character()

# Reassemble and parse as a standard CSV
df_usda <- read_csv(I(paste(c(col_name, lignes), collapse = "\n")),
                    show_col_types = FALSE)


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 2 — AGGREGATE TO WORLD TOTALS
# The PSD database contains one row per country per crop year
# per attribute. Summing across all countries yields world
# totals for the four variables of interest.
# Consumption for crop year 2000 is set to NA due to
# incomplete EU reporting in the PSD for that year.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

df_usda_world <- df_usda %>%
  filter(Attribute_Description %in% c("Production", "Domestic Consumption",
                                       "Exports", "Ending Stocks"),
         Market_Year >= 2000, Market_Year <= 2024) %>%
  group_by(Market_Year, Attribute_Description) %>%
  summarise(valeur = sum(Value, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>%
  # Reshape from long to wide: one column per supply-demand variable
  pivot_wider(names_from = Attribute_Description, values_from = valeur) %>%
  rename(annee         = Market_Year,
         production    = Production,
         consommation  = `Domestic Consumption`,
         exportations  = Exports,
         ending_stocks = `Ending Stocks`) %>%
  arrange(annee) %>%
  # Flag year-2000 consumption as missing (incomplete source data)
  mutate(consommation = ifelse(annee == 2000, NA, consommation))


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 3 — EXPAND TO MONTHLY FREQUENCY
# USDA data are published at annual crop-year frequency.
# Each year's value is repeated across the 12 calendar months
# of that year, reflecting the assumption that market
# participants incorporate annual supply-demand estimates
# into pricing decisions throughout the crop year.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

df_usda_monthly <- df_usda_world %>%
  rowwise() %>%
  do({
    annee <- .$annee
    data.frame(
      date          = format(seq(as.Date(paste0(annee, "-01-01")),
                                 as.Date(paste0(annee, "-12-01")),
                                 by = "month"), "%Y-%m"),
      production    = .$production,
      consommation  = .$consommation,
      exportations  = .$exportations,
      ending_stocks = .$ending_stocks
    )
  }) %>%
  ungroup()


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 4 — FOUR-PANEL PLOT OF ANNUAL WORLD TOTALS
# The plot uses the annual (non-expanded) data for clarity.
# Each point represents one crop year. Consumption starts
# at 2001 to avoid plotting the documented NA for 2000.
# A minimum y-axis floor of 90,000 is applied to consumption
# to prevent the axis from starting at zero and compressing
# the visible variation in the series.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

df_usda_plot <- df_usda_world %>%
  mutate(date_fmt = as.Date(paste0(annee, "-01-01")))

gridExtra::grid.arrange(

  ggplot(df_usda_plot, aes(date_fmt, production)) +
    geom_line(color = "#8B4513", linewidth = 0.8, na.rm = TRUE) +
    geom_point(size = 1.5, color = "#8B4513", na.rm = TRUE) +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
    labs(title = "World production (1,000 bags)", x = NULL, y = NULL) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 9),

  # Filter out 2000 NA so the consumption chart starts cleanly at 2001
  ggplot(filter(df_usda_plot, !is.na(consommation)),
         aes(date_fmt, consommation)) +
    geom_line(color = "#2ca25f", linewidth = 0.8) +
    geom_point(size = 1.5, color = "#2ca25f") +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma, limits = c(90000, NA)) +
    labs(title = "World consumption (1,000 bags)", x = NULL, y = NULL) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 9),

  ggplot(df_usda_plot, aes(date_fmt, exportations)) +
    geom_line(color = "#43a2ca", linewidth = 0.8, na.rm = TRUE) +
    geom_point(size = 1.5, color = "#43a2ca", na.rm = TRUE) +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
    labs(title = "World exports (1,000 bags)", x = NULL, y = NULL) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 9),

  ggplot(df_usda_plot, aes(date_fmt, ending_stocks)) +
    geom_line(color = "#e34a33", linewidth = 0.8, na.rm = TRUE) +
    geom_point(size = 1.5, color = "#e34a33", na.rm = TRUE) +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
    labs(title = "World ending stocks (1,000 bags)", x = NULL, y = NULL) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 9),

  ncol = 2,
  top  = "USDA FAS supply and demand fundamentals, 2000–2024"
)

This expansion procedure rests on the assumption that market participants incorporate annual supply-demand fundamentals into their pricing decisions gradually over the crop year, rather than reacting only at the point of the USDA’s annual release. Since these fundamentals are only reported at crop-year frequency, carrying the same value forward to each month preserves the dataset’s monthly structure while still allowing this information to enter the models.

3.4.4 Speculative Positioning

The Commitments of Traders (COT) report is a weekly publication of the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) (CFTC, 2026), the US regulatory authority for futures markets, disclosing the aggregate open positions held by different categories of market participants in futures and options contracts traded on US exchanges.

This study uses the Disaggregated Futures-Only report, which splits market participants into four categories: Producer/Merchant/Processor/User (physical commercials), Swap Dealers, Managed Money (speculative funds) and Other Reportables (CFTC, n.d.). Managed Money covers commodity trading advisors, commodity pool operators and hedge funds holding positions for speculative or investment purposes rather than physical exposure to the underlying commodity (CFTC, n.d.), and historical data for this category only go back to June 2006, which sets the start date for the speculative positioning variable used in this dataset.

A long position is a contract to buy the underlying commodity at a set price, profiting if the price rises; a short position is a contract to sell, profiting if the price falls. The variable constructed here is the net position of the Managed Money category on the Coffee C contract (ICE Futures U.S., contract symbol KC), computed as the average, across all weekly reports published within a given calendar month, of the difference between its long and short holdings:

\[COT_{netMM}(t) = \frac{1}{N_t} \sum_{k \in t} \left[ Long_{MM}(k) - Short_{MM}(k) \right]\]

where \(Long_{MM}(k)\) and \(Short_{MM}(k)\) denote the number of long and short Coffee C contracts held by the Managed Money category at weekly reporting date \(k\), and \(N_t\) is the number of weekly reports published within calendar month \(t\). Aggregating by taking this arithmetic mean, rather than simply using the last weekly observation of the month, is more robust to the position adjustments that tend to cluster around contract expiry at month-end.

A positive net position means speculative funds hold more long contracts than short, implying a net expectation of rising prices; a negative net position signals the opposite, a net bearish stance.

This chunk reads and consolidates the ten CFTC Disaggregated COT files, extracts the Coffee C contract rows, computes the Managed Money net position for each weekly report, and aggregates to monthly frequency. Each file covers a different time span, one consolidated historical file for 2006–2015 and one annual file per year from 2016 onward, so all ten are stacked into a single data frame before any aggregation takes place. The resulting monthly series is saved to disk and visualised as a ribbon chart distinguishing net long from net short positioning.

Show code 
cat("Running COT chunk — reading and consolidating 10 files, this may take a few minutes...\n")

# ----------------------------------------------------------
# READING FUNCTION — CFTC DISAGGREGATED COT FILE
# Each COT file contains weekly position data for all
# commodity contracts traded on US exchanges. The function
# filters to Coffee C rows only, retains the three columns
# needed to compute the net Managed Money position, and
# converts the Excel date serial number to a proper R Date.
# The same date conversion used for Refinitiv files applies
# here: Refinitiv and the CFTC both use the Excel 1899-12-30
# origin for date serials.
#
# The Managed Money category encompasses commodity trading
# advisors, commodity pool operators and hedge funds (i.e.
# purely speculative participants with no physical exposure
# to the underlying commodity).
# ----------------------------------------------------------

lire_cot_fichier <- function(fichier) {

  df_raw <- read_excel(fichier, col_names = FALSE)
  colnames(df_raw) <- as.character(df_raw[1, ])
  df_raw <- df_raw[-1, ]

  df_raw %>%
    # Retain only rows corresponding to the Coffee C contract
    filter(grepl("COFFEE C", Market_and_Exchange_Names,
                 ignore.case = TRUE)) %>%
    # Keep only the three columns needed for the net position calculation
    select(date_raw = Report_Date_as_MM_DD_YYYY,
           long_mm  = M_Money_Positions_Long_ALL,
           short_mm = M_Money_Positions_Short_ALL) %>%
    mutate(
      # Convert Excel date serial to R Date (same origin as Refinitiv)
      date_raw = as.Date(as.POSIXct(as.numeric(date_raw) * 86400,
                                     origin = "1899-12-30", tz = "UTC")),
      long_mm  = as.numeric(long_mm),
      short_mm = as.numeric(short_mm)
    ) %>%
    filter(!is.na(date_raw), !is.na(long_mm), !is.na(short_mm))
}


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 1 — READ AND STACK ALL TEN COT FILES
# lapply() applies the reading function to each file in
# FICHIERS_COT and returns a list of data frames.
# bind_rows() stacks them into a single frame.
# distinct() on date_raw removes any duplicate weekly reports
# that may appear at the boundary between the consolidated
# 2006-2015 file and the 2016 annual file.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

liste_cot  <- lapply(FICHIERS_COT, lire_cot_fichier)

df_cot_all <- bind_rows(liste_cot) %>%
  # Remove duplicate observations at file boundaries
  distinct(date_raw, .keep_all = TRUE) %>%
  arrange(date_raw) %>%
  # Compute the net Managed Money position for each weekly report:
  # Net_MM = Long_MM - Short_MM
  # Positive values indicate a net bullish stance among speculative funds;
  # negative values indicate a net bearish stance.
  mutate(net_mm = long_mm - short_mm)


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 2 — AGGREGATE TO MONTHLY FREQUENCY
# Weekly reports are averaged within each calendar month.
# Averaging is preferred over end-of-month values because it
# is more robust to position adjustments associated with
# contract expiry in the final week of the month.
# n_rapports records how many weekly reports contributed to
# each monthly average, which can be used to flag months
# with unusually few observations.
# The series is filtered to start at DATE_DEBUT_COT (June
# 2006), the first date for which the Disaggregated report
# is available.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

df_cot_monthly <- df_cot_all %>%
  mutate(date = format(date_raw, "%Y-%m")) %>%
  group_by(date) %>%
  summarise(cot_net_mm   = mean(net_mm,   na.rm = TRUE),
            cot_long_mm  = mean(long_mm,  na.rm = TRUE),
            cot_short_mm = mean(short_mm, na.rm = TRUE),
            n_rapports   = n(),            # Number of weekly reports in the month
            .groups = "drop") %>%
  filter(date >= DATE_DEBUT_COT & date <= DATE_FIN) %>%
  arrange(date)

# Save to disk for reuse in the final assembly chunk
write.csv(df_cot_monthly,
          file.path(PATH_OUTPUT, "cot_net_mm_2006_2023.csv"),
          row.names = FALSE)


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 3 — NET POSITION RIBBON PLOT
# Green ribbon fills the area above zero (net long periods);
# red ribbon fills the area below zero (net short periods).
# This dual-ribbon design makes it immediately visible when
# speculative funds switch between bullish and bearish stances,
# and allows identifying sustained positioning episodes that
# may have driven or amplified price trends.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

df_cot_plot <- df_cot_monthly %>%
  mutate(date_fmt = as.Date(paste0(date, "-01")))

ggplot(df_cot_plot, aes(x = date_fmt)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey40", linetype = "dashed") +
  # Green ribbon: net long periods (COT > 0)
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = 0,
                  ymax = ifelse(cot_net_mm > 0, cot_net_mm, 0)),
              fill = "#2ca25f", alpha = 0.3) +
  # Red ribbon: net short periods (COT < 0)
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = ifelse(cot_net_mm < 0, cot_net_mm, 0),
                  ymax = 0),
              fill = "#de2d26", alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_line(aes(y = cot_net_mm), color = "grey20", linewidth = 0.6) +
  labs(title    = "Managed Money net position — Coffee C (CFTC COT), 2006–2023",
       subtitle = "Net contracts = Long − Short (monthly average of weekly reports). Green = net long, Red = net short.",
       x = NULL, y = "Net contracts") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "2 years", date_labels = "%Y") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma)

The Managed Money net position on the Coffee C contract shows considerable variation over 2006–2023, ranging from a peak of roughly +55,000 net long contracts in 2008 to a trough of nearly −108,000 net short contracts in 2018–2019, its most extreme episode of the period. The series moves through several distinct phases: predominantly long positioning in 2007–2008 coinciding with the commodity price boom, a net short episode in 2012–2013 during that period’s price decline, a recovery toward net long positions from 2014 onward, then the sharp net short swing of 2018–2019 itself, followed by a gradual return to net long positioning from 2020 onward.

3.4.5 Climate Variables

3.4.5.1 Selection of Producer Countries

Climate conditions in coffee-producing regions directly affect supply through their impact on cherry development, flowering and yield, with temperature and precipitation standing out as the two primary determinants at the agronomic level. Rather than relying on a single country or a global average, this study constructs weighted climate indices that aggregate conditions across the 14 countries accounting for the largest share of world coffee production.

These 14 countries are selected using a simple, data-driven rule: only those whose average annual share of world coffee production exceeds 1% over 2000–2024 are included. The threshold is computed directly from the USDA FAS PSD data already used for the supply fundamentals variables, which keeps the production weights fully consistent with their underlying data source. The table below reports the resulting production shares and confirms the selection.

This chunk derives the country selection criterion for the climate indices directly from the USDA PSD data already loaded in the previous chunk. For each crop year, each country’s share of world production is computed, and the 25-year average of that share is then calculated across the full 2000–2024 period. Only countries whose average share meets or exceeds the 1% threshold are retained.

Show code 
# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 1 — COMPUTE ANNUAL PRODUCTION SHARES BY COUNTRY
# For each crop year, world total production is computed
# first as a denominator, then each country's share is
# expressed as a percentage of that total.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

prod_by_country <- df_usda %>%
  filter(Attribute_Description == "Production",
         Market_Year >= 2000, Market_Year <= 2024) %>%
  group_by(Market_Year) %>%
  # Compute world total for the denominator within each year
  mutate(world_total = sum(Value, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  # Each country's share as a percentage of world production
  mutate(share_pct = Value / world_total * 100) %>%

# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 2 — AVERAGE SHARE OVER 2000-2024 AND APPLY THRESHOLD
# Averaging over 25 years smooths out year-to-year production
# fluctuations caused by weather or disease, yielding stable
# structural weights that reflect each country's long-run
# contribution to global supply.
# The 1% threshold is applied to exclude countries whose
# individual contribution is too small to have a meaningful
# impact on the aggregated climate indices.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

  group_by(Country_Name) %>%
  summarise(avg_share = round(mean(share_pct, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
            .groups = "drop") %>%
  arrange(desc(avg_share)) %>%
  filter(avg_share >= 1.0) %>%
  # Correct encoding of Côte d'Ivoire (stored without accent in USDA PSD)
  mutate(Country_Name = if_else(Country_Name == "Cote d'Ivoire",
                                 "Côte d'Ivoire",
                                 Country_Name))


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 3 — DISPLAY THE SELECTION TABLE
# The caption dynamically computes the combined production
# share of the selected countries, confirming that the 14
# retained countries collectively represent ~90.8% of world
# production over the analysis period.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

kable(prod_by_country,
      caption = paste0("Countries with average annual production share ≥ 1%, ",
                       "2000–2024 (USDA FAS PSD). ",
                       "Total: ", round(sum(prod_by_country$avg_share), 1), "%."),
      col.names = c("Country", "Avg. share (%)"),
      booktabs  = TRUE) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"),
                font_size = 11, full_width = FALSE)
Countries with average annual production share ≥ 1%, 2000–2024 (USDA FAS PSD). Total: 90.8%.

Mexico 2.79
Uganda 2.73
Guatemala 2.64
Peru 2.50

Costa Rica 1.17

This chunk converts the raw production shares computed in the previous chunk into normalised weights that sum exactly to one. These weights are the core of the climate index construction: every weighted average in the subsequent climate chunks is computed using POIDS_PRODUCTION. Two parallel vectors map official country names as they appear in the USDA PSD database to the internal identifiers used in the file lists defined in the setup chunk, ensuring that the correct weight is always matched to the correct file.

Show code 
# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 1 — DEFINE THE NAME MAPPING BETWEEN USDA AND FILES
# The USDA PSD database uses official English country names,
# while the climate file lists (FICHIERS_PRECIP, FICHIERS_TEMP)
# use shorter internal identifiers without accents, defined
# in the setup chunk. The two vectors below establish the
# one-to-one correspondence between the two naming systems.
# The order in both vectors must be identical.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

pays_retenus  <- c("Brazil", "Vietnam", "Colombia", "Indonesia", "Ethiopia",
                   "India", "Honduras", "Mexico", "Uganda", "Guatemala",
                   "Peru", "Côte d'Ivoire", "Nicaragua", "Costa Rica")

noms_internes <- c("bresil", "vietnam", "colombie", "indonesie", "ethiopie",
                   "inde", "honduras", "mexique", "uganda", "guatemala",
                   "perou", "cote_ivoire", "nicaragua", "costa_rica")


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 2 — BUILD THE RAW PRODUCTION SHARE VECTOR
# match() looks up each country name from prod_by_country
# in pays_retenus and returns its position, which is then
# used to retrieve the corresponding internal identifier.
# setNames() attaches those identifiers as vector names,
# so that PARTS_PRODUCTION["bresil"] returns Brazil's share.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

PARTS_PRODUCTION <- setNames(
  prod_by_country$avg_share,
  noms_internes[match(prod_by_country$Country_Name, pays_retenus)]
)


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 3 — NORMALISE TO UNIT SUM (PRODUCTION WEIGHTS)
# Dividing by the total ensures the weights sum exactly to 1,
# as required by the weighted index formula. This normalisation
# step is necessary because the 14 selected countries do not
# collectively account for 100% of world production — the
# remaining ~9% belongs to countries below the 1% threshold.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

POIDS_PRODUCTION <- PARTS_PRODUCTION / sum(PARTS_PRODUCTION)


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# VERIFICATION
# Confirms that all 14 internal names were matched correctly
# and that no NA values were introduced by the name mapping.
# Any NA in the output would indicate a mismatch between
# pays_retenus and the country names in prod_by_country.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

cat("Names of POIDS_PRODUCTION:", names(POIDS_PRODUCTION), "\n")

The 14 selected countries collectively account for 90.8% of world coffee production on average over 2000–2024. Countries below the 1% threshold contribute too little to global supply to matter here, and including them would only add noise without improving the explanatory power of the climate indices.

Before building variety-specific production weights, the Arabica and Robusta shares of each of the 14 retained countries are computed directly from the USDA FAS PSD data, using the separate Arabica Production and Robusta Production line items already present in the raw dataset. This keeps the variety split empirical rather than assumed, and fully consistent with the data already used for the global production weights. The table below reports the resulting variety shares for each country over 2000–2024.

Show code 
# ----------------------------------------------------------
# VARIETY SPLITS — ARABICA VS ROBUSTA PER COUNTRY
# The USDA FAS PSD dataset contains separate line items for
# "Arabica Production" and "Robusta Production" per country.
# Summing across 2000-2024 and computing shares yields the
# empirical variety split for each of the 14 retained countries.
# These splits are used downstream to assign each country
# to the correct variety-specific climate index.
# The recode of Cote d'Ivoire is applied BEFORE the filter
# to ensure the country is correctly matched to pays_retenus.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

splits_variete <- df_usda %>%
  filter(Attribute_Description %in% c("Arabica Production",
                                       "Robusta Production"),
         Market_Year >= 2000, Market_Year <= 2024) %>%
  group_by(Country_Name, Attribute_Description) %>%
  summarise(total = sum(Value, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from  = Attribute_Description,
              values_from = total,
              values_fill = 0) %>%
  rename(arabica = `Arabica Production`,
         robusta = `Robusta Production`) %>%
  mutate(
    Country_Name = if_else(Country_Name == "Cote d'Ivoire",
                            "Côte d'Ivoire",
                            Country_Name),
    total        = arabica + robusta,
    pct_arabica  = round(arabica / total * 100, 1),
    pct_robusta  = round(robusta / total * 100, 1)
  ) %>%
  filter(Country_Name %in% pays_retenus) %>%
  # Share of each country in the combined Arabica / Robusta
  # production of the 14 retained countries (denominators
  # computed across the filtered set, not world totals).
  mutate(
    pct_monde_arabica = round(arabica / sum(arabica) * 100, 1),
    pct_monde_robusta = round(robusta / sum(robusta) * 100, 1),
    arabica_disp = paste0(format(round(arabica), big.mark = ","),
                          " (", pct_arabica, "%)"),
    robusta_disp = paste0(format(round(robusta), big.mark = ","),
                          " (", pct_robusta, "%)")
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(total))

kable(splits_variete %>%
        select(Country_Name, arabica_disp, pct_monde_arabica,
               robusta_disp, pct_monde_robusta),
      caption   = "Variety splits — Arabica vs Robusta production share per country (2000–2024, USDA FAS PSD)",
      booktabs  = TRUE,
      col.names = c("Country", "Volume (% of country)", "% of group total",
                    "Volume (% of country)", "% of group total"),
      align     = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r")) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"),
                font_size = 11, full_width = FALSE) %>%
  add_header_above(c(" "       = 1,
                     "Arabica" = 2,
                     "Robusta" = 2),
                   bold       = TRUE,
                   color      = c("black", "#8B4513", "#2E8B57"),
                   background = c("white", "#f5ece6", "#e8f5ec"))

The variety split table confirms the expected production geography of the two coffee varieties. Eight countries produce exclusively or near-exclusively Arabica, Colombia, Ethiopia, Honduras, Peru, Costa Rica, Guatemala, Nicaragua and Mexico all report Arabica shares above 90% and are assigned entirely to the Arabica group as a result. Brazil, the world’s largest producer, stands out as the only major country with genuinely mixed production, splitting 72.3% Arabica and 27.7% Robusta over 2000–2024. On the Robusta side, Vietnam and Côte d’Ivoire come close to being pure Robusta producers at 96.8% and 100% respectively, while Indonesia (87.7%), Uganda (80.9%) and India (67.8%) lean heavily toward Robusta without being exclusive to it.

Four countries feed into both variety-specific indices: Brazil, India, Uganda and Indonesia. For these, the production weight assigned to each group is scaled by the empirically computed variety share rather than assumed from external sources, while countries with a variety share above 90% are treated as pure producers and assigned entirely to their dominant group, a simplification justified by how little the minority variety contributes to their total output. This variety-aware weighting keeps the climate indices used in each model specification tied to the regions that actually produce the variety in question, rather than averaging over areas that are climatically irrelevant to it.

The variety-specific production weights are now constructed for each group. For the Arabica group, the twelve contributing countries are assigned weights proportional to their Arabica production share, adjusted by the empirically computed variety splits for mixed producers. The resulting weights sum to one and reflect the long-run structural contribution of each country to global Arabica supply over 2000–2024.

Show code

# share are treated as pure producers (split = 1.0).
# Mixed producers (Brazil, India, Uganda, Indonesia) receive
# their empirically computed Arabica share as a scaling factor.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

split_arabica <- c(
  bresil      = 0.723,
  colombie    = 1.000,
  ethiopie    = 1.000,
  inde        = 0.322,
  honduras    = 1.000,
