Isolating the effect of neuron count alone, at each variety’s selected decay, tells a clearer story than the aggregate tuning search does on its own.

For Arabica, the relationship is essentially flat and mildly monotonic: validation MSE rises smoothly from 0.0353 at 2 neurons to 0.0359 at 15, a difference small enough to suggest the network is not particularly sensitive to width once decay is properly tuned, and the compact 2-neuron architecture is chosen mainly because it is marginally better rather than dramatically so.

Robusta behaves quite differently. Validation MSE jumps more than fourfold between 2 neurons (0.0450) and 3 (0.1832), the single largest deviation anywhere in either grid, before falling back down through 5, 8, 10 and 15 neurons without ever recovering to the 2-neuron level. This is not the smooth, monotonic degradation seen for Arabica; it looks more like an isolated instability at one specific width, plausibly a poor local optimum reached during training at that particular size and decay combination, given that nnet’s weight initialisation is random and its optimiser offers no guarantee of finding the global minimum on a non-convex loss surface. The 2-neuron architecture remains the best choice for Robusta regardless, but the size of the gap to its nearest neighbour should be read with some caution rather than as evidence that odd numbers of neurons are inherently worse than even ones.

7.4.2 ANN Network Depth

The ANN specification estimated above relies on a single hidden layer, the only architecture nnet is able to fit. This leaves open a natural question: does adding depth, rather than just width, change how well the network forecasts either series. Testing this requires a different package, neuralnet, which accepts a vector of hidden layer sizes and can therefore be configured with an arbitrary number of layers. Three depths are tested here, two, five and ten hidden layers, all with a fixed width of two neurons per layer so that the comparison isolates depth on its own rather than mixing it with a change in the number of neurons at each layer.

One trade-off is worth flagging before looking at the results. neuralnet has no direct equivalent of the decay parameter that drove the improvement in the single-layer ANN earlier in this document, from an \(R^2\) of 0.453 to 0.728 for Arabica. Without that L2 regularisation, deeper networks estimated on the same training samples, 168 to 211 observations for Arabica and 153 to 192 for Robusta depending on the walk-forward step, are a demanding specification, and some degree of instability or non-convergence at individual walk-forward steps would not be a surprising outcome.

This chunk defines the three hidden-layer configurations as a named list and implements the walk-forward estimation function for neuralnet. The function mirrors the expanding-window loop used for the other models in this document, with a tryCatch() wrapper around each re-fit so that a non-convergent step at one iteration returns NA and moves on rather than halting the whole loop.

Show code 
# ----------------------------------------------------------
# ANN MULTI-LAYER — PACKAGE SWITCH REQUIRED
# nnet (baseline ANN) only supports a single hidden layer, so it
# cannot test network depth. neuralnet supports multiple hidden
# layers via a vector, e.g. hidden = c(2,2,2) for 3 layers of 2
# neurons each. neuralnet has no direct L2 regularisation
# (no `decay` argument like nnet); if these deeper networks show
# instability similar to the pre-regularisation single-layer ANN,
# this is flagged as a limitation rather than worked around.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

library(neuralnet)

# Depth configurations to test.
# Width is held fixed at 2 neurons per layer across all three
# depths, so that any performance difference observed between
# configurations reflects depth alone, not a confound between
# depth and width.
configs_profondeur <- list(
  "2 layers"  = c(2, 2),        # 2 hidden layers, 2 neurons each
  "5 layers"  = rep(2, 5),      # 5 hidden layers, 2 neurons each
  "10 layers" = rep(2, 10)      # 10 hidden layers, 2 neurons each
)


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# WALK-FORWARD ESTIMATION FUNCTION — MULTI-LAYER ANN
#
# Arguments:
#   df         : levels dataset (one row per month)
#   var_dep    : name of the dependent variable column
#                ("arabica_price" or "robusta_price")
#   n_train    : size of the initial training window (number of
#                rows), computed earlier in the preprocessing chunk
#   hidden_vec : vector of neurons per layer, e.g. rep(2, 5) for
#                5 layers of 2 neurons — this is what changes
#                between the three calls made in the next chunk
#
# What the function returns:
#   actual    : the observed (scaled) prices in the test period
#   predicted : the walk-forward one-step-ahead forecasts, with
#               NA for any step where the network failed to
#               converge (see tryCatch() in STEP 5 below)
# ----------------------------------------------------------

fit_ann_multilayer <- function(df, var_dep, n_train, hidden_vec) {

  # STEP 1 — Restrict the dataset to the columns this model needs:
  # the dependent variable plus the 14 exogenous predictors defined
  # in vars_exo. intersect() is a safety check in case a predictor
  # is ever missing from df; it is silently skipped rather than
  # causing the function to error out.
  vars_exo_disponibles <- intersect(vars_exo, colnames(df))
  vars_a_garder        <- c(var_dep, vars_exo_disponibles)
  df_modele            <- df[, vars_a_garder]

  # STEP 2 — Min-Max scale every column, including the dependent
  # variable, to the [0, 1] range. neuralnet, like the other ML
  # models in this document, is sensitive to input scale: without
  # this step, variables with large absolute values (e.g. ending
  # stocks, in thousands of bags) would dominate the loss function
  # over variables with small values (e.g. the ONI index, roughly
  # -3 to +3). sapply() applies minmax_scale() column by column and
  # returns a matrix, which as.data.frame() converts back to a
  # data frame so it can be used in a formula-based model call.
  df_modele_scaled <- as.data.frame(sapply(df_modele, minmax_scale))

  # STEP 3 — Split the scaled data into the initial training set
  # and the held-out test set, using the row count n_train computed
  # once in the preprocessing chunk and shared across all six main
  # models for a consistent train/test partition.
  n_total       <- nrow(df_modele_scaled)
  donnees_train <- df_modele_scaled[1:n_train, ]
  donnees_test  <- df_modele_scaled[(n_train + 1):n_total, ]
  n_test        <- nrow(donnees_test)

  # STEP 4 — Build the model formula explicitly by pasting together
  # the dependent variable and all 14 predictor names with "+".
  # This is done instead of using the shorthand "var_dep ~ ."
  # because neuralnet's support for the "." (all other columns)
  # notation is inconsistent across package versions, so writing
  # the formula out explicitly avoids a possible silent failure.
  formule <- as.formula(paste(var_dep, "~",
                              paste(vars_exo_disponibles, collapse = " + ")))

  # STEP 5 — Walk-forward loop. This follows the same expanding-
  # window logic used throughout the document: at each step i, the
  # network is retrained from scratch on the initial training set
  # plus every test-period row already passed, then used to predict
  # a single next observation. Two things are specific to this
  # function: (a) neuralnet's own model syntax, and (b) a tryCatch()
  # safety net, since deeper networks (5 or 10 layers) are more
  # likely to fail to converge within the iteration budget on the
  # small samples available here, and a single failed step should
  # not stop the whole walk-forward run.
  predictions <- numeric(n_test)   # empty vector to be filled in

  set.seed(42)   # fixed once, before the loop starts, so that the
                 # entire sequence of random weight initialisations
                 # across all walk-forward steps is reproducible

  for (i in 1:n_test) {

    # Number of test-period rows already "seen" before this step:
    # 0 at step 1, 1 at step 2, and so on, exactly as in fit_ann().
    nb_lignes_test_vues  <- i - 1
    lignes_test_vues     <- donnees_test[seq_len(nb_lignes_test_vues), ]

    # The expanding training window: the fixed initial training set
    # plus every test row already passed.
    fenetre_entrainement <- rbind(donnees_train, lignes_test_vues)

    # Re-fit the network from scratch on the current window.
    # tryCatch() returns NULL instead of raising an error if the
    # network fails to converge within stepmax iterations, which
    # becomes more likely as hidden_vec grows longer (10 layers).
    #   linear.output = TRUE : identity activation on the output
    #                           neuron, required for a regression
    #                           target rather than classification
    #   stepmax = 1e6         : raised well above neuralnet's
    #                           default (1e5) because deeper
    #                           networks need more backpropagation
    #                           steps to converge
    #   threshold = 0.05      : the partial derivative convergence
    #                           criterion, relaxed from the default
    #                           (0.01) so that deep networks on a
    #                           small sample can converge within a
    #                           reasonable time rather than hitting
    #                           stepmax without reaching a tighter
    #                           threshold
    modele_nn <- tryCatch(
      neuralnet(formule, data = fenetre_entrainement,
               hidden        = hidden_vec,
               linear.output = TRUE,
               stepmax       = 1e6,
               threshold     = 0.05),
      error = function(e) NULL
    )

    # If convergence failed, record NA for this step and move on
    # to the next one rather than stopping the whole loop.
    if (is.null(modele_nn)) {
      predictions[i] <- NA
      next
    }

    # Predict the single next observation (row i of the test set).
    # Only the predictor columns are passed to predict(), since
    # neuralnet's predict() does not expect the dependent variable
    # column to be present in newdata.
    ligne_a_predire <- donnees_test[i, vars_exo_disponibles, drop = FALSE]
    predictions[i]  <- as.numeric(predict(modele_nn, newdata = ligne_a_predire))
  }

  # STEP 6 — Return the observed and predicted test values. NA
  # entries from any non-converged step are kept in the output;
  # calculer_metriques() drops them via complete.cases() when
  # computing R², MSE and MAE downstream.
  valeurs_observees <- donnees_test[[var_dep]]
  list(actual = valeurs_observees, predicted = predictions)
}

This chunk runs the three depth configurations for both coffee varieties, six walk-forward estimations in total, storing the results in two named lists for use in the comparison table below.

Show code 
# ----------------------------------------------------------
# RUN ALL THREE DEPTHS, BOTH SERIES
# The outer for() loop iterates over the three named configurations
# in configs_profondeur ("2 layers", "5 layers", "10 layers"), and
# for each one calls fit_ann_multilayer() twice, once per coffee
# variety, storing the results in two named lists keyed by
# configuration name for easy lookup in the comparison table below.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

resultats_ml_ara <- list()
resultats_ml_rob <- list()

for (nom_config in names(configs_profondeur)) {

  cat("Running", nom_config, "- Arabica...\n")
  resultats_ml_ara[[nom_config]] <- fit_ann_multilayer(
    df_arabica_levels, "arabica_price", n_train_ara_lev,
    configs_profondeur[[nom_config]])

  cat("Running", nom_config, "- Robusta...\n")
  resultats_ml_rob[[nom_config]] <- fit_ann_multilayer(
    df_robusta_levels, "robusta_price", n_train_rob_lev,
    configs_profondeur[[nom_config]])
}

This chunk compiles the walk-forward results from all three depth configurations, together with the single-layer ANN baseline already estimated earlier in the document (res_ann_ara, res_ann_rob), into a single comparison table, grouped by variety with pack_rows() for readability, consistent with the comparative performance table earlier in the document.

Show code 
# ----------------------------------------------------------
# COMPILE COMPARISON TABLE — BASELINE (1 LAYER, nnet) VS
# 2/5/10 LAYERS (neuralnet)
# The baseline row reuses the walk-forward results already stored
# in res_ann_ara and res_ann_rob from the main ANN chunk earlier in
# the document, so the single-layer specification is not re-run
# here. Rows are built variety by variety (all Arabica architectures
# first, then all Robusta architectures) rather than alternating,
# so that pack_rows() below can group each variety into its own
# labelled block instead of interleaving them row by row.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

# Ordered architecture labels, shared by both varieties so the
# row order is identical within each variety block.
labels_architecture <- c("1 layer (baseline, nnet)", names(configs_profondeur))

df_ann_depth <- rbind(
  # Arabica block: baseline row followed by the 3 depth configs
  rbind(
    data.frame(Architecture = "1 layer (baseline, nnet)",
               calculer_metriques(res_ann_ara$actual, res_ann_ara$predicted)),
    do.call(rbind, lapply(names(configs_profondeur), function(nom) {

  # Robusta block: same structure, same architecture order
  rbind(
    data.frame(Architecture = "1 layer (baseline, nnet)",
               calculer_metriques(res_ann_rob$actual, res_ann_rob$predicted)),
    do.call(rbind, lapply(names(configs_profondeur), function(nom) {
      data.frame(Architecture = nom,
                 calculer_metriques(resultats_ml_rob[[nom]]$actual,
                                    resultats_ml_rob[[nom]]$predicted))
    }))
  ) %>% mutate(Series = "Robusta", .after = Architecture)
)

# Render with pack_rows() grouping instead of an interleaved Series
# column, so all 4 Arabica rows appear together, then all 4 Robusta
# rows, matching the convention used in the comparative_performance
# and robustness check tables earlier in the document.
df_ann_depth %>%
  select(Architecture, R2, MSE, MAE) %>%
  kable(caption   = "ANN depth comparison — 1 layer (nnet baseline) vs 2/5/10 layers (neuralnet)",

  pack_rows("Arabica", 1, 4,
            bold       = TRUE,
            color      = "#8B4513",
            background = "#f5ece6") %>%

            bold       = TRUE,

            background = "#e8f5ec")

The results show a clear and monotonic pattern: performance deteriorates as depth increases, for both varieties and at every step. For Arabica, \(R^2\) falls from 0.728 at the single-layer baseline to 0.598 at 2 layers, 0.305 at 5 layers, and turns negative at −0.393 for 10 layers. Robusta follows the same trajectory, dropping from 0.456 to 0.335 at 2 layers, then to a negative \(R^2\) of −0.128 at 5 layers and −0.275 at 10 layers. A negative \(R^2\) means the model performs worse than simply predicting the mean of the test period, so the 5 and 10 layer networks are not just weaker, they are actively harmful specifications for this forecasting task.

This pattern is consistent with the trade-off flagged before running the comparison. neuralnet offers no L2 regularisation equivalent to the decay parameter that turned the single-layer ANN from an unstable specification (Arabica \(R^2\) = 0.453) into the current baseline (0.728). Adding hidden layers without any mechanism to constrain weight growth increases the number of parameters substantially while the training sample stays fixed at 168 to 211 observations for Arabica and 153 to 192 for Robusta depending on the walk-forward step. Each additional layer gives the network more capacity to fit noise in an already small sample, and the walk-forward protocol compounds this: the network is re-initialised and retrained from scratch at every step, so a deeper, less constrained architecture is asked to reach a stable solution dozens of times over on training windows that shrink to well under 200 observations at the earliest steps. A second, compounding factor is the choice of activation function: neuralnet defaults to a logistic (sigmoid) activation in the hidden layers, whose derivative is bounded well below 1 and shrinks the backpropagated gradient at every layer it passes through. In a ten-layer network this vanishing gradient problem can leave the earliest layers with almost no learning signal at all, compounding the overfitting risk already discussed rather than substituting for it.

Depth alone, in other words, does not help here, and by 5 layers it actively hurts. This is not evidence that deeper networks are unsuited to coffee price forecasting in general, but that depth without regularisation is the wrong lever to pull given the sample sizes available in this study.

This chunk re-estimates the three depth configurations using RSNNS::mlp() instead of neuralnet, adding L2 weight decay via the BackpropWeightDecay learning function. Unlike neuralnet, RSNNS::mlp() supports both a vector of hidden layer sizes and weight decay simultaneously, closing the regularisation gap identified as the likely cause of the depth-related degradation observed above. The decay values reuse those already selected by cross-validation for the single-layer ANN, 0.1 for Arabica and 0.001 for Robusta, so the comparison isolates the effect of adding regularisation to the same depths already tested.

Show code 
# ----------------------------------------------------------
# ANN MULTI-LAYER WITH WEIGHT DECAY — RSNNS PACKAGE
# neuralnet has no weight decay mechanism, which is the most
# likely explanation for the monotonic R² collapse observed as
# depth increased (see ann_multilayer_table results above).
# RSNNS::mlp() accepts a vector of hidden layer sizes, like
# neuralnet, AND supports L2-style weight decay through the
# "BackpropWeightDecay" learning function, closing that gap.
#
# learnFuncParams order for BackpropWeightDecay, confirmed from
# the SNNS User Manual (parameters of the learning functions):
#   [1] eta   : learning rate, typical range 0.1-1
#   [2] d     : weight decay term, typical range 0.005-0.3
#   [3] dmin  : minimum tolerated weight for a link before it is
#               pruned — set to 0 here to disable pruning, so
#               only weight decay is tested, not link removal
#   [4] dmax  : maximum output-target difference tolerated before
#               being backpropagated as error, typical 0/0.1/0.2
# ----------------------------------------------------------

library(RSNNS)


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# WALK-FORWARD ESTIMATION FUNCTION — MULTI-LAYER ANN WITH DECAY
#
# Arguments:
#   df         : levels dataset (one row per month)
#   var_dep    : name of the dependent variable column
#   n_train    : size of the initial training window
#   hidden_vec : vector of neurons per layer (same configs as
#                configs_profondeur, defined in the neuralnet
#                chunk above and reused here)
#   decay      : L2 weight decay strength. Reuses the value
#                already selected by cross-validation for the
#                single-layer ANN (tuning_ann_ara$decay = 0.1,
#                tuning_ann_rob$decay = 0.001), so the same
#                regularisation strength that stabilised the
#                1-layer network is tested at greater depths.
#
# What the function returns:
#   actual    : the observed (scaled) prices in the test period
#   predicted : the walk-forward one-step-ahead forecasts, with
#               NA for any step where training failed
# ----------------------------------------------------------

fit_ann_multilayer_decay <- function(df, var_dep, n_train, hidden_vec, decay) {

  # STEP 1 — Restrict the dataset to the columns this model needs,
  # identical to fit_ann_multilayer() above.
  vars_exo_disponibles <- intersect(vars_exo, colnames(df))
  vars_a_garder        <- c(var_dep, vars_exo_disponibles)
  df_modele            <- df[, vars_a_garder]

  # STEP 2 — Min-Max scale every column to [0, 1], identical to
  # every other ML model in this document.
  df_modele_scaled <- as.data.frame(sapply(df_modele, minmax_scale))

  # STEP 3 — Split into the initial training set and the test set.
  n_total       <- nrow(df_modele_scaled)
  donnees_train <- df_modele_scaled[1:n_train, ]
  donnees_test  <- df_modele_scaled[(n_train + 1):n_total, ]
  n_test        <- nrow(donnees_test)

  # STEP 4 — Walk-forward loop. RSNNS::mlp() requires x (predictors)
  # and y (target) as separate numeric matrices rather than a single
  # data frame with a formula, unlike neuralnet or nnet, so the
  # matrix construction happens inside the loop for each expanding
  # window rather than once outside it.
  predictions <- numeric(n_test)

  set.seed(42)   # fixed once, before the loop starts

  for (i in 1:n_test) {

    nb_lignes_test_vues  <- i - 1
    lignes_test_vues     <- donnees_test[seq_len(nb_lignes_test_vues), ]
    fenetre_entrainement <- rbind(donnees_train, lignes_test_vues)

    # RSNNS::mlp() expects the predictor matrix and target matrix
    # as separate arguments, not a formula on a single data frame.
    x_train <- as.matrix(fenetre_entrainement[, vars_exo_disponibles])
    y_train <- as.matrix(fenetre_entrainement[[var_dep]])

    # Fit the network with weight decay. learnFuncParams order
    # confirmed against the SNNS User Manual: c(eta, decay, dmin,
    # dmax). dmin is fixed at 0 to disable link pruning, so the
    # comparison isolates weight decay alone.
    modele_rsnns <- tryCatch(
      mlp(x = x_train, y = y_train,
          size            = hidden_vec,
          maxit           = 500,
          learnFunc       = "BackpropWeightDecay",
          learnFuncParams = c(0.2, decay, 0, 0.1),
          linOut          = TRUE),
      error = function(e) NULL
    )

    if (is.null(modele_rsnns)) {
      predictions[i] <- NA
      next
    }

    # Predict the single next observation. RSNNS's predict() also
    # requires a matrix input, consistent with the training call.
    ligne_a_predire <- as.matrix(donnees_test[i, vars_exo_disponibles,
                                               drop = FALSE])
    predictions[i]  <- as.numeric(predict(modele_rsnns, ligne_a_predire))
  }

  # STEP 5 — Return observed and predicted test values.
  valeurs_observees <- donnees_test[[var_dep]]
  list(actual = valeurs_observees, predicted = predictions)
}

This chunk runs the three depth configurations with weight decay for both coffee varieties, six additional walk-forward estimations, using the decay values already selected for the single-layer ANN baseline.

resultats_ml_decay_rob <- list()

for (nom_config in names(configs_profondeur)) {

Adding weight decay through RSNNS::mlp() was intended to test whether regularisation restores some of the performance lost at depth, using the same decay values already selected for the single-layer baseline, 0.1 for Arabica and 0.001 for Robusta. The results do not support this. Every decayed configuration underperforms its undecayed neuralnet counterpart at the same depth, and by a wide margin: Arabica falls to \(R^2\) values of −1.206, −1.054 and −1.220 at 2, 5 and 10 layers respectively, while Robusta falls to −0.423, −0.264 and −0.367. As with the undecayed depth comparison earlier in this section, a negative \(R^2\) means the model performs worse than simply predicting the mean of the test period; here, every single decayed configuration falls into that category, and several do so by a wider margin than the worst undecayed network. Rather than narrowing the gap with the single-layer baseline, adding decay widens it substantially.

This outcome most likely reflects a methodological confound rather than a genuine effect of weight decay. Gaining access to BackpropWeightDecay required switching from neuralnet to RSNNS, and the two packages differ not only in their support for regularisation but in their default training algorithm. neuralnet trains by resilient backpropagation (Rprop+), an adaptive method whose step size is adjusted per weight and typically converges efficiently even on small samples. BackpropWeightDecay, by contrast, is a variant of standard gradient descent with a fixed learning rate, a considerably less efficient optimiser that generally requires more iterations to reach a comparable solution. This difficulty is compounded by the sigmoid activation shared by both packages: BackpropWeightDecay’s fixed-step updates have no mechanism to compensate for a gradient that is already shrinking with depth, unlike Rprop+, which adapts to the sign rather than the magnitude of the gradient and is comparatively more robust to this effect. The 500-iteration budget carried over unchanged from the neuralnet specification was calibrated for the faster of the two algorithms, and is plausibly insufficient for the slower one, particularly on the deeper architectures tested here. The RSNNS results are therefore better read as evidence of under-optimisation than as evidence against the value of regularisation at depth. Future work could test whether tuning the learning rate (eta) for BackpropWeightDecay, or extending the iteration budget specifically for this optimiser, resolves the convergence issues observed here, rather than concluding that weight decay itself is unhelpful at depth.

7.4.3 ANN Activation Function (neuralnet)

Every ANN specification estimated so far, whether one layer or several, has used nnet and neuralnet’s shared default: the logistic (sigmoid) function, \(\sigma(x) = 1/(1+e^{-x})\), which squashes its input into the \((0,1)\) range. This is one of two activation functions neuralnet supports natively without requiring a custom function definition, the other being the hyperbolic tangent, \(\tanh(x) = (e^x - e^{-x})/(e^x + e^{-x})\), which squashes its input into \((-1,1)\) instead. ReLU and other piecewise-linear activations are not available in neuralnet without writing and differentiating a custom activation function by hand, and RSNNS, the package that does offer a wider range of activations, was already shown earlier in this section to introduce convergence problems of its own; this comparison is therefore restricted to sigmoid and tanh, tested within the same package and optimiser already used for every other ANN result in this document, so that any difference observed reflects the activation function itself rather than a confound with a different training algorithm.

The choice between the two is not purely cosmetic. Tanh is zero-centred while sigmoid is not, which in principle produces more balanced gradient updates during backpropagation: a sigmoid-activated neuron’s output is always positive, so the gradient with respect to any weight feeding into it is always the same sign as the error signal, which can slow convergence in a zig-zagging pattern. Tanh’s steeper derivative, with a maximum value of 1 compared to sigmoid’s 0.25, also means less of the gradient is lost at each layer it passes through, the same vanishing-gradient mechanism already flagged as a likely contributor to the collapse observed at greater depth earlier in this section. At the single-layer, two-neuron architecture tested here, this difference is expected to matter less than it did across ten stacked layers, but it is still worth testing directly rather than assuming sigmoid remains the better default.

This chunk defines the walk-forward estimation function for a single-hidden-layer ANN with a configurable activation function, mirroring fit_ann_multilayer() from the depth comparison above with the hidden layer fixed at 2 neurons, the architecture confirmed optimal earlier in this section. It then runs both activation functions, sigmoid and tanh, for both coffee varieties, four walk-forward estimations in total.

Show code 
library(neuralnet)


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# WALK-FORWARD ESTIMATION FUNCTION — ANN WITH CONFIGURABLE
# ACTIVATION FUNCTION
# Mirrors fit_ann_multilayer() from the depth comparison above,
# with the hidden layer fixed at a single layer of 2 neurons
# (the architecture confirmed optimal earlier in this section)
# and act.fct exposed as an argument so the same function can
# be called with "logistic" or "tanh".
# ----------------------------------------------------------

fit_ann_activation <- function(df, var_dep, n_train, act_fct) {

  vars_exo_disponibles <- intersect(vars_exo, colnames(df))
  vars_a_garder        <- c(var_dep, vars_exo_disponibles)
  df_modele            <- df[, vars_a_garder]

  df_modele_scaled <- as.data.frame(sapply(df_modele, minmax_scale))

  n_total       <- nrow(df_modele_scaled)
  donnees_train <- df_modele_scaled[1:n_train, ]
  donnees_test  <- df_modele_scaled[(n_train + 1):n_total, ]
  n_test        <- nrow(donnees_test)

  formule <- as.formula(paste(var_dep, "~",
                              paste(vars_exo_disponibles, collapse = " + ")))

  predictions <- numeric(n_test)

  set.seed(42)

  for (i in 1:n_test) {

    nb_lignes_test_vues  <- i - 1
    lignes_test_vues     <- donnees_test[seq_len(nb_lignes_test_vues), ]
    fenetre_entrainement <- rbind(donnees_train, lignes_test_vues)

    modele_nn <- tryCatch(
      neuralnet(formule, data = fenetre_entrainement,
               hidden        = 2,
               act.fct       = act_fct,
               linear.output = TRUE,
               stepmax       = 1e6,
               threshold     = 0.05),
      error = function(e) NULL
    )

    if (is.null(modele_nn)) {
      predictions[i] <- NA
      next
    }

    ligne_a_predire <- donnees_test[i, vars_exo_disponibles, drop = FALSE]
    predictions[i]  <- as.numeric(predict(modele_nn, newdata = ligne_a_predire))
  }

  valeurs_observees <- donnees_test[[var_dep]]
  list(actual = valeurs_observees, predicted = predictions)
}


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# RUN — SIGMOID AND TANH, BOTH VARIETIES
# ----------------------------------------------------------

cat("Running sigmoid activation - Arabica...\n")
res_activation_sigmoid_ara <- fit_ann_activation(
  df_arabica_levels, "arabica_price", n_train_ara_lev, act_fct = "logistic")

cat("Running tanh activation - Arabica...\n")
res_activation_tanh_ara <- fit_ann_activation(
  df_arabica_levels, "arabica_price", n_train_ara_lev, act_fct = "tanh")

cat("Running sigmoid activation - Robusta...\n")
res_activation_sigmoid_rob <- fit_ann_activation(
  df_robusta_levels, "robusta_price", n_train_rob_lev, act_fct = "logistic")

cat("Running tanh activation - Robusta...\n")
res_activation_tanh_rob <- fit_ann_activation(
  df_robusta_levels, "robusta_price", n_train_rob_lev, act_fct = "tanh")

        calculer_metriques(res_activation_tanh_ara$actual, res_activation_tanh_ara$predicted)),

            bold       = TRUE,

Tanh 0.6176 0.0171 0.1052

The results do not point to a single winner across both varieties. For Arabica, tanh outperforms sigmoid (\(R^2\) = 0.618 vs 0.577), consistent with the zero-centred, steeper-derivative rationale outlined above: better-conditioned gradients translate into a modest but real improvement over the sigmoid default. For Robusta, the direction reverses: sigmoid outperforms tanh (\(R^2\) = 0.334 vs 0.288), the opposite of what the gradient-flow argument alone would predict.

Two things are worth keeping in mind before reading too much into this reversal. First, both specifications here are unregularised, neuralnet offers no decay mechanism, so both numbers sit well below the tuned, regularised baseline reported earlier in this section (0.728 for Arabica, 0.456 for Robusta); the comparison isolates the activation function only, and should not be read as a claim about the best achievable ANN specification for either series. Second, sigmoid and tanh differ not just in gradient behaviour but in output range, and at only two hidden neurons, the network has very little redundancy to fall back on if either activation happens to saturate on a handful of extreme input values during a particular walk-forward window, especially given Robusta’s shorter, more volatile training sample. The theoretical advantage of tanh is real, but with this little capacity, the outcome for a specific series and specific random weight initialisation can still go either way. What the comparison does establish is that the choice of activation function is not neutral: the gap between the two ranges from 0.041 to 0.045 in \(R^2\) for both varieties, comparable in size to some of the gains obtained from more heavily engineered changes elsewhere in this analysis, so it is a lever worth documenting explicitly rather than leaving at its untested default.

7.4.4 ANN Activation Function with L2 Regularisation (keras)

The comparison above isolates the effect of the activation function on its own, but leaves open a natural follow-up question: does the direction of that effect survive once regularisation is added back in? neuralnet cannot answer this, since it has no weight decay mechanism. This section uses keras3, via reticulate, which supports both a configurable activation function and L2 regularisation on the same layer, to test all four combinations of activation (sigmoid, tanh) and regularisation (none, L2 penalty of 0.01) at the same 1-layer, 2-neuron architecture used throughout this section, with the Adam optimiser rather than the less robust fixed-step gradient descent that produced the inconclusive RSNNS results earlier in this document.

This chunk defines a walk-forward estimation function for a single-hidden-layer Keras network, with activation function and L2 penalty exposed as arguments, then runs all four combinations for both coffee varieties. Each network is rebuilt from scratch at every walk-forward step, consistent with every other model in this document; Keras’s own random weight initialisation is seeded via tensorflow::set_random_seed() for reproducibility. Each network trains for up to 200 epochs, with early stopping halting training after 10 consecutive epochs without improvement in training loss, restoring the weights from the best epoch observed rather than the final one.

Show code 
library(keras3)
library(tensorflow)

# ----------------------------------------------------------
# ANN VIA KERAS — ACTIVATION FUNCTION x L2 REGULARISATION
# keras3 supports both a configurable activation function per layer
# and L2 weight regularisation simultaneously, closing the gap left
# by neuralnet (no regularisation) and RSNNS (regularisation
# available but with an under-optimising fixed-step gradient
# descent algorithm, as documented in the depth comparison earlier
# in this section). Keras's default Adam optimiser is adaptive,
# similar in spirit to neuralnet's Rprop+, avoiding the
# under-optimisation problem encountered with RSNNS.
# ----------------------------------------------------------


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# WALK-FORWARD ESTIMATION FUNCTION — KERAS ANN
#
# Arguments:
#   df           : levels dataset (one row per month)
#   var_dep      : name of the dependent variable column
#   n_train      : size of the initial training window
#   activation   : "sigmoid" or "tanh"
#   l2_penalty   : L2 regularisation strength; 0 disables it
#
# What the function returns:
#   actual    : the observed (scaled) prices in the test period
#   predicted : the walk-forward one-step-ahead forecasts
# ----------------------------------------------------------

fit_ann_keras <- function(df, var_dep, n_train, activation, l2_penalty = 0) {

  vars_exo_disponibles <- intersect(vars_exo, colnames(df))
  vars_a_garder         <- c(var_dep, vars_exo_disponibles)
  df_modele              <- df[, vars_a_garder]

  df_modele_scaled <- as.data.frame(sapply(df_modele, minmax_scale))

  n_total       <- nrow(df_modele_scaled)
  donnees_train <- df_modele_scaled[1:n_train, ]
  donnees_test  <- df_modele_scaled[(n_train + 1):n_total, ]
  n_test        <- nrow(donnees_test)

  predictions <- numeric(n_test)

  for (i in 1:n_test) {

    nb_lignes_test_vues  <- i - 1
    lignes_test_vues     <- donnees_test[seq_len(nb_lignes_test_vues), ]
    fenetre_entrainement <- rbind(donnees_train, lignes_test_vues)

    x_train <- as.matrix(fenetre_entrainement[, vars_exo_disponibles])
    y_train <- as.matrix(fenetre_entrainement[[var_dep]])

    tensorflow::set_random_seed(42)

    # STEP — build the model layer by layer.
    modele_keras <- keras_model_sequential() %>%
      layer_dense(
        units              = 2,
        activation         = activation,
        kernel_regularizer = if (l2_penalty > 0) regularizer_l2(l2_penalty) else NULL,
        input_shape        = ncol(x_train)
      ) %>%
      layer_dense(units = 1, activation = "linear")

    # STEP — compile, model passed as a named argument (object = )
    # for compatibility with keras3's stricter API.
    compile(
      object    = modele_keras,
      optimizer = optimizer_adam(),
      loss      = "mse"
    )

    # STEP — early stopping: training halts once the training loss
    # fails to improve for 10 consecutive epochs (patience = 10),
    # restoring the weights from the best epoch observed. A hard
    # cap of 200 epochs is retained as an upper bound in case
    # convergence has not triggered early stopping by then.
    early_stop <- callback_early_stopping(
      monitor              = "loss",
      patience             = 10,
      restore_best_weights = TRUE
    )

    fit(
      object    = modele_keras,
      x         = x_train,
      y         = y_train,
      epochs    = 200,
      callbacks = list(early_stop),
      verbose   = 0
    )

    ligne_a_predire <- as.matrix(donnees_test[i, vars_exo_disponibles, drop = FALSE])
    predictions[i]  <- as.numeric(predict(modele_keras, ligne_a_predire, verbose = 0))
  }

  valeurs_observees <- donnees_test[[var_dep]]
  list(actual = valeurs_observees, predicted = predictions)
}

This chunk runs all four activation/regularisation combinations for both coffee varieties, eight walk-forward estimations in total.

This chunk compiles the eight results into a single comparison table, grouped by variety.

Show code 
construire_bloc_keras <- function(nom_serie, res_list) {
  do.call(rbind, lapply(names(res_list), function(nom) {
    data.frame(Configuration = nom,
               calculer_metriques(res_list[[nom]]$actual, res_list[[nom]]$predicted))
  })) %>% mutate(Series = nom_serie, .before = Configuration)
}

df_keras_comparison <- rbind(
  construire_bloc_keras("Arabica", resultats_keras_ara),
  construire_bloc_keras("Robusta", resultats_keras_rob)
)

df_keras_comparison %>%
  select(Configuration, R2, MSE, MAE) %>%
  kable(caption   = "ANN (Keras) — activation function x L2 regularisation (1 layer, 2 neurons)",
        booktabs  = TRUE, row.names = FALSE,
        col.names = c("Configuration", "R²", "MSE", "MAE")) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"),
                font_size = 11, full_width = TRUE) %>%
  row_spec(4, extra_css = "border-bottom: 2px solid #333;") %>%
  pack_rows("Arabica", 1, 4,
            bold       = TRUE,
            color      = "#8B4513",
            background = "#f5ece6") %>%
  pack_rows("Robusta", 5, 8,
            bold       = TRUE,
            color      = "#2E8B57",
            background = "#e8f5ec")
ANN (Keras) — activation function x L2 regularisation (1 layer, 2 neurons)
Configuration R² MSE MAE
Arabica
Sigmoid, no L2 -0.2168 0.0543 0.1682
Sigmoid, L2 -0.2348 0.0551 0.1887
Tanh, no L2 0.7124 0.0128 0.0942
Tanh, L2 0.3944 0.0270 0.1292
Robusta
Sigmoid, no L2 0.2227 0.0514 0.1950
Sigmoid, L2 0.2127 0.0521 0.1982
Tanh, no L2 0.5215 0.0316 0.1470
Tanh, L2 0.4869 0.0339 0.1514

The regularised specifications are uniformly worse than their unregularised counterparts here, the opposite of what the tuned single-layer ANN showed earlier in this section. For Arabica, tanh without L2 reaches \(R^2\) = 0.712, the strongest result in the table, while adding L2 at 0.1 drops it to 0.394. Sigmoid fares even worse and never recovers: \(R^2\) = \(-0.217\) without L2 and \(-0.235\) with it, both negative regardless of regularisation. For Robusta, the same pattern holds at a smaller scale: tanh without L2 reaches 0.522, falling to 0.487 with L2, and sigmoid falls from 0.223 to 0.213.

This is not a contradiction of the earlier finding that decay improved the tuned ANN substantially (from 0.453 to 0.728 for Arabica), but a difference in training regime. The tuned nnet specification trains to convergence via a fixed-step full-batch procedure with no early stopping, so weight decay was doing necessary work: without it, the network kept fitting noise for as long as training continued. The Keras specification here already includes early stopping, which halts training as soon as further epochs stop improving the loss, providing a form of implicit regularisation on its own. Adding an explicit L2 penalty on top of that likely does what regularisation always risks doing when applied to a model that is not actually overfitting: it introduces additional bias without a corresponding reduction in variance, since early stopping had already contained the variance problem the penalty was designed to address.

Comparing this table to the sigmoid-versus-tanh comparison run earlier in neuralnet also shows that the specific \(R^2\) values, and even the ranking between activations, are sensitive to the choice of package and optimiser rather than reflecting a stable property of the activation function alone. neuralnet’s Rprop+ optimiser found sigmoid mildly preferable to tanh for Robusta (0.334 vs 0.288); Keras’s Adam optimiser, with early stopping, finds the reverse (0.223 vs 0.522). For Arabica, both packages agree that tanh outperforms sigmoid, but by a very different margin (0.041 in neuralnet, closer to 0.9 in Keras, driven mainly by sigmoid’s collapse to a negative \(R^2\) here). Taken together, these results confirm that the choice of activation function matters, consistent with the earlier comparison, but they also show that the size and even the direction of that effect cannot be separated cleanly from the optimiser and training procedure used to fit the network, a limitation worth stating plainly rather than picking whichever package’s ranking looks most convincing.

The most interesting takeaway from comparing the two activation tests is that the direction and size of the effect depend on the package and optimiser used, not on the activation function alone. neuralnet’s Rprop+ optimiser and Keras’s Adam optimiser do not agree on which activation performs better for Robusta. This is worth stating plainly rather than presenting either result as the definitive answer: the choice of activation function matters, but its effect cannot be cleanly separated from the training procedure used to fit the network.

The following plots report the full permutation importance rankings for all 14 predictors across the six models and both coffee varieties. Each bar represents the increase in MSE when the corresponding variable is randomly permuted on the test set.

plot_importance_appendix <- function(imp_df, color, bg_color,
                                      title, subtitle = NULL) {

  # Format labels: round to 4 decimal places for ML models,
  # round to 0 for ARIMAX which has very large values
  imp_df <- imp_df %>%
    mutate(label = ifelse(abs(Importance) > 100,
                          format(round(Importance, 0), big.mark = ","),
                          as.character(round(Importance, 4))))

  ggplot(imp_df, aes(x = reorder(Variable, Importance),
                     y = Importance)) +
    geom_bar(stat = "identity",
             fill = ifelse(imp_df$Importance >= 0, color, "grey70"),
             alpha = 0.85, width = 0.65) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey40",
               linewidth = 0.5, linetype = "dashed") +
    geom_text(aes(label = label),
              hjust = ifelse(imp_df$Importance >= 0, -0.15, 1.15),
              size = 3, color = "grey30") +
    coord_flip() +
    scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.2, 0.3))) +
    labs(title    = title,
         subtitle = subtitle,
         x = NULL, y = "ΔMSE") +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
    theme(
      panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
      panel.grid.minor   = element_blank(),
      panel.background   = element_rect(fill = "#fafafa", color = NA),
      strip.background   = element_rect(fill = bg_color, color = NA),
      plot.title         = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12),
      plot.subtitle      = element_text(size = 9, color = "grey50"),
      axis.text.y        = element_text(size = 10, color = "grey20"),
      axis.text.x        = element_text(size = 9, color = "grey40"),
      plot.margin = ggplot2::margin(10, 20, 10, 10)
    )
}

7.6 Partial Dependence Plots — Per-Model Detail

Show code 
# ----------------------------------------------------------
# PARTIAL DEPENDENCE PLOTS — APPENDIX (PER-MODEL DETAIL)
# Unlike the main text, which is restricted to a few consensus
# variables, this section produces the PDP for the three variables
# specific to EACH individual model, as already identified by top3_ara
# and top3_rob in the Variable Importance section. One figure is
# produced per model and per variety (4 + 4 = 8 figures), each showing
# that model's three variables as separate panels.
# Unlike the main-text figures, no facet_grid2()/independent = "x"
# workaround is needed here: facet_wrap() with scales = "free_x"
# already frees the x-axis per panel rather than per row or column,
# since each panel in a facet_wrap() grid is independent by
# construction. out.width = "100%" caps the rendered width to the
# page's text width, consistent with the main-text PDP chunks.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

# STEP 1 — Reverse mapping from label to internal variable name.
# labels_mlr already maps each internal name (e.g. "ending_stocks") to
# its readable label (e.g. "Ending stocks"). labels_inverse builds the
# opposite mapping, needed here because top3_ara$Variable stores the
# readable labels, while calculer_pdp() needs the internal name to
# pull the right column from the training set.
labels_inverse <- setNames(names(labels_mlr), labels_mlr)


# STEP 2 — Compute the PDP for the 3 variables of ONE given model.
# For nom_modele, first filter top3_df down to its 3 most important
# variables (top3_df$Model == nom_modele), convert their labels to
# internal names via labels_inverse, then compute the PDP for each one
# using the same calculer_pdp() function as in the main text, stacking
# the 3 results with rbind().
generer_pdp_appendice <- function(nom_modele, modele, top3_df,
                                  donnees_full, donnees_predicteurs,
                                  bornes_vars, bornes_cible) {

  # Internal names of this model's 3 most important variables
  vars_internes <- labels_inverse[
    as.character(top3_df$Variable[top3_df$Model == nom_modele])
  ]

  # Appropriate input dataset (matrix for XGBoost, full data frame
  # otherwise), resolved once here and reused for all 3 variables of
  # this model
  donnees_pdp <- obtenir_donnees_pdp(nom_modele, donnees_full,
                                      donnees_predicteurs)

  # Loop over the 3 variables: compute the PDP, then attach the
  # readable label (rather than the internal name) for display in the
  # plot
  do.call(rbind, lapply(vars_internes, function(var_int) {
    res <- calculer_pdp(nom_modele, modele, donnees_pdp, var_int,
                        bornes_vars[[var_int]], bornes_cible)
    res$Variable <- labels_mlr[var_int]
    res
  }))
}


# STEP 3 — Generic plotting function, reused for all 8 figures (4
# models x 2 varieties). facet_wrap() lays out a model's 3 variables
# side by side, each panel with its own free x-axis since the 3
# variables don't share the same unit.
plot_pdp_appendice <- function(df_pdp, couleur, bg_couleur, titre, unite_y) {
  ggplot(df_pdp, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
    geom_line(color = couleur, linewidth = 0.9) +
    facet_wrap(~ Variable, scales = "free_x", ncol = 3) +
    labs(title = titre, x = NULL, y = unite_y) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
    theme(
      strip.text       = element_text(face = "bold", size = 9),
      strip.background = element_rect(fill = bg_couleur, color = NA),
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      panel.background = element_rect(fill = "#fafafa", color = NA)
    )
}


# STEP 4 — Generate the 4 Arabica figures (one per ML model).
# Using a for() loop here rather than lapply(), since each iteration
# needs to display a plot immediately via print() — this is required
# for ggplot2 to actually render a plot inside an R Markdown / Quarto
# chunk when called from within a loop rather than at the chunk's top
# level.
for (nom in names(modeles_ara)) {
  df_pdp_modele <- generer_pdp_appendice(nom, modeles_ara[[nom]], top3_ara,
                                         train_ara, train_ara_xgb,
                                         bornes_ara, bornes_prix_ara)
  print(plot_pdp_appendice(df_pdp_modele, "#8B4513", "#f5ece6",
                           paste0("Partial dependence — ", nom, " (Arabica)"),
                           "Predicted price (USD/lb)"))
}
Show code

for (nom in names(modeles_rob)) {
  df_pdp_modele <- generer_pdp_appendice(nom, modeles_rob[[nom]], top3_rob,
                                         train_rob, train_rob_xgb,
                                         bornes_rob, bornes_prix_rob)
  print(plot_pdp_appendice(df_pdp_modele, "#2E8B57", "#e8f5ec",
                           paste0("Partial dependence — ", nom, " (Robusta)"),
                           "Predicted price (USD/tonne)"))
}

7.7 Robustness Checks

7.7.1 Disaggregated Climate Variables

The main model specifications rely on two production-weighted climate indices that aggregate temperature and precipitation conditions across 14 producer countries into single monthly series. While this aggregation is methodologically motivated, as it avoids endogeneity, reduces dimensionality, and is consistent with the fixed-weight approach documented in the data section, it raises the question of whether relevant country-specific climate information is lost in the process.

To assess this, the four ML models are re-estimated under an alternative specification in which the two aggregated indices are replaced by the 28 individual national series (14 countries × 2 climate variables), holding all other predictors constant. A comparison of out-of-sample \(R^2\) between the two configurations provides direct evidence on whether disaggregation improves predictive accuracy. ARIMAX and MLR are excluded from this comparison: ARIMAX is computationally prohibitive with 40 regressors in a walk-forward loop, and MLR is ill-conditioned with 40 predictors on approximately 170 training observations.

The chunk below re-estimates the four ML models using the disaggregated variable list and stores the results for comparison with the baseline specification. The model functions are identical in structure to those used in the main results, with a vars_exo_vec argument replacing the global vars_exo list.

Show code 
# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 1 — LOAD THE DISAGGREGATED CLIMATE SERIES AND BUILD
# THE DISAGGREGATED DATASET
# The two production-weighted indices (indice_precip,
# indice_temp) are dropped from the monthly dataset and
# replaced by the 28 individual national series, 14 for
# precipitation and 14 for temperature.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

df_precip_dis <- read_csv(
  file.path(PATH_OUTPUT, "precip_disaggregated_2000_2023.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE)

df_temp_dis <- read_csv(
  file.path(PATH_OUTPUT, "temp_disaggregated_2000_2023.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE)

dataset_disagg <- dataset_mensuel %>%
  select(-indice_precip, -indice_temp) %>%
  left_join(df_precip_dis, by = "date") %>%
  left_join(df_temp_dis,   by = "date")


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 2 — DEFINE THE DISAGGREGATED EXOGENOUS VARIABLE LIST
# vars_climate_dis lists the 28 national climate columns
# (precip_bresil, precip_vietnam, ..., temp_bresil, ...).
# vars_exo_dis replaces indice_precip and indice_temp in the
# baseline vars_exo list with these 28 columns, keeping the
# other 12 baseline predictors unchanged.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

vars_climate_dis <- c(
  paste0("precip_", names(POIDS_PRODUCTION)),
  paste0("temp_",   names(POIDS_PRODUCTION))
)

vars_exo_dis <- c(
  "sugar_price", "cocoa_price", "cpi", "wti", "fed_funds_rate",
  "dxy", "production", "consumption", "exports",
  "ending_stocks", "oni", "cot_net_mm",
  vars_climate_dis
)


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 3 — PREPARE THE DISAGGREGATED DATASETS
# Same logic as preparer_niveaux() in the preprocessing chunk:
# keep the dependent variable and the 40 exogenous predictors,
# drop rows with any missing value, and sort by date.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

preparer_niveaux_dis <- function(df, var_dep) {
  colonnes_a_garder <- c("date", var_dep, vars_exo_dis)
  df_modele         <- df[, colonnes_a_garder]
  df_modele         <- df_modele[complete.cases(df_modele), ]
  df_modele[order(df_modele$date), ]
}

df_arabica_dis <- preparer_niveaux_dis(dataset_disagg, "arabica_price")
df_robusta_dis <- preparer_niveaux_dis(
  dataset_disagg[!is.na(dataset_disagg$robusta_price), ], "robusta_price")

n_train_ara_dis <- floor(nrow(df_arabica_dis) * split_ratio)
n_train_rob_dis <- floor(nrow(df_robusta_dis) * split_ratio)


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 4 — GENERIC MODEL FUNCTIONS
# Identical in structure to the main model functions, with
# an added vars_exo_vec argument so the same function can
# be reused with different predictor lists without copying
# the function body.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

fit_rf_generique <- function(df, var_dep, vars_exo_vec, n_train) {
  vars_exo_disponibles <- intersect(vars_exo_vec, colnames(df))
  df_modele            <- df[, c(var_dep, vars_exo_disponibles)]
  df_modele            <- df_modele[complete.cases(df_modele), ]
  df_modele_scaled     <- as.data.frame(sapply(df_modele, minmax_scale))

  n_total       <- nrow(df_modele_scaled)
  donnees_train <- df_modele_scaled[1:n_train, ]
  donnees_test  <- df_modele_scaled[(n_train + 1):n_total, ]
  n_test        <- nrow(donnees_test)

  predictions <- numeric(n_test)
  formule     <- as.formula(paste(var_dep, "~ ."))

  for (i in 1:n_test) {
    nb_lignes_test_vues  <- i - 1
    lignes_test_vues     <- donnees_test[seq_len(nb_lignes_test_vues), ]
    fenetre_entrainement <- rbind(donnees_train, lignes_test_vues)
    set.seed(42)
    foret <- randomForest(formule, data = fenetre_entrainement,
                          ntree = 500, importance = TRUE)
    predictions[i] <- predict(foret, newdata = donnees_test[i, ])
  }

  list(actual = donnees_test[[var_dep]], predicted = predictions)
}

fit_xgb_generique <- function(df, var_dep, vars_exo_vec, n_train) {
  vars_exo_disponibles <- intersect(vars_exo_vec, colnames(df))
  df_modele            <- df[, c(var_dep, vars_exo_disponibles)]
  df_modele            <- df_modele[complete.cases(df_modele), ]
  df_modele_scaled     <- as.data.frame(sapply(df_modele, minmax_scale))

  colonnes_predicteurs <- setdiff(colnames(df_modele_scaled), var_dep)
  X       <- as.matrix(df_modele_scaled[, colonnes_predicteurs])
  y       <- df_modele_scaled[[var_dep]]
  n_total <- length(y)
  n_test  <- n_total - n_train

  predictions <- numeric(n_test)

  for (i in 1:n_test) {
    indices_fenetre  <- 1:(n_train + i - 1)
    indice_a_predire <- n_train + i
    modele_xgb <- xgboost(data      = X[indices_fenetre, ],
                          label     = y[indices_fenetre],
                          nrounds   = 100, max_depth = 4,
                          eta       = 0.1, subsample = 0.8,
                          verbose   = 0,
                          objective = "reg:squarederror")
    ligne_a_predire <- matrix(X[indice_a_predire, ], nrow = 1)
    predictions[i]  <- predict(modele_xgb, newdata = ligne_a_predire)
  }

  list(actual = y[(n_train + 1):n_total], predicted = predictions)
}

fit_svm_generique <- function(df, var_dep, vars_exo_vec, n_train) {
  vars_exo_disponibles <- intersect(vars_exo_vec, colnames(df))
  df_modele            <- df[, c(var_dep, vars_exo_disponibles)]
  df_modele            <- df_modele[complete.cases(df_modele), ]
  df_modele_scaled     <- as.data.frame(sapply(df_modele, minmax_scale))

  n_total       <- nrow(df_modele_scaled)
  donnees_train <- df_modele_scaled[1:n_train, ]
  donnees_test  <- df_modele_scaled[(n_train + 1):n_total, ]
  n_test        <- nrow(donnees_test)

  predictions <- numeric(n_test)
  formule     <- as.formula(paste(var_dep, "~ ."))

  for (i in 1:n_test) {
    nb_lignes_test_vues  <- i - 1
    lignes_test_vues     <- donnees_test[seq_len(nb_lignes_test_vues), ]
    fenetre_entrainement <- rbind(donnees_train, lignes_test_vues)
    modele_svm <- svm(formule, data = fenetre_entrainement,
                      kernel = "radial", cost = 1, gamma = 0.1)
    predictions[i] <- predict(modele_svm, newdata = donnees_test[i, ])
  }

  list(actual = donnees_test[[var_dep]], predicted = predictions)
}

fit_ann_generique <- function(df, var_dep, vars_exo_vec, n_train) {
  vars_exo_disponibles <- intersect(vars_exo_vec, colnames(df))
  df_modele            <- df[, c(var_dep, vars_exo_disponibles)]
  df_modele            <- df_modele[complete.cases(df_modele), ]
  df_modele_scaled     <- as.data.frame(sapply(df_modele, minmax_scale))

  n_total       <- nrow(df_modele_scaled)
  donnees_train <- df_modele_scaled[1:n_train, ]
  donnees_test  <- df_modele_scaled[(n_train + 1):n_total, ]
  n_test        <- nrow(donnees_test)

  predictions <- numeric(n_test)
  formule     <- as.formula(paste(var_dep, "~ ."))

  set.seed(42)
  for (i in 1:n_test) {
    nb_lignes_test_vues  <- i - 1
    lignes_test_vues     <- donnees_test[seq_len(nb_lignes_test_vues), ]
    fenetre_entrainement <- rbind(donnees_train, lignes_test_vues)
    modele_ann <- nnet(formule, data = fenetre_entrainement,
                       size = 5, linout = TRUE, maxit = 500, trace = FALSE)
    predictions[i] <- predict(modele_ann, newdata = donnees_test[i, ])
  }

  list(actual = donnees_test[[var_dep]], predicted = predictions)
}


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 5 — RUN ALL FOUR MODELS ON BOTH SERIES
# ----------------------------------------------------------

# STEP 6 — COMPILE RESULTS INTO A COMPARISON TABLE

df_robustness <- data.frame(
  Model  = rep(c("Random Forest", "XGBoost", "SVM", "ANN"), each = 2),
  Series = rep(c("Arabica", "Robusta"), 4),
  R2_baseline = as.numeric(c(
    metriques_all %>% filter(Model == "Random Forest", Series == "Arabica") %>% pull(R2),
    metriques_all %>% filter(Model == "Random Forest", Series == "Robusta") %>% pull(R2),
    metriques_all %>% filter(Model == "XGBoost",       Series == "Arabica") %>% pull(R2),
    metriques_all %>% filter(Model == "XGBoost",       Series == "Robusta") %>% pull(R2),
    metriques_all %>% filter(Model == "SVM",           Series == "Arabica") %>% pull(R2),
    metriques_all %>% filter(Model == "SVM",           Series == "Robusta") %>% pull(R2),
    metriques_all %>% filter(Model == "ANN",           Series == "Arabica") %>% pull(R2),
    metriques_all %>% filter(Model == "ANN",           Series == "Robusta") %>% pull(R2)
  )),
  R2_disaggregated = c(
    calculer_metriques(res_rf_dis_ara$actual,  res_rf_dis_ara$predicted)$R2,
    calculer_metriques(res_rf_dis_rob$actual,  res_rf_dis_rob$predicted)$R2,
    calculer_metriques(res_xgb_dis_ara$actual, res_xgb_dis_ara$predicted)$R2,
    calculer_metriques(res_xgb_dis_rob$actual, res_xgb_dis_rob$predicted)$R2,
    calculer_metriques(res_svm_dis_ara$actual, res_svm_dis_ara$predicted)$R2,
    calculer_metriques(res_svm_dis_rob$actual, res_svm_dis_rob$predicted)$R2,
    calculer_metriques(res_ann_dis_ara$actual, res_ann_dis_ara$predicted)$R2,
    calculer_metriques(res_ann_dis_rob$actual, res_ann_dis_rob$predicted)$R2
  )
) %>%
  mutate(
    Delta_R2         = round(R2_disaggregated - R2_baseline, 4),
    R2_baseline      = round(R2_baseline, 4),
    R2_disaggregated = round(R2_disaggregated, 4)
  )

The robustness check confirms that the production-weighted aggregation of climate indices is the appropriate specification. Disaggregation systematically deteriorates out-of-sample \(R^2\) across all four ML models and both coffee varieties, with every \(ΔR^2\) value negative. The deterioration is moderate for Random Forest (\(ΔR^2\) of −0.052 for Arabica, −0.097 for Robusta) and XGBoost (−0.014 and −0.059), but severe for SVM and ANN, both of which fall to negative \(R^2\) values for both varieties under the disaggregated specification, indicating performance worse than a naive mean forecast.

This pattern is consistent with the curse of dimensionality: with 40 regressors and approximately 170 training observations, models sensitive to input dimensionality become severely overparameterised and fail to generalise to the test period. The ensemble methods Random Forest and XGBoost are more robust to this problem through their built-in variable selection mechanisms, but still suffer a meaningful performance loss. These results suggest that the production-weighted aggregation improves the climate signal by filtering out country-specific noise, and that the information gain from disaggregation is outweighed by the dimensionality cost at the sample sizes available in this study.

7.7.2 Variety-Specific Model Specification

The robustness check conducted in the preceding section validated the production-weighted aggregation methodology by showing that disaggregated climate indices systematically deteriorate out-of-sample performance. A second robustness check is now conducted by re-estimating all six models under a variety-specific specification. Rather than using global climate indices and world supply-and-demand fundamentals, this specification assigns each model its own set of variety-relevant predictors: the Arabica models use climate indices and fundamentals aggregated across the twelve Arabica-producing countries, while the Robusta models use the equivalent aggregates for the six Robusta-producing countries. This specification is motivated by the structural concentration of Robusta production in a small number of countries, chiefly Vietnam and Indonesia, compared with the broader geographic diversification of Arabica production across twelve countries. Using global indices for Robusta in particular dilutes the climate and supply signal by including conditions in countries that produce virtually no Robusta.

This chunk defines the variety-specific exogenous variable lists and prepares the two datasets used in the re-estimation below. Sample sizes are printed to the console for verification.

Show code 
# ----------------------------------------------------------
# VARIETY-SPECIFIC EXOGENOUS VARIABLE LISTS
# Two separate lists replace the global vars_exo: one for
# Arabica models (climate indices and fundamentals aggregated
# across the 10 Arabica-producing countries) and one for
# Robusta models (aggregated across the 6 Robusta-producing
# countries). All other predictors (sugar, cocoa, macro
# variables, ONI, COT) are unchanged from the baseline.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

vars_exo_ara_vs <- c(
  "sugar_price", "cocoa_price", "cpi", "wti", "fed_funds_rate",
  "dxy", "production_ara", "consommation_ara", "exportations_ara",
  "ending_stocks_ara", "indice_precip_arabica", "indice_temp_arabica",
  "oni", "cot_net_mm"
)

vars_exo_rob_vs <- c(
  "sugar_price", "cocoa_price", "cpi", "wti", "fed_funds_rate",
  "dxy", "production_rob", "consommation_rob", "exportations_rob",
  "ending_stocks_rob", "indice_precip_robusta", "indice_temp_robusta",
  "oni", "cot_net_mm"
)

# ----------------------------------------------------------
# PREPARE THE VARIETY-SPECIFIC DATASETS
# Same logic as preparer_niveaux() used throughout the
# document: keep the dependent variable and the relevant
# exogenous predictors, drop rows with any missing value,
# and sort by date.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

preparer_niveaux_vs <- function(df, var_dep, vars_exo_vec) {
  colonnes_a_garder <- c("date", var_dep, vars_exo_vec)
  df_modele         <- df[, colonnes_a_garder]
  df_modele         <- df_modele[complete.cases(df_modele), ]
  df_modele[order(df_modele$date), ]
}

  "robusta_price", vars_exo_rob_vs)

# 80/20 split, using the same split_ratio as every other model

Sample sizes for the variety-specific datasets mirror those of the baseline specification, 168 training and 43 test observations for Arabica, and 153 training and 39 test observations for Robusta, confirming that the variety-specific variable substitution does not alter the temporal coverage of either dataset.

All six models are re-estimated under this specification using the same walk-forward protocol as the baseline. The Random Forest, XGBoost, SVM and ANN models reuse the generic functions already defined in the disaggregated robustness check above, called here with the variety-specific variable lists. ARIMAX and MLR are generalised below by adding a vars_exo_vec argument following the same pattern.

The chunk below defines the generic ARIMAX and MLR functions and re-estimates all six models under the variety-specific specification.

Show code 
# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 1 — GENERIC ARIMAX FUNCTION — FIXED ORDER
# Mirrors fit_arimax() from the main results: the (p,d,q)
# order is selected once via an exhaustive search on the
# initial training window, then held fixed for the rest of
# the walk-forward loop, with only the coefficients
# re-estimated at each step via Arima(). This keeps the
# ARIMAX methodology used in this robustness check consistent
# with the main results, rather than falling back to the
# earlier, re-adaptive auto.arima() search abandoned there.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

fit_arimax_generique <- function(df, var_dep, vars_exo_vec, n_train) {

  serie_dependante    <- df[[var_dep]]
  matrice_regresseurs <- as.matrix(df[, vars_exo_vec])

  colonnes_valides    <- apply(matrice_regresseurs, 2,
                               function(col) !all(is.na(col)))
  matrice_regresseurs <- matrice_regresseurs[, colonnes_valides, drop = FALSE]

  n_total    <- length(serie_dependante)
  y_train    <- serie_dependante[1:n_train]
  y_test     <- serie_dependante[(n_train + 1):n_total]
  xreg_train <- matrice_regresseurs[1:n_train, ]
  xreg_test  <- matrice_regresseurs[(n_train + 1):n_total, ]
  n_test     <- length(y_test)

  # Select and fix the (p,d,q) order once, on the initial
  # training set only, using the same widened search as the
  # main ARIMAX specification (stepwise = FALSE,
  # approximation = FALSE, max.p = max.q = 5, max.d = 2).
  modele_ordre_initial <- auto.arima(y_train, xreg = xreg_train,
                                     stepwise      = FALSE,
                                     approximation = FALSE,
                                     max.p = 5, max.q = 5, max.d = 2)

  ordre_fixe <- arimaorder(modele_ordre_initial)[c("p", "d", "q")]

  # Walk-forward loop with the order held fixed: only the
  # coefficients are re-estimated via Arima() at each step.
  predictions <- numeric(n_test)

  for (i in 1:n_test) {
    nb_observations_vues <- i - 1
    indices_vus          <- seq_len(nb_observations_vues)
    y_vu                 <- y_test[indices_vus]
    xreg_vu              <- xreg_test[indices_vus, , drop = FALSE]
    y_fenetre            <- c(y_train, y_vu)
    xreg_fenetre         <- rbind(xreg_train, xreg_vu)

    modele_arima <- tryCatch(
      Arima(y_fenetre, order = as.numeric(ordre_fixe), xreg = xreg_fenetre),
      error = function(e) NULL
    )

    if (is.null(modele_arima)) { predictions[i] <- NA; next }

    ligne_regresseurs_futurs <- matrix(xreg_test[i, ], nrow = 1)
    prevision <- forecast(modele_arima, h = 1,
                          xreg = ligne_regresseurs_futurs)
    predictions[i] <- prevision$mean[1]
  }

  list(actual = y_test, predicted = predictions, ordre_fixe = ordre_fixe)
}


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 2 — GENERIC MLR FUNCTION
# Identical to fit_mlr() defined earlier, except that the
# predictor list is passed in as vars_exo_vec. intersect()
# ensures only columns present in df are used, guarding
# against any name mismatch between the variable list and
# the dataset columns.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

fit_mlr_generique <- function(df, var_dep, vars_exo_vec, n_train) {

  vars_exo_disponibles <- intersect(vars_exo_vec, colnames(df))
  df_modele            <- df[, c(var_dep, vars_exo_disponibles)]
  df_modele            <- df_modele[complete.cases(df_modele), ]

  n_total       <- nrow(df_modele)
  donnees_train <- df_modele[1:n_train, ]
  donnees_test  <- df_modele[(n_train + 1):n_total, ]
  n_test        <- nrow(donnees_test)

  predictions <- numeric(n_test)
  formule     <- as.formula(paste(var_dep, "~ ."))

  for (i in 1:n_test) {
    nb_lignes_test_vues  <- i - 1
    lignes_test_vues     <- donnees_test[seq_len(nb_lignes_test_vues), ]
    fenetre_entrainement <- rbind(donnees_train, lignes_test_vues)
    modele_ols           <- lm(formule, data = fenetre_entrainement)
    predictions[i]       <- predict(modele_ols, newdata = donnees_test[i, ])
  }

  list(actual = donnees_test[[var_dep]], predicted = predictions)
}


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 3 — RUN ALL SIX MODELS ON BOTH SERIES
# Each model is called twice: once for Arabica using
# df_arabica_vs and vars_exo_ara_vs, and once for Robusta
# using df_robusta_vs and vars_exo_rob_vs. The four ML
# generic functions were defined in the disaggregated
# robustness check chunk and are reused here unchanged.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

cat("Running variety-specific ARIMAX - Arabica...\n")

# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 4 — STACK PERFORMANCE METRICS
# calculer_metriques() is applied to each model's actual and
# predicted vectors. Results are stacked into a single 12-row
# data frame (6 models × 2 series) and numeric columns are
# coerced from character to numeric as in metriques_all.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

metriques_vs_all <- rbind(
  cbind(Model = "ARIMAX", Series = "Arabica",
        calculer_metriques(res_arimax_ara_vs$actual, res_arimax_ara_vs$predicted)),
  cbind(Model = "ARIMAX", Series = "Robusta",
        calculer_metriques(res_arimax_rob_vs$actual, res_arimax_rob_vs$predicted)),
  cbind(Model = "MLR", Series = "Arabica",
        calculer_metriques(res_mlr_ara_vs$actual, res_mlr_ara_vs$predicted)),
  cbind(Model = "MLR", Series = "Robusta",
        calculer_metriques(res_mlr_rob_vs$actual, res_mlr_rob_vs$predicted)),
  cbind(Model = "Random Forest", Series = "Arabica",
        calculer_metriques(res_rf_ara_vs$actual, res_rf_ara_vs$predicted)),
  cbind(Model = "Random Forest", Series = "Robusta",
        calculer_metriques(res_rf_rob_vs$actual, res_rf_rob_vs$predicted)),
  cbind(Model = "XGBoost", Series = "Arabica",
        calculer_metriques(res_xgb_ara_vs$actual, res_xgb_ara_vs$predicted)),
  cbind(Model = "XGBoost", Series = "Robusta",
        calculer_metriques(res_xgb_rob_vs$actual, res_xgb_rob_vs$predicted)),
  cbind(Model = "SVM", Series = "Arabica",
        calculer_metriques(res_svm_ara_vs$actual, res_svm_ara_vs$predicted)),
  cbind(Model = "SVM", Series = "Robusta",
        calculer_metriques(res_svm_rob_vs$actual, res_svm_rob_vs$predicted)),
  cbind(Model = "ANN", Series = "Arabica",
        calculer_metriques(res_ann_ara_vs$actual, res_ann_ara_vs$predicted)),
  cbind(Model = "ANN", Series = "Robusta",
        calculer_metriques(res_ann_rob_vs$actual, res_ann_rob_vs$predicted))
) %>%
  mutate(across(c(R2, MSE, MAE), as.numeric))
