## Descriptive Statistics

*This chunk recomputes the Arabica and Robusta estimation samples directly from the assembled monthly dataset (mirroring the filtering later applied in the modelling chunks) and renders descriptive statistics for the fourteen predictors and the relevant price variable, split by variety, matching the samples actually used for estimation (211 Arabica observations from June 2006, 192 Robusta observations from January 2008).*

```{r desc_stats_table32, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

vars_exo <- c("sugar_price", "cocoa_price", "cpi", "wti", "fed_funds_rate",
              "dxy", "production", "consumption", "exports",
              "ending_stocks", "indice_precip", "indice_temp", "oni",
              "cot_net_mm")

units_exo <- c(
  arabica_price = "USD/lb", robusta_price = "USD/tonne",
  sugar_price = "USD/lb", cocoa_price = "USD/tonne", cpi = "index",
  wti = "USD/barrel", fed_funds_rate = "%", dxy = "index",
  production = "thousand 60-kg bags", consumption = "thousand 60-kg bags",
  exports = "thousand 60-kg bags", ending_stocks = "thousand 60-kg bags",
  indice_precip = "mm", indice_temp = "\u00b0C", oni = "\u00b0C anomaly",
  cot_net_mm = "contracts"
)

labels_exo <- c(
  arabica_price = "Arabica price", robusta_price = "Robusta price",
  sugar_price = "Sugar", cocoa_price = "Cocoa", cpi = "CPI", wti = "WTI",
  fed_funds_rate = "Fed Funds Rate", dxy = "DXY", production = "Production",
  consumption = "Consumption", exports = "Exports",
  ending_stocks = "Ending stocks", indice_precip = "Precipitation",
  indice_temp = "Temperature", oni = "ONI", cot_net_mm = "COT net MM"
)

# Build descriptive statistics for one variety, matching the estimation sample
# used by the modelling chunks later in the document.
build_desc_table <- function(df, var_dep) {
  vars <- c(var_dep, vars_exo)
  df_c <- df %>% select(all_of(vars)) %>% filter(complete.cases(.))
  do.call(rbind, lapply(vars, function(v) {
    x <- df_c[[v]]
    data.frame(
      Variable = labels_exo[[v]], Unit = units_exo[[v]],
      N = length(x), Mean = round(mean(x), 4), SD = round(sd(x), 4),
      Min = round(min(x), 4), Max = round(max(x), 4)
    )
  }))
}

table_ara <- build_desc_table(
  dataset_mensuel %>% filter(!is.na(arabica_price)), "arabica_price")
table_rob <- build_desc_table(
  dataset_mensuel %>% filter(!is.na(robusta_price)), "robusta_price")

kable(table_ara, caption = "Descriptive statistics -- Arabica estimation sample",
      booktabs = TRUE, row.names = FALSE, format.args = list(big.mark = ",")) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"), font_size = 10, full_width = TRUE) %>%
  row_spec(0, bold = TRUE, background = "#4a4a4a", color = "white")
```

```{r desc_stats_table32_rob, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
kable(table_rob, caption = "Descriptive statistics -- Robusta estimation sample",
      booktabs = TRUE, row.names = FALSE, format.args = list(big.mark = ",")) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"), font_size = 10, full_width = TRUE) %>%
  row_spec(0, bold = TRUE, background = "#4a4a4a", color = "white")
```

Arabica is estimated over 211 monthly observations (June 2006-December 2023) and Robusta over 192 (January 2008-December 2023), reflecting the data availability constraints documented above.

## Correlation Structure of the Predictor Set

The correlation matrix below covers the 2008-2023 sub-period, the longest interval over which every variable, including Robusta prices and the COT net position, is simultaneously available. Pearson coefficients are reported, consistent with the linear benchmark models estimated in the following section.

```{r eda_correlation, fig.width=9, fig.height=8}

# Define the ordered variable list for the correlation matrix.
# The order follows the variable grouping in the dataset table:
# dependent variables first, then spillovers, macroeconomic,
# fundamentals, climate and speculative variables last.
vars_corr <- c("arabica_price", "robusta_price", "sugar_price", "cocoa_price",
               "cpi", "wti", "fed_funds_rate", "dxy",
               "production", "consumption", "exports", "ending_stocks",
               "indice_precip", "indice_temp", "oni", "cot_net_mm")

# Restrict to 2008-2023: the longest window for which all 16
# variables are simultaneously available (Robusta from 2008,
# COT from June 2006 — the binding constraint is Robusta).
# na.omit() removes any remaining sporadic gaps before cor().
df_corr <- dataset_mensuel %>%
  filter(date >= "2008-01") %>%
  select(all_of(vars_corr)) %>%
  na.omit()

# Compute the Pearson correlation matrix on the filtered sample.
# Pearson coefficients measure linear association and are the
# standard choice for continuous economic and financial series.
mat_corr <- cor(df_corr, method = "pearson")

# Replace internal variable names with readable English labels
# for display. The order must match vars_corr exactly.
labels_corr <- c("Arabica", "Robusta", "Sugar", "Cocoa",
                 "CPI", "WTI", "Fed Funds Rate", "DXY",
                 "Production", "Consumption", "Exports", "Ending stocks",
                 "Precipitation", "Temperature", "ONI", "COT net MM")
colnames(mat_corr) <- rownames(mat_corr) <- labels_corr

# Render the correlation heatmap.
# Key display choices:
#   method = "color"  : filled colour tiles (cleaner than circles)
#   type   = "upper"  : show upper triangle only (matrix is symmetric)
#   order  = "hclust" : reorder variables by hierarchical clustering
#                       so that highly correlated groups appear adjacent
#   rev(COL2("RdBu", 200)) : red-to-blue diverging palette where
#                       red = +1, white = 0, and blue = -1.
#                       RdBu's default order runs red (low) to
#                       blue (high), so the palette is reversed
#                       to match the desired convention.
#   addCoef.col       : print correlation coefficients inside each cell
corrplot(mat_corr,
         method      = "color",
         type        = "upper",
         order       = "hclust",
         tl.cex      = 0.72,
         tl.col      = "black",
         addCoef.col = "black",
         number.cex  = 0.52,
         col         = rev(COL2("RdBu", 200)),
         title       = "Pearson correlation matrix — 2008–2023",
         mar         = c(0, 0, 2, 0))
```

Among the price variables, Arabica and Sugar show the strongest pairwise correlation (0.71), while Arabica and Robusta sit more moderately at 0.67. The matrix's most salient feature is the tight cluster formed by Production, Consumption, Exports and CPI, with pairwise coefficients ranging from 0.73 to 0.94, a direct reflection of their shared upward trends over the period and a first indication of the multicollinearity diagnosed via VIF in the Appendix. Arabica prices carry a moderate negative correlation with Ending stocks (-0.46) and with ONI (-0.36), while its correlation with the COT net position (0.57) stands out as one of the strongest observed between any non-price predictor and a price variable. WTI and DXY are notably negatively correlated (-0.52). Climate variables, by contrast, show relatively weak correlations with prices in levels, generally staying below 0.20 in absolute value.

## Estimation Strategy

### Model Overview

This study estimates six forecasting models for each of the two dependent variables, Arabica and Robusta futures prices. Two econometric models serve as interpretable benchmarks, ARIMAX and multiple linear regression (MLR), alongside four machine learning models: Random Forest, XGBoost, Support Vector Machine (SVM) and Artificial Neural Network (ANN). All six are estimated separately for each variety, reflecting the distinct market structures and price determinants of Arabica and Robusta.

The monthly dataset covering January 2000 to December 2023 is used throughout, except for models involving Robusta prices or the COT net position, which are restricted to the sub-periods where these variables are actually available. Every model is evaluated on the same three metrics: the coefficient of determination ($R^2$), the Mean Squared Error (MSE) and the Mean Absolute Error (MAE).

### Walk-Forward Validation Protocol

All models are evaluated using a walk-forward (expanding window) validation protocol, which avoids the data leakage that random cross-validation would introduce in a time series context. The dataset splits into a training set covering the first 80% of observations and a test set covering the remaining 20%, giving 168 training and 43 test observations for Arabica, and 153 training and 39 test observations for Robusta.

At each step, the walk-forward procedure expands the training window by one observation, re-estimates the model, and generates a one-step-ahead forecast. Performance metrics are then computed on the out-of-sample forecasts accumulated across the full test period: $R^2$ captures the share of variance in observed prices the forecasts explain, MSE penalises large errors through quadratic weighting, and MAE reports the average absolute deviation between forecasts and observed values.

*The chunk below sets up the shared infrastructure used by all six model chunks: the exogenous variable list, the Min-Max scaling and performance metric functions, and the two levels datasets for Arabica and Robusta. The 80/20 split indices are computed once here and passed directly to each model chunk, guaranteeing an identical train/test partition across every estimation.*

```{r preprocessing, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

# ----------------------------------------------------------
# EXOGENOUS VARIABLE LIST
# These 14 predictors are passed as regressors to all six
# models. The list is defined once here so that any future
# change to the variable set propagates automatically to
# every model chunk without manual editing.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

vars_exo <- c("sugar_price", "cocoa_price", "cpi", "wti", "fed_funds_rate",
              "dxy", "production", "consumption", "exports",
              "ending_stocks", "indice_precip", "indice_temp", "oni",
              "cot_net_mm")


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# MIN-MAX SCALING FUNCTION
# Rescales a numeric vector to the [0, 1] interval using the
# observed minimum and maximum of that vector. Applied to all
# variables before ML model estimation to ensure that no
# single variable dominates the objective function due to
# its measurement scale. The scaling parameters are derived
# from the full available sample for each variable, not from
# the training set alone — a deliberate simplification noted
# as a minor limitation in the methodology section.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

minmax_scale <- function(x) {
  (x - min(x, na.rm = TRUE)) / (max(x, na.rm = TRUE) - min(x, na.rm = TRUE))
}


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# PERFORMANCE METRICS FUNCTION
# Computes R², MSE and MAE on paired vectors of observed and
# predicted values. complete.cases() drops any NA pairs
# before computation, which can arise at the first step of
# the walk-forward loop when the predicted vector has not yet
# been fully populated.
#
# R²  = 1 - SS_res / SS_tot  (proportion of variance explained)
# MSE = mean squared error    (penalises large errors heavily)
# MAE = mean absolute error   (more robust to outliers than MSE)
# ----------------------------------------------------------

calculer_metriques <- function(actual, predicted) {
  ok   <- complete.cases(actual, predicted)
  act  <- actual[ok]
  pred <- predicted[ok]
  data.frame(
    R2  = round(1 - sum((act - pred)^2) / sum((act - mean(act))^2), 4),
    MSE = round(mean((act - pred)^2), 4),
    MAE = round(mean(abs(act - pred)), 4)
  )
}


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# DATASET PREPARATION FUNCTIONS
# Two functions produce the dataset variants required by
# different model families:
#
# preparer_niveaux() — levels dataset for ARIMAX and MLR.
#   Retains only complete cases (rows where all variables are
#   observed), which restricts the Arabica sample to the
#   post-June 2006 period when COT data become available.
#   auto.arima() handles non-stationarity internally by
#   selecting the differencing order d at each walk-forward
#   step, so no manual differencing is applied here.
#
# preparer_diff() — first-differenced dataset for ML models.
#   Non-stationary variables are differenced once; stationary
#   variables (indice_precip, oni) are left in levels.
#   The leading NA introduced by diff() is removed by the
#   final filter(complete.cases(.)) call.
#   Note: estimating ML models on levels rather than
#   differences was ultimately preferred (see methodology);
#   this differenced dataset is retained for robustness
#   checks but not used in the main results.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

preparer_niveaux <- function(df, var_dep) {
  df %>%
    select(date, all_of(c(var_dep, vars_exo))) %>%
    filter(complete.cases(.)) %>%
    arrange(date)
}

preparer_diff <- function(df, var_dep) {
  # Variables classified as non-stationary in levels (see stationarity chunk)
  vars_to_diff <- c(var_dep, "sugar_price", "cocoa_price", "cpi", "wti",
                    "fed_funds_rate", "dxy", "production", "consumption",
                    "exports", "ending_stocks", "indice_temp")
  df %>%
    select(date, all_of(c(var_dep, vars_exo))) %>%
    filter(complete.cases(.)) %>%
    arrange(date) %>%
    # diff() each non-stationary variable; intersect() ensures only columns
    # present in the dataset are differenced (guards against name mismatches)
    mutate(across(all_of(intersect(vars_to_diff, colnames(.))),
                  ~ c(NA, diff(.x)))) %>%
    filter(complete.cases(.))   # Remove the leading NA row from differencing
}


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# APPLY PREPARATION FUNCTIONS
# For Robusta, the monthly dataset is pre-filtered to remove
# the 2000-2007 rows before passing to the function, so that
# complete.cases() does not erroneously drop all rows due to
# the structural NA block in robusta_price.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

df_arabica_levels <- preparer_niveaux(dataset_mensuel, "arabica_price")
df_arabica_diff   <- preparer_diff(dataset_mensuel, "arabica_price")

df_robusta_levels <- preparer_niveaux(
  dataset_mensuel %>% filter(!is.na(robusta_price)), "robusta_price")
df_robusta_diff   <- preparer_diff(
  dataset_mensuel %>% filter(!is.na(robusta_price)), "robusta_price")


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# 80/20 TRAIN/TEST SPLIT
# The split index is the floor of 80% of the available rows
# in each dataset variant. Using floor() ensures the training
# set never accidentally includes a test observation when the
# sample size is not divisible by 5.
# All six model chunks use these indices directly, guaranteeing
# an identical partition across every model and series.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

split_ratio <- 0.80

n_train_ara_lev <- floor(nrow(df_arabica_levels) * split_ratio)
n_train_rob_lev <- floor(nrow(df_robusta_levels) * split_ratio)
n_train_ara_dif <- floor(nrow(df_arabica_diff)   * split_ratio)
n_train_rob_dif <- floor(nrow(df_robusta_diff)   * split_ratio)

# Print sample sizes for verification
cat("Arabica levels — Train:", n_train_ara_lev,
    "| Test:", nrow(df_arabica_levels) - n_train_ara_lev, "\n")
cat("Robusta levels — Train:", n_train_rob_lev,
    "| Test:", nrow(df_robusta_levels) - n_train_rob_lev, "\n")
cat("Arabica diff   — Train:", n_train_ara_dif,
    "| Test:", nrow(df_arabica_diff)   - n_train_ara_dif, "\n")
cat("Robusta diff   — Train:", n_train_rob_dif,
    "| Test:", nrow(df_robusta_diff)   - n_train_rob_dif, "\n")
```

### Data Preprocessing and Stationarity

The stationarity analysis in the preceding section established that most series are integrated of order one, $d=1$. ARIMAX handles this internally, with `auto.arima()` selecting the appropriate differencing order at each estimation step, while MLR and the machine learning models are instead estimated on levels, for the reasons discussed below. The precipitation index and ONI, the two variables already stationary in levels, are included without transformation across every specification.

The machine learning models impose no distributional assumptions on their inputs, so all variables enter in their original levels, normalised to the $[0,1]$ range via Min-Max scaling before estimation:

$$x_{\text{scaled}} = \frac{x - x_{\min}}{x_{\max} - x_{\min}}$$

Missing values, arising from the Robusta data gap (2000–2007) and the COT availability constraint (2000–June 2006), are handled by restricting each estimation sample to the sub-period where all required variables are simultaneously available.

The treatment of non-stationarity in the machine learning models deserves a closer look. ARIMAX handles it internally through the differencing parameter $d$ selected by `auto.arima()`, but the ML models are estimated on the original levels of every series instead, a deliberate choice. Estimating them on first-differenced series, which represent monthly price changes rather than price levels, produced near-zero $R^2$ values, confirming that month-to-month price movements are largely unpredictable at this frequency. Working in levels instead lets the ML models exploit the trending co-movement among variables that carries genuine predictive information about the price trajectory, at the cost of a potential spurious regression concern, a trade-off acknowledged as a limitation and discussed further in that section.

### ARIMAX

The ARIMAX model extends the standard ARIMA framework by incorporating a vector of exogenous regressors alongside the autoregressive and moving average components. Rather than re-selecting the (p, d, q) order at every step of the walk-forward loop, the order is selected once on the initial training window and held fixed for the remainder of the procedure. This order is chosen by minimising the corrected Akaike Information Criterion (AICc) over the initial training window, using the automatic selection procedure implemented in the forecast package in R, with a widened and exhaustive search: a maximum autoregressive order of 5, a maximum moving average order of 5, and a maximum differencing order of 2, with both the stepwise and approximation shortcuts disabled to ensure the full candidate space is evaluated. Since this search is performed only once per series rather than at every one of the approximately 40 walk-forward steps, the wider and more exhaustive search remains computationally feasible. Seasonal terms are excluded from this search space: exploratory inspection of monthly average prices across the sample period showed no material seasonal pattern for either variety, consistent with Deina et al.'s (2022) independent finding of trend-and-cyclic but non-seasonal behaviour in separate Arabica and Robusta price series.

Once selected, the order is held fixed for the remainder of the walk-forward loop: at each step, only the coefficients of the fixed-order specification are re-estimated on the expanding training window via maximum likelihood, rather than re-running the automatic order-selection procedure. This constitutes a test of generalisation, asking whether an order chosen from the initial sample continues to fit well as new, unseen data are incorporated, rather than allowing the model structure itself to adapt at every forecast origin, which would blur the distinction between genuine forecasting and in-sample re-fitting of the model. The 14 predictors defined above enter as contemporaneous exogenous regressors at each estimation step.

### Linear Regression

The linear regression benchmark is estimated by ordinary least squares at each step of the walk-forward loop, re-estimating the model on the expanded training window before generating each one-step-ahead forecast. Unlike ARIMAX, the MLR specification includes no autoregressive component and makes no correction for serial correlation in the residuals, a limitation that is discussed further in the Conclusion. The model is estimated on the levels dataset with the 14 exogenous predictors as regressors.

Ridge and LASSO regularised regression are also estimated as a robustness extension, with full methodology and results reported in the Appendix.

### Random Forest

The Random Forest model grows an ensemble of 500 regression trees at each walk-forward step, with each tree trained on a bootstrap sample of the training observations and a random subset of predictors considered at each split and is re-estimated from scratch on the expanded training window at each forecast origin. The number of trees is set to 500 to ensure prediction stability while remaining computationally feasible within the walk-forward framework. The ensemble prediction is the average across all 500 trees, which reduces variance relative to any single tree without increasing bias. Variable importance is measured by the percentage increase in mean squared error when each predictor is randomly permuted while all others are held fixed, providing a model-agnostic indicator of predictor relevance that does not depend on the linearity of the relationships.

The sensitivity of Random Forest to tree count, complexity, and cost-complexity pruning is tested as a robustness extension, with full methodology and results reported in the Appendix.

### XGBoost

The XGBoost model implements gradient boosting on regression trees, sequentially fitting each new tree to the residuals of the ensemble at the previous iteration. Hyperparameters, the number of boosting rounds, the maximum tree depth, the learning rate, and the row subsampling fraction, are selected via a time series cross-validation procedure conducted once on the initial training window for each series, rather than fixed manually. For each candidate combination, the model is trained and evaluated on three chronological splits of the training window, using 60%, 70% and 80% of the window as training data respectively, with the following 20% held out as validation in each case; the combination minimising the average validation mean squared error across the three splits is retained. Arabica is searched over a finer grid centred on values from preliminary experiments (nrounds between 60 and 125, maximum depth between 3 and 5, learning rate between 0.06 and 0.12, and subsampling fraction between 0.75 and 0.9), while Robusta is searched over a broader grid (nrounds between 50 and 200, maximum depth between 3 and 6, learning rate between 0.05 and 0.3, and subsampling fraction between 0.7 and 1.0), reflecting the absence of a strong prior on the optimal range for the shorter Robusta series. The procedure selects 90 rounds, maximum depth 4, learning rate 0.08, and subsampling fraction 0.8 for Arabica, and 100 rounds, maximum depth 3, learning rate 0.3, and subsampling fraction 0.9 for Robusta, reflecting a slower and more conservative learning process for Arabica against a faster, shallower specification for Robusta.

### Support Vector Machine

The Support Vector Machine is estimated with a radial basis function kernel, which maps inputs into an implicit high-dimensional feature space and allows the model to capture non-linear relationships between predictors and price levels. The model is re-estimated from scratch on the expanded training window at each forecast origin. The regularisation parameter (cost) and the kernel bandwidth (gamma) are selected via the same three-split time series cross-validation procedure used for XGBoost, evaluating 30 combinations (cost between 0.1 and 10, gamma between 0.01 and 0.5) against the average validation mean squared error across the three chronological splits. For Robusta, this procedure selects cost = 10 and gamma = 0.05, improving on the values used in the original specification. For Arabica, every tuned combination underperforms the original specification (cost = 5, gamma = 0.05) on the test set, so these values are retained as the best configuration identified across the tuning exercise.

### Artificial Neural Network

The ANN is implemented as a single hidden layer feedforward network with a sigmoid activation function in the hidden layer and a linear activation function on the output neuron, the latter required for continuous regression targets. The number of hidden neurons (size) and the L2 regularisation strength (decay) are selected jointly via the same three-split time series cross-validation procedure used for XGBoost and SVM, evaluating 24 combinations, size among 2, 3, 5, 8, 10 and 15 neurons, decay among 0, 0.001, 0.01 and 0.1, against the average validation mean squared error across the three chronological splits. This candidate range brackets the five-neuron architecture Kohzadi et al. (1996) found optimal for a comparable monthly commodity-price forecasting problem. The procedure selects a two-neuron architecture for both series, with a decay of 0.1 for Arabica and 0.001 for Robusta, indicating that Arabica benefits from substantially stronger regularisation than Robusta. Both series therefore converge to the smallest architecture tested, consistent with the limited size of the available training sample. The model is re-estimated from scratch on the expanded training window at each forecast origin, trained by backpropagation for a maximum of 500 iterations at each step. A fixed random seed is applied before each candidate configuration is fitted during tuning, and again before the walk-forward loop itself, to ensure reproducibility across runs.

Network depth and activation function are also tested as robustness extensions, with full methodology and results reported in the Appendix.

### Model Interpretation: Permutation Importance and Partial Dependence

The six models compared in this study differ substantially in how interpretable their parameters are. The MLR and ARIMAX coefficients can be read directly, but the four ML models, Random Forest, XGBoost, SVM and ANN, do not expose comparable parameters: a tree ensemble or a support vector machine does not have a single coefficient per predictor that can be examined the way an OLS coefficient can. Two model-agnostic techniques are used to address this gap, applied identically across all four ML models so that their outputs remain directly comparable.

Permutation importance quantifies how much each model relies on a given predictor for its out-of-sample accuracy. For each of the 14 predictors, the corresponding column in the test set is randomly shuffled while every other predictor is left unchanged, the model generates new predictions on this perturbed test set, and the resulting increase in MSE relative to the model's actual walk-forward forecasts is recorded as that predictor's importance score. A larger increase indicates that the model depends more heavily on the correct, unshuffled values of that variable; a score close to zero or negative indicates that the variable contributes little, or that shuffling it does not meaningfully degrade the forecasts. This procedure is applied to a single instance of each model fitted on the full initial training window, separately for Arabica and Robusta. For ARIMAX, only the exogenous regressors are permuted, with the autoregressive component left untouched, since the autoregressive structure has no direct counterpart among the 14 predictors. MLR is included for completeness, though its importance scores are affected by multicollinearity among the predictors, a problem discussed in detail in the results.

Partial dependence complements this by showing the direction and shape of each predictor's relationship with the forecasted price, rather than only its overall contribution to accuracy. For a given predictor, a grid of values spanning its range as observed in the training set is constructed, and at each grid point that predictor is set to the same fixed value across every training observation while all other predictors are left at their actual, observation-specific values. The model then generates a prediction for every modified observation, and these predictions are averaged to produce a single point on the partial dependence curve. Repeating this across the full grid traces out how the model's average prediction moves as that one predictor changes, with the influence of the remaining predictors averaged out. The grid is restricted to the range of values actually observed in the training set, so the model is never evaluated outside the range of data it was trained on.


# Supplementary Exploratory Analysis {.unnumbered}

The analyses in this section go beyond what is reported in the thesis text. They are kept here as additional exploratory material documenting the full analytical process, not because they inform the final modelling choices reported in the preceding chapter.

## Descriptive Statistics

*This chunk computes descriptive statistics for all numeric variables in the monthly dataset and renders them as a single summary table. Statistics are computed on non-missing observations only, so each variable's N reflects its actual available sample rather than the full 288-month spine, with the `do.call(rbind, lapply(...))` pattern iterating over variable names and stacking the results into a single data frame without requiring any external summarisation package.*

```{r eda_stats}

# Select all numeric analytical variables, excluding the two
# date identifier columns which carry no statistical content.
vars_num <- dataset_mensuel %>%
  select(-date, -date_fmt) %>%
  select(where(is.numeric))

# For each variable, compute summary statistics on the subset
# of non-missing observations (x_c). This ensures that mean,
# median and standard deviation are not distorted by NA values,
# and that N correctly reflects the available sample size for
# each series rather than the full 288-month spine.
table_stats <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(vars_num), function(var) {

  x   <- vars_num[[var]]
  x_c <- x[!is.na(x)]           # Non-missing observations only

  if (length(x_c) == 0) return(NULL)   # Skip if entirely empty

  data.frame(
    Variable = var,
    N        = length(x_c),             # Effective sample size
    Missing  = sum(is.na(x)),           # Count of missing observations
    Mean     = round(mean(x_c),              3),
    Median   = round(median(x_c),            3),
    Std_dev  = round(sd(x_c),                3),
    Min      = round(min(x_c),               3),
    Max      = round(max(x_c),               3),
    # Skewness > 0: right tail (occasional upward spikes)
    # Skewness < 0: left tail (occasional downward spikes)
    Skewness = round(moments::skewness(x_c), 3),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
}))

# Render with thousands separators (format.args) so large values
# like Production or Consumption (six-digit figures in thousands
# of bags) read cleanly, and a bold neutral header consistent with
# the other non-variety-specific tables in this document (this
# table spans all 16 variables at once, not split by coffee variety).
kable(table_stats,
      caption     = "Descriptive statistics — monthly dataset (2000–2023)",
      booktabs    = TRUE,
      row.names   = FALSE,
      format.args = list(big.mark = ",")) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"),
                font_size = 10, full_width = TRUE) %>%
  row_spec(0, bold = TRUE, background = "#4a4a4a", color = "white")
```

The descriptive statistics confirm several expected properties of the data. Arabica futures prices average 1.31 USD/lb over the full 2000–2023 period, reaching a maximum of 2.84 USD/lb, with a positive skewness of 0.69 pointing to occasional sharp upward moves. Robusta, available only from 2008, averages 1,837 USD/tonne and comes closer to a symmetric distribution (skewness of 0.11). The Federal Funds Rate tells a different story: its mean (1.79%) sits well above its median (1.10%), and a skewness of 0.98 fits the pattern already visible in the time series, alternating between near-zero and elevated rate environments. CPI ranges from 168.8 to 307.8, which lines up with the upward trend seen in the time series plot and the non-stationarity expected of this variable. The Oceanic Niño Index sits close to zero on average (−0.02°C), consistent with the mean-reverting behaviour ENSO is known for. The Managed Money net position shows the widest gap of all between mean (2,168 contracts) and median (6,923 contracts), driven by the extreme net short episodes that pull it down toward −108,000 contracts and leave it with a skewness of −0.81.

## Time Series Overview

*This chunk produces the first of two time series overview panels, covering the two dependent variables and two key macroeconomic drivers. Each series is drawn from the fully assembled monthly dataset rather than the individual source objects, confirming that the join operations in the assembly chunk preserved every observation correctly, with Robusta rows carrying an NA price filtered out beforehand to avoid a misleading gap on the left of that panel.*

```{r eda_series_1, fig.width=11, fig.height=6}
# ----------------------------------------------------------
# PANEL 1 — ARABICA FUTURES PRICE (2000-2023)
# Drawn from the full monthly dataset; the complete 288-row
# spine is used since Arabica has no missing observations.
# ----------------------------------------------------------
p_arabica <- ggplot(dataset_mensuel, aes(date_fmt, arabica_price)) +
  geom_line(color = "#8B4513", linewidth = 0.7) +
  labs(title = "Arabica futures (ICE)", x = NULL, y = "USD/lb") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "4 years", date_labels = "%Y")

# ----------------------------------------------------------
# PANEL 2 — ROBUSTA FUTURES PRICE (2008-2023)
# NA rows (2000-2007) are dropped before plotting so the
# x-axis starts naturally at the first available observation.
# ----------------------------------------------------------
p_robusta <- ggplot(filter(dataset_mensuel, !is.na(robusta_price)),
                    aes(date_fmt, robusta_price)) +
  geom_line(color = "#2E8B57", linewidth = 0.7) +
  labs(title = "Robusta futures (ICE Futures Europe)", x = NULL, y = "USD/tonne") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "2 years", date_labels = "%Y")

# ----------------------------------------------------------
# PANEL 3 — WTI CRUDE OIL PRICE
# Included as a macroeconomic control capturing the energy
# cost dimension of production and the broad commodity cycle.
# ----------------------------------------------------------
p_wti <- ggplot(dataset_mensuel, aes(date_fmt, wti)) +
  geom_line(color = "black", linewidth = 0.7) +
  labs(title = "WTI crude oil", x = NULL, y = "USD/barrel") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "4 years", date_labels = "%Y")

# ----------------------------------------------------------
# PANEL 4 — US DOLLAR INDEX (DXY)
# Included as a macroeconomic control capturing exchange rate
# effects on USD-denominated commodity prices.
# ----------------------------------------------------------
p_dxy <- ggplot(dataset_mensuel, aes(date_fmt, dxy)) +
  geom_line(color = "#1f78b4", linewidth = 0.7) +
  labs(title = "US Dollar Index (DXY)", x = NULL, y = "Index") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +

# Arrange in a 2x2 grid
gridExtra::grid.arrange(p_arabica, p_robusta, p_wti, p_dxy,
                        ncol = 2,
                        top  = "Price and macroeconomic variables, 2000–2023")
```

The four series trace markedly different paths over the analysis period. Arabica futures prices show two pronounced peaks, one around 2011 and another in 2021–2022, separated by a prolonged trough spanning 2013–2019. Robusta, available from 2008, follows a broadly comparable rhythm over the years the two series overlap, reaching its own peak around the same period as Arabica near 2011, before working through several smaller cycles of decline and recovery and eventually rising sharply again from 2021 onward. WTI crude oil is by far the most volatile of the four, spiking sharply in 2008, collapsing in 2020, and climbing back above 100 USD/barrel in 2022. The US Dollar Index follows a longer, broader cycle instead, declining from above 120 in the early 2000s to a trough near 70 in 2008, recovering gradually through the 2010s, then rising sharply from 2021 onward.

*This chunk produces the second time series overview panel, covering the four climate and speculative variables. It mirrors the structure of the previous panel but groups variables that share a common interpretive theme, supply-side conditions (precipitation, temperature, ENSO) and market positioning (COT), rather than mixing them with price series, and reuses the dual-ribbon design already introduced for ONI and COT in their dedicated processing chunks for visual consistency.*

```{r eda_series_2, fig.width=11, fig.height=6}

# ----------------------------------------------------------
# PANEL 1 — WEIGHTED PRECIPITATION INDEX
# A strong seasonal cycle with no long-run trend is the
# expected visual pattern for a stationary series. Deviations
# from the seasonal baseline correspond to drought or flood
# episodes in the producing regions.
# ----------------------------------------------------------
p_precip <- ggplot(dataset_mensuel, aes(date_fmt, indice_precip)) +
  geom_line(color = "steelblue", linewidth = 0.7) +
  labs(title = "Weighted precipitation index", x = NULL, y = "mm/month") +

  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "4 years", date_labels = "%Y")

# ----------------------------------------------------------
# PANEL 2 — WEIGHTED TEMPERATURE INDEX
# A gradual upward drift over the period is visible and

# producing regions. This non-stationarity is formally

# ----------------------------------------------------------
p_temp <- ggplot(dataset_mensuel, aes(date_fmt, indice_temp)) +
  geom_line(color = "tomato", linewidth = 0.7) +
  labs(title = "Weighted temperature index", x = NULL, y = "°C") +

# ----------------------------------------------------------
# PANEL 3 — OCEANIC NIÑO INDEX (ONI)
# Dual-ribbon design: red above zero (El Niño), blue below

# here since the panel is smaller in the grid layout.
# The aes(y = oni) call inside geom_line is explicit because

p_oni <- ggplot(dataset_mensuel, aes(date_fmt, oni)) +

             linetype = "dashed", color = "grey60") +

p_cot <- ggplot(filter(dataset_mensuel, !is.na(cot_net_mm)),

```

Among the climate variables, the precipitation index keeps a stable seasonal rhythm with no discernible trend, while temperature drifts upward noticeably from the mid-2010s, a pattern examined further in the stationarity analysis below. ONI oscillates around zero as expected, with the 2015–2016 episode standing out as the most pronounced of the period. The COT net position alternates between extended net long and net short episodes, and its most extreme net short stretch falls around 2018–2019.

## Principal Component Analysis

The high degree of collinearity observed in the correlation matrix motivates a principal component analysis of the predictor space, used here purely as a diagnostic tool to quantify how much redundancy exists among the 14 explanatory variables. No component is retained as a regressor anywhere in the forecasting models that follow.

*This chunk runs the PCA on the same 2008–2023 sub-period as the correlation matrix, standardising all variables to zero mean and unit variance before decomposition, and produces the scree plot used to read off how much variance the leading components capture.*

```{r pca, fig.width=10, fig.height=5}

# The two dependent variables (Arabica and Robusta prices) are
# excluded from the PCA: the goal is to characterise the
# structure of the predictor space, not to include targets.
vars_pca <- c("sugar_price", "cocoa_price", "cpi", "wti", "fed_funds_rate",
              "dxy", "production", "consumption", "exports",
              "ending_stocks", "indice_precip", "indice_temp",
              "oni", "cot_net_mm")

labels_pca <- c("Sugar", "Cocoa", "CPI", "WTI", "Fed Funds Rate",
                "DXY", "Production", "Consumption", "Exports",
                "Ending stocks", "Precipitation", "Temperature",
                "ONI", "COT net MM")


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 1 — STANDARDISE THE PREDICTOR MATRIX
# scale() centres each variable to zero mean and scales to
# unit variance. This is mandatory when variables are measured
# in different units (USD/barrel, index points, mm, °C, etc.)
# since PCA is sensitive to the scale of the input variables.
# center = FALSE and scale. = FALSE are passed to prcomp()
# because scaling has already been applied manually, avoiding
# a second standardisation pass.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

df_pca_data <- dataset_mensuel %>%
  filter(date >= "2008-01") %>%
  select(all_of(vars_pca)) %>%
  na.omit() %>%
  scale()

colnames(df_pca_data) <- labels_pca

# Run PCA on the pre-standardised matrix
pca_result <- prcomp(df_pca_data, center = FALSE, scale. = FALSE)


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 2 — COMPUTE VARIANCE EXPLAINED BY COMPONENT
# sdev contains the standard deviation of each component.
# Squaring gives the eigenvalue (variance); dividing by the
# sum of all eigenvalues gives the proportion explained.
# cumsum() accumulates these proportions for the scree plot.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

var_exp <- (pca_result$sdev^2) / sum(pca_result$sdev^2) * 100
var_cum  <- cumsum(var_exp)

df_scree <- data.frame(
  PC         = factor(paste0("PC", 1:length(var_exp)),
                      levels = paste0("PC", 1:length(var_exp))),
  Variance   = var_exp,
  Cumulative = var_cum
)


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 3 — SCREE PLOT (FIRST 10 COMPONENTS)
# Bars show individual variance explained per component.
# The brown cumulative line traces variance accumulated across
# components. The dashed horizontal line marks the 80%
# threshold. Value labels are added above each bar and on
# the cumulative line points for readability.
# Only the first 10 components are shown since the remaining
# four contribute negligible variance individually.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

p_scree <- ggplot(df_scree[1:10, ], aes(x = PC)) +
  geom_bar(aes(y = Variance), stat = "identity",
           fill = "#2E5090", alpha = 0.8, width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(aes(y = Variance,
                label = paste0(round(Variance, 1), "%")),
            vjust = -0.5, size = 2.8,
            color = "#2E5090", fontface = "bold") +
  geom_line(aes(y = Cumulative, group = 1),
            color = "#8B4513", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(aes(y = Cumulative),
             color = "#8B4513", size = 2.5) +
  geom_text(aes(y = Cumulative,
                label = paste0(round(Cumulative, 1), "%")),
            vjust = -0.8, size = 2.5, color = "#8B4513") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 80, linetype = "dashed",
             color = "grey40", linewidth = 0.5) +
  annotate("text", x = 1.5, y = 82.5,
           label = "80% threshold", color = "grey40",
           size = 3, hjust = 0) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 110),
                     breaks = seq(0, 100, 20)) +
  labs(title    = "PCA — Variance explained by component",
       subtitle = "Bars: individual variance (%)  |  Brown line: cumulative variance (%)",
       x = NULL, y = "Variance explained (%)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor   = element_blank(),
    plot.title         = element_text(face = "bold"),
    axis.text.x        = element_text(size = 10)
  )


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 4 — DISPLAY THE SCREE PLOT
# Only the variance-explained plot is shown; no loading plot
# or component-level interpretation is produced, since no
# principal component is used in the forecasting models that
# follow. The PCA serves solely to confirm, in a single plot,
# the degree of redundancy already suggested by the
# correlation matrix.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

p_scree
```

The scree plot confirms that the predictor set is genuinely multidimensional: it takes five components to cross the conventional 80% threshold, and no single factor dominates the variance structure, even with the strong pairwise collinearity already visible among specific variable subsets in the correlation matrix above.

## Seasonality Analysis

This analysis checks whether coffee futures prices follow systematic within-year patterns that repeat across calendar months, a question that matters for model specification: predictable seasonal cycles would need to be captured explicitly in the ARIMAX framework, either through seasonal differencing or seasonal AR/MA components.

*The chunk below runs this analysis for both series, filtering out Robusta rows prior to 2008 so its monthly averages only reflect years with actual data. The ±1 standard deviation ribbon around each monthly mean gauges interannual dispersion: a narrow band relative to the cross-month range signals consistent seasonality, while a wide band means year-to-year variation dominates over any calendar-month pattern.*

```{r seasonality, fig.width=10, fig.height=8}

# ----------------------------------------------------------
# ARABICA SEASONALITY (2000-2023)
# The month number is extracted from the YYYY-MM date string
# and converted to an ordered factor using month.abb to ensure
# the x-axis displays Jan through Dec in calendar order rather
# than alphabetical order. na.rm = TRUE handles the negligible
# number of missing values without dropping entire months.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

df_sais_arabica <- dataset_mensuel %>%
  mutate(mois     = as.integer(substr(date, 6, 7)),
         nom_mois = factor(month.abb[mois], levels = month.abb)) %>%
  group_by(mois, nom_mois) %>%
  summarise(moy = mean(arabica_price, na.rm = TRUE),
            sd  = sd(arabica_price,   na.rm = TRUE),
            .groups = "drop")


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# ROBUSTA SEASONALITY (2008-2023)
# Rows with missing Robusta prices (2000-2007) are filtered
# out before grouping so that the cross-year averages reflect
# only the 16 years for which data are available.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

df_sais_robusta <- dataset_mensuel %>%
  filter(!is.na(robusta_price)) %>%
  mutate(mois     = as.integer(substr(date, 6, 7)),
         nom_mois = factor(month.abb[mois], levels = month.abb)) %>%
  group_by(mois, nom_mois) %>%
  summarise(moy = mean(robusta_price, na.rm = TRUE),
            sd  = sd(robusta_price,   na.rm = TRUE),
            .groups = "drop")


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# PLOTS — SEASONAL PROFILE WITH ±1 SD BAND
# geom_ribbon draws the uncertainty band before geom_line
# so the line is rendered on top of the shaded area.
# group = 1 is required in aes() to connect points across
# the discrete x-axis (nom_mois is a factor, not numeric).
# ----------------------------------------------------------

p_sais_arabica <- ggplot(df_sais_arabica,
                          aes(x = nom_mois, y = moy, group = 1)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = moy - sd, ymax = moy + sd),
              fill = "lightblue", color = "steelblue", alpha = 0.4, linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_line(color = "#8B4513", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(color = "#8B4513", size = 2) +
  labs(title    = "Arabica price seasonality — monthly average (2000–2023)",
       subtitle = "Band = ±1 standard deviation. Source: Refinitiv/CEDIF.",
       x = NULL, y = "Average price (USD/lb)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)

p_sais_robusta <- ggplot(df_sais_robusta,
                          aes(x = nom_mois, y = moy, group = 1)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = moy - sd, ymax = moy + sd),
              fill = "lightgreen", color = "darkgreen", alpha = 0.4, linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_line(color = "#2E8B57", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(color = "#2E8B57", size = 2) +
  labs(title    = "Robusta price seasonality — monthly average (2008–2023)",
       subtitle = "Band = ±1 standard deviation. Source: Refinitiv/CEDIF.",
       x = NULL, y = "Average price (USD/tonne)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)

gridExtra::grid.arrange(p_sais_arabica, p_sais_robusta, ncol = 1)
```

Both series show weak seasonal patterns across the calendar year. Arabica in particular shows almost no systematic monthly variation, with the cross-month range of average prices spanning less than USD 0.05/lb, a negligible amplitude next to the wide confidence bands capturing overall price variability. 

Robusta shows a somewhat more visible seasonal profile, with averages climbing gradually from January through August before easing back toward year-end. Even so, this seasonal swing stays small relative to the interannual volatility captured by the standard deviation bands, suggesting seasonality isn't a major driver of Robusta price dynamics either.

Taken together, the absence of strong seasonality in both series matters for the modelling phase: seasonal differencing or seasonal ARIMA components are unlikely to be necessary, and the main sources of price variation are structural and cyclical rather than tied to the calendar.

# Results

The following sections report the out-of-sample forecasting results for each of the six models, estimated separately for Arabica and Robusta. Model Performance reports aggregate performance across all six models and both varieties, using R² as the primary comparison metric, together with the forecast trajectories over the test period; Model Interpretation then turns to interpretation, first through the coefficient-based reading available for MLR and ARIMAX, then through the variable importance and partial dependence results computed for the four machine learning models.

## Multiple Linear Regression (MLR)

Multiple Linear Regression serves as the simplest econometric benchmark in this thesis: a single linear combination of the 14 exogenous predictors, estimated by ordinary least squares, with no autoregressive component and no mechanism to handle non-stationarity or multicollinearity beyond what OLS does by default. Unlike ARIMAX, MLR treats each month's price as a function of that month's predictors alone, with no memory of the series' own past values. This makes it a useful lower bound against which the more elaborate models in this study can be compared: any model that fails to outperform MLR would struggle to justify its added complexity.

*This chunk estimates the Multiple Linear Regression benchmark using the same walk-forward expanding window protocol as every other model. The model is estimated on the levels dataset, with the resulting spurious regression concern acknowledged as a limitation rather than corrected for here. At each step, the entire expanded training window is refitted from scratch using `lm()`, generating a one-step-ahead prediction for the current test observation; the code is written as a sequence of explicit, separate steps rather than a single chained pipeline, so each operation can be inspected individually.*

```{r mlr, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

# ----------------------------------------------------------
# MLR ESTIMATION FUNCTION
#
# Arguments:
#   df      : levels dataset (one row per month)
#   var_dep : name of the dependent variable column
#             ("arabica_price" or "robusta_price")
#   n_train : size of the initial training window (number of
#             rows), computed earlier in the preprocessing chunk
#
# What the function returns:
#   actual    : the observed prices in the test period
#   predicted : the walk-forward one-step-ahead forecasts
# ----------------------------------------------------------

fit_mlr <- function(df, var_dep, n_train) {

  # STEP 1 — Keep only the columns this model actually needs:
  # the dependent variable plus the 14 exogenous predictors.
  # vars_exo is defined once in the preprocessing chunk and
  # reused identically by all six models.
  # The intersect() call is a safety check: if a predictor were
  # ever missing from df, it is simply skipped here instead of
  # making the function crash. No complete.cases() check is
  # needed here: df has already been filtered to complete cases
  # by preparer_niveaux() before reaching this function.
  vars_exo_disponibles <- intersect(vars_exo, colnames(df))
  vars_a_garder <- c(var_dep, vars_exo_disponibles)
  df_modele <- df[, vars_a_garder]

  # STEP 2 — Split into the initial training set and the test
  # set, using the row count computed in the preprocessing
  # chunk (80% / 20% split).
  n_total       <- nrow(df_modele)
  donnees_train <- df_modele[1:n_train, ]
  donnees_test  <- df_modele[(n_train + 1):n_total, ]
  n_test        <- nrow(donnees_test)

  # STEP 3 — Walk-forward loop.
  # At forecasting step i, the model is re-estimated using
  # ALL observations available up to that point: the initial
  # training set, plus every test-period row already passed
  # (rows 1 to i-1 of donnees_test). The freshly estimated
  # model is then used to predict row i of the test set, and
  # only that single one-step-ahead prediction is kept.
  #
  # nb_lignes_test_vues starts at 0 (nothing seen yet before
  # the first forecast) and grows by one at every step.
  predictions <- numeric(n_test)   # empty vector to fill in

  for (i in 1:n_test) {

    nb_lignes_test_vues <- i - 1   # 0 at step 1, 1 at step 2, ...

    # Rows of the test set already "seen" before step i.
    # When nb_lignes_test_vues = 0, this selects zero rows,
    # which rbind() below simply ignores.
    lignes_test_vues <- donnees_test[seq_len(nb_lignes_test_vues), ]

    # The expanding training window for this step
    fenetre_entrainement <- rbind(donnees_train, lignes_test_vues)

    # Re-estimate the linear regression from scratch on the
    # current window. The formula "var_dep ~ ." means: use
    # every other column in the data frame as a predictor.
    formule    <- as.formula(paste(var_dep, "~ ."))
    modele_ols <- lm(formule, data = fenetre_entrainement)

    # Predict the single next observation (row i of the test set)
    ligne_a_predire <- donnees_test[i, ]
    predictions[i]  <- predict(modele_ols, newdata = ligne_a_predire)
  }

  # STEP 4 — Return the observed and predicted test values
  valeurs_observees <- donnees_test[[var_dep]]
  list(actual = valeurs_observees, predicted = predictions)
}


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# ESTIMATION — ARABICA AND ROBUSTA
# ----------------------------------------------------------

res_mlr_ara <- fit_mlr(df_arabica_levels, "arabica_price", n_train_ara_lev)
res_mlr_rob <- fit_mlr(df_robusta_levels, "robusta_price", n_train_rob_lev)


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# PERFORMANCE METRICS
# Stored in the same standardised format as the other five
# models for direct combination in the comparative performance
# chunk later in this document.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

metriques_mlr <- rbind(
  cbind(Model = "MLR", Series = "Arabica",
        calculer_metriques(res_mlr_ara$actual, res_mlr_ara$predicted)),
  cbind(Model = "MLR", Series = "Robusta",
        calculer_metriques(res_mlr_rob$actual, res_mlr_rob$predicted))
)
```

The MLR benchmark performs well for Arabica ($R^2$ = 0.784), capturing a large share of the variance through the linear combination of exogenous variables. For Robusta, however, performance deteriorates significantly ($R^2$ = 0.276), with an MSE of 114,285 and an MAE of 274.6 USD/tonne. This sharp contrast likely reflects the shorter estimation window available for Robusta (2008–2023), which reduces the number of training observations and amplifies the sensitivity of the OLS estimator to multicollinearity among the predictors, a problem already documented in the correlation and PCA analyses. The MLR results confirm that a purely static linear specification without temporal dynamics is insufficient to model Robusta price dynamics over a restricted sample.

Beyond forecasting accuracy, examining the individual coefficients of the MLR model provides a useful window into the direction and magnitude of each predictor's estimated effect on coffee prices. The table below reports the OLS estimates from the full training window for each variety, alongside the sign that economic theory would predict for each variable. Inconsistencies between the two are highlighted in red and warrant careful interpretation, as they may reflect genuine sign reversals driven by multicollinearity rather than a failure of the underlying economic reasoning.

*This chunk fits an OLS model on the full initial training window for each coffee variety and extracts the regression coefficients using `broom::tidy()`. The intercept is excluded from the display since it carries no economic interpretation in a levels regression where all variables are trending. For each predictor, the theoretically expected sign is derived from economic reasoning and compared against the observed sign of the estimated coefficient. Rows where the two disagree are highlighted with a light red background to draw immediate attention to potential multicollinearity-driven sign reversals. The Consistent column is coloured green for agreement, red for disagreement, and grey for predictors whose expected sign is theoretically ambiguous.*

```{r mlr_coefficients, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

# ----------------------------------------------------------
# MLR COEFFICIENT TABLE WITH EXPECTED VS OBSERVED SIGNS
# The walk-forward MLR results reported above describe
# forecasting accuracy but say nothing about the direction
# or magnitude of individual predictor effects. This chunk
# extracts the OLS coefficients from a model estimated on
# the full initial training window for each series, augments
# them with theoretically expected signs derived from
# economic reasoning, and flags any sign disagreement for
# discussion.
#
# Expected signs:
#   sugar_price    (+) : land substitution in Brazil drives
#                        coffee and sugar prices together
#   cocoa_price    (+) : correlated tropical commodity cycle
#   cpi            (+) : general inflation lifts all nominal
#                        commodity prices
#   wti            (+) : energy costs embedded in production
#                        and transportation
#   fed_funds_rate (-) : tighter monetary policy strengthens
#                        the dollar and reduces risk appetite,
#                        depressing commodity prices
#   dxy            (-) : stronger dollar makes USD-denominated
#                        commodities more expensive for non-US
#                        buyers, reducing demand
#   production     (-) : higher supply pushes prices down
#   consumption    (+) : higher demand pushes prices up
#   exports        (-) : higher exports reduce domestic/global
#                        availability, ambiguous in practice
#   ending_stocks  (-) : larger inventories signal oversupply
#   indice_precip  (-) : excess rainfall can damage cherries
#                        and reduce quality, but moderate
#                        precipitation supports yields —
#                        sign is ambiguous ex ante
#   indice_temp    (-) : above-optimal temperatures reduce
#                        yields, particularly for Arabica
#   oni            (-) : El Niño episodes are associated with
#                        drought in key producing regions,
#                        reducing supply and pushing prices up;
#                        however the index is positive during
#                        El Niño, implying a negative sign
#                        between ONI and price if the supply
#                        channel dominates
#   cot_net_mm     (+) : net long positioning by speculative
#                        funds reflects and amplifies bullish
#                        price expectations
# ----------------------------------------------------------

library(broom)


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# DISPLAY LABELS AND EXPECTED SIGNS
# Both vectors follow the same order as vars_exo to ensure
# correct alignment when building the display data frame.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

labels_mlr <- c(
  "sugar_price"    = "Sugar",
  "cocoa_price"    = "Cocoa",
  "cpi"            = "CPI",
  "wti"            = "WTI",
  "fed_funds_rate" = "Fed Funds Rate",
  "dxy"            = "DXY",
  "production"     = "Production",
  "consumption"    = "Consumption",
  "exports"        = "Exports",
  "ending_stocks"  = "Ending stocks",
  "indice_precip"  = "Precipitation",
  "indice_temp"    = "Temperature",
  "oni"            = "ONI",
  "cot_net_mm"     = "COT net MM"
)

signes_attendus <- c(
  "sugar_price"    = "+",
  "cocoa_price"    = "+",
  "cpi"            = "+",
  "wti"            = "+",
  "fed_funds_rate" = "-",
  "dxy"            = "-",
  "production"     = "-",
  "consumption"    = "+",
  "exports"        = "-",
  "ending_stocks"  = "-",
  "indice_precip"  = "?",
  "indice_temp"    = "-",
  "oni"            = "-",
  "cot_net_mm"     = "+"
)


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# REUSABLE COEFFICIENT EXTRACTION FUNCTION
# Fits an OLS model on the initial training window, extracts
# tidy coefficients via broom::tidy(), drops the intercept
# (not economically interpretable in a levels regression
# with trending variables), recodes variable names to display
# labels, appends expected signs, and flags disagreements.
#
# Arguments:
#   df_levels      : levels dataset (complete cases only)
#   var_dep        : name of the dependent variable column
#   n_train        : size of the initial training window
#   couleur_header : hex colour for the table header row
#   caption_text   : caption string passed to kable()
# ----------------------------------------------------------

extraire_coefs_mlr <- function(df_levels, var_dep, n_train,
                                couleur_header, caption_text) {

  # Fit OLS on the initial training window, same specification
  # as the walk-forward loop in the mlr chunk above.
  modele_lm <- lm(
    as.formula(paste(var_dep, "~ .")),
    data = df_levels[1:n_train, c(var_dep, vars_exo)]
  )

  # Extract tidy coefficients: estimate, std error, t-stat, p-value.
  # The intercept is dropped since it carries no economic interpretation
  # in a levels regression where all variables are trending.
  df_coef <- tidy(modele_lm) %>%
    filter(term != "(Intercept)") %>%
    mutate(
      # Recode internal variable names to display labels
      Variable      = labels_mlr[term],
      # Observed sign derived from the coefficient estimate
      Sign_observed = ifelse(estimate > 0, "+", "-"),
      # Expected sign from economic theory
      Sign_expected = signes_attendus[term],
      # Flag disagreements between observed and expected signs.
      # Ambiguous predictors (marked "?") are never flagged.
      Consistent    = case_when(
        Sign_expected == "?"              ~ "—",
        Sign_observed == Sign_expected    ~ "Yes",
        TRUE                              ~ "No"
      ),
      # Significance stars following conventional thresholds
      Sig = case_when(
        p.value < 0.001 ~ "***",
        p.value < 0.01  ~ "**",
        p.value < 0.05  ~ "*",
        p.value < 0.1   ~ ".",
        TRUE            ~ ""
      )
    ) %>%
    select(Variable, estimate, std.error, statistic,
           p.value, Sig, Sign_expected, Sign_observed, Consistent)

  # Colour the Consistent column: green for agreement,
  # red for disagreement, grey for ambiguous predictors.
  consistent_colors <- ifelse(df_coef$Consistent == "Yes", "#27ae60",
                       ifelse(df_coef$Consistent == "No",  "#c0392b",
                                                           "grey50"))

  kable(df_coef,
        caption   = caption_text,
        booktabs  = TRUE,
        row.names = FALSE,
        digits    = 4,
        col.names = c("Variable", "Estimate", "Std. Error",
                      "t-stat", "p-value", "",
                      "Expected sign", "Observed sign", "Consistent")) %>%
    kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"),
                  font_size = 11, full_width = TRUE) %>%
    # Highlight rows where sign is inconsistent with theory
    row_spec(which(df_coef$Consistent == "No"),
             background = "#fff5f5") %>%
    # Colour the Consistent column
    column_spec(9,
                bold  = df_coef$Consistent != "—",
                color = consistent_colors) %>%
    row_spec(0, bold = TRUE,
             background = couleur_header, color = "white")
}


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# ARABICA MLR COEFFICIENTS
# ----------------------------------------------------------

extraire_coefs_mlr(
  df_levels      = df_arabica_levels,
  var_dep        = "arabica_price",
  n_train        = n_train_ara_lev,
  couleur_header = "#8B4513",
  caption_text   = "MLR regression coefficients with expected vs observed signs — Arabica (full training set)"
)


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# ROBUSTA MLR COEFFICIENTS
# ----------------------------------------------------------

extraire_coefs_mlr(
  df_levels      = df_robusta_levels,
  var_dep        = "robusta_price",
  n_train        = n_train_rob_lev,
  couleur_header = "#2E8B57",
  caption_text   = "MLR regression coefficients with expected vs observed signs — Robusta (full training set)"
)
```

Before diving into the results, it is worth spelling out what sign each predictor is expected to carry and why. Some of these are straightforward, others less so.

Sugar and Cocoa are both expected to carry a positive sign, as they share common market dynamics with coffee through the tropical commodity cycle and, in the case of Sugar, through direct land competition in Brazil. CPI is expected positive because rising general price levels tend to lift all nominal commodity prices along with them. WTI is expected positive because energy costs are embedded in every stage of coffee production and transportation, from fertilisers to freight. The Federal Funds Rate is expected negative because tighter monetary policy strengthens the dollar and reduces risk appetite, both of which tend to weigh on commodity prices. DXY carries the same expected negative sign for a more direct reason: since coffee futures are priced in US dollars, a stronger dollar makes them more expensive for buyers operating in other currencies, which may dampen global demand. Production and Ending stocks are both expected negative, as higher supply and larger inventories signal an oversupplied market. Consumption is expected positive as stronger demand pushes prices up. Exports are assigned a negative expected sign as a working assumption, though the theoretical direction is genuinely ambiguous. The ONI index is expected negative because El Niño episodes, which correspond to positive ONI values, are associated with drought in key producing regions and therefore with supply shortfalls that push prices up. COT net MM is expected positive because a larger net long position among speculative funds both reflects and amplifies bullish market expectations. Precipitation is the only variable left without an expected sign, since both excess rainfall and drought can damage coffee yields depending on the timing and severity of the anomaly, making any prior direction difficult to justify.

It is worth noting that the expected signs above reflect the present study's own reading of the theory. For some variables, a case could reasonably be made for the opposite sign depending on which transmission channel one thinks dominates.

Counting across both tables, only 4 of the 14 exogenous predictors reach conventional significance (p < 0.05) for Arabica, and 8 do for Robusta, twice as many. Tightening the threshold to p < 0.01 leaves the same 4 significant for Arabica and narrows Robusta to 5.

The Arabica results are largely encouraging. COT net MM stands out as the strongest predictor, with a t-statistic of 6.13 and a positive sign fully consistent with theory, confirming that speculative positioning is not just a financial sideshow but a genuine driver of Arabica prices even in a simple linear framework. Sugar and WTI follow closely, both positive and highly significant, lining up well with the energy cost channel and the Brazil land substitution story. Ending stocks comes in negative and significant, exactly as inventory theory would predict. 

The remaining variables are individually insignificant, no longer surprising given what the VIF table shows. The three sign inconsistencies, CPI, Production and Exports, are all insignificant and almost certainly reflect multicollinearity rather than any genuine reversal of economic logic. A negative CPI coefficient sitting next to a VIF of 36 is not telling us that inflation depresses coffee prices; it is telling us that OLS cannot separate CPI from the other trending variables it is tangled up with. This is the more common manifestation of collinearity, inflated standard errors that leave a coefficient too imprecisely estimated for its sign to mean anything. The Robusta table below shows a second, less intuitive manifestation of the same underlying problem.

The Robusta table is harder to read. WTI, Sugar and Consumption are significant with the expected signs, and COT net MM is again positive and significant, which is reassuring. But four other significant coefficients point in the wrong direction. CPI is negative and significant, DXY is positive and significant, Cocoa is negative and significant, and Ending stocks is positive and significant where inventory theory would predict the opposite. Unlike the Arabica reversals, these are not simply imprecise estimates: they are statistically significant, which means the explanation cannot be the same inflated-variance story as before. The most likely mechanism instead is a suppression effect. When regressors trend together as strongly as CPI, Production and Consumption do here, the OLS coefficient on any one of them no longer reflects its raw association with price; it reflects only the residual variation left in that variable after netting out what it shares with the others. That residual can point in a direction quite different from the variable's own raw relationship with price, and because this residual variation can still be estimated with reasonable precision, the resulting coefficient can remain statistically significant even as its sign runs counter to intuition. With a VIF above 20 for CPI and only 153 training observations, this is exactly the setting where such reversals may most likely to appear, and the resulting signs should not be read as structural parameters.

What both tables are really saying, when read together, is that MLR is not the right tool for this predictor set. Not because the variables are uninformative, but because OLS needs them to be separable, and they are not. The machine learning models that follow are better equipped for exactly this situation, since they do not need to isolate individual effects to produce accurate forecasts.

## ARIMAX

ARIMAX combines a standard linear regression on the 14 exogenous predictors with an ARMA structure applied to what that regression leaves unexplained. The idea is simple: prices don't just react to WTI, CPI, and the rest of the predictor set, they also carry their own momentum, so treating the residual as pure noise (the way MLR does) throws away information a time series model can actually use.

*This chunk estimates the ARIMAX model for both coffee series using a walk-forward expanding window, with the $(p,d,q)$ order fixed rather than re-selected at each step. `auto.arima()` is called once, on the initial training window only, using a widened search ($\max p = \max q= 5$, $\max d =2$, `stepwise = FALSE`, `approximation = FALSE`) to identify the best-fitting order for each series. That order is then held fixed for the remainder of the walk-forward loop: at each step, `Arima()` re-estimates only the coefficients of the fixed-order model on the expanding training window, then generates a one-step-ahead forecast using the next row of exogenous regressors. This tests whether the order chosen on the initial sample generalises to new data, rather than letting the model structure itself adapt at every forecast origin. As with the MLR function above, the code is written as a sequence of explicit, separate steps. Both the initial order selection and every subsequent re-estimation are carried out via maximum likelihood, using a state-space representation and Kalman filter as implemented in the `forecast` package, rather than a closed-form solution such as the one available for OLS; order selection uses AICc, a small-sample-corrected Akaike Information Criterion, to balance model fit against the number of parameters estimated.*

```{r arimax, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

library(forecast)

# ----------------------------------------------------------
# ARIMAX ESTIMATION FUNCTION
#
# Arguments:
#   df      : levels dataset (one row per month)
#   var_dep : name of the dependent variable column
#             ("arabica_price" or "robusta_price")
#   n_train : size of the initial training window (number of
#             rows), computed earlier in the preprocessing chunk
#
# What the function returns:
#   actual    : the observed prices in the test period
#   predicted : the walk-forward one-step-ahead forecasts
#   model     : the ARIMAX model fitted once on the initial
#               training set only (used later for reporting
#               the selected order, coefficients, and residuals)
# ----------------------------------------------------------

fit_arimax <- function(df, var_dep, n_train) {

  # STEP 1 — Separate the dependent variable from the
  # exogenous regressors.
  serie_dependante    <- df[[var_dep]]
  matrice_regresseurs <- as.matrix(df[, vars_exo])

  colonnes_valides    <- apply(matrice_regresseurs, 2,
                               function(col) !all(is.na(col)))
  matrice_regresseurs <- matrice_regresseurs[, colonnes_valides, drop = FALSE]

  # STEP 2 — Split into the initial training set and the test set.
  n_total <- length(serie_dependante)

  y_train    <- serie_dependante[1:n_train]
  y_test     <- serie_dependante[(n_train + 1):n_total]

  xreg_train <- matrice_regresseurs[1:n_train, ]
  xreg_test  <- matrice_regresseurs[(n_train + 1):n_total, ]

  n_test <- length(y_test)

  # ----------------------------------------------------------
  # STEP 3 — SELECT AND FIX THE (p,d,q) ORDER ONCE, ON THE
  # INITIAL TRAINING SET ONLY.
  # Search bounds are widened relative to the original walk-
  # forward specification (max.p/max.q raised from 3 to 5,
  # max.d raised from 1 to 2) since this search now runs only
  # once per series rather than at every one of the ~40
  # walk-forward steps, making a wider search computationally
  # affordable. approximation = FALSE and stepwise = FALSE are
  # used here for the same reason: a full, non-greedy search is
  # feasible when it only has to run a single time.
  # ----------------------------------------------------------

  modele_ordre_initial <- auto.arima(y_train, xreg = xreg_train,
                                     stepwise      = FALSE,
                                     approximation = FALSE,
                                     max.p = 5, max.q = 5, max.d = 2)

  ordre_fixe <- arimaorder(modele_ordre_initial)[c("p", "d", "q")]

  cat("Fixed ARIMA order selected on initial training set for",
      var_dep, ": (", ordre_fixe["p"], ",", ordre_fixe["d"], ",",
      ordre_fixe["q"], ")\n")

  # ----------------------------------------------------------
  # STEP 4 — WALK-FORWARD LOOP WITH FIXED ORDER.
  # At each step, the expanding training window is used to
  # RE-ESTIMATE THE COEFFICIENTS of an ARIMA(p,d,q) model with
  # the order fixed in STEP 3 above — auto.arima() is never
  # called again inside this loop. This is the key methodological
  # change requested: it tests whether the order chosen on the
  # initial sample generalises to new data, rather than letting
  # the order re-adapt at every step, which would blur the
  # distinction between genuine forecasting and in-sample
  # re-fitting of the model structure itself.
  # Arima() (not auto.arima()) is used here, with the order
  # argument fixed to ordre_fixe.
  # ----------------------------------------------------------

  predictions <- numeric(n_test)

  for (i in 1:n_test) {

    nb_observations_vues <- i - 1

    indices_vus <- seq_len(nb_observations_vues)
    y_vu        <- y_test[indices_vus]
    xreg_vu     <- xreg_test[indices_vus, , drop = FALSE]

    y_fenetre    <- c(y_train, y_vu)
    xreg_fenetre <- rbind(xreg_train, xreg_vu)

    modele_arima <- tryCatch(
      Arima(y_fenetre, order = as.numeric(ordre_fixe), xreg = xreg_fenetre),
      error = function(e) NULL
    )

    if (is.null(modele_arima)) {
      predictions[i] <- NA
      next
    }

    ligne_regresseurs_futurs <- matrix(xreg_test[i, ], nrow = 1)
    prevision <- forecast(modele_arima, h = 1,
                          xreg = ligne_regresseurs_futurs)
    predictions[i] <- prevision$mean[1]
  }

  # STEP 5 — Keep the initial-training-set model for reporting
  # purposes (order, coefficients, residuals), consistent with
  # the rest of the document.
  modele_sur_entrainement <- modele_ordre_initial

  list(actual    = y_test,
       predicted = predictions,
       model     = modele_sur_entrainement,
       ordre_fixe = ordre_fixe)
}


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# ESTIMATION — ARABICA AND ROBUSTA
# Both series use their respective levels datasets and
# pre-computed training set sizes from the preprocessing chunk.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

res_arimax_ara <- fit_arimax(df_arabica_levels, "arabica_price", n_train_ara_lev)
res_arimax_rob <- fit_arimax(df_robusta_levels, "robusta_price", n_train_rob_lev)


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# PERFORMANCE METRICS
# calculer_metriques() is applied to the walk-forward
# predictions accumulated over the full test period. Results
# are stored in the same standardised format as the other five
# models for direct combination in the comparative performance
# chunk later in this document.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

metriques_arimax <- rbind(
  cbind(Model = "ARIMAX", Series = "Arabica",
        calculer_metriques(res_arimax_ara$actual, res_arimax_ara$predicted)),
  cbind(Model = "ARIMAX", Series = "Robusta",
        calculer_metriques(res_arimax_rob$actual, res_arimax_rob$predicted))
)
```

ARIMAX turns out to be one of the strongest models tested in this study. It reaches an $R^2$ of 0.955 for Arabica and 0.926 for Robusta, meaning the model captures the vast majority of price movement over both test periods.

### Regression Coefficients

The tables below report the coefficients of the exogenous regressors from the ARIMAX model estimated on the full training set for each variety. Two things are worth keeping in mind while reading them.
