XGBoost, Random Forest and SVM form a second tier, all capturing the broad direction of the price but with a more noticeable lag at turning points, a typical feature of one-step-ahead walk-forward forecasts. Random Forest and MLR in particular compress the peaks and troughs relative to the actual series, producing smoother forecasts that miss the amplitude of short-term movements. SVM tracks the general direction reasonably well but with larger deviations visible around the 2022 peak. The ANN panel is cleaner than in the baseline specification: L2 regularisation has substantially reduced the instability that previously dominated the forecasts, and the model now follows the general price trajectory more consistently, which explains the improvement from 0.453 to 0.728, though it remains the weakest ML model for Arabica.

#### Actual vs Predicted — Robusta

The six panels below show the same comparison for Robusta over its shorter test period. The strong and persistent upward trend that characterises this series from 2022 onward makes it a particularly demanding forecasting exercise, and the plots reveal important differences in how each model handles this kind of sustained price acceleration.

*This chunk produces the equivalent six-panel plot for Robusta. The shorter test period (approximately 39 months) makes the visual comparison more compressed, but the same alignment logic applies. The sharp upward trend visible from 2022 onward is a key diagnostic: models that fail to track this trend will show a pronounced divergence in the right portion of each panel.*

The Robusta plots tell a more varied story than Arabica. ARIMAX is clearly the strongest model, tracking the observed price closely throughout the test period including the sharp acceleration from 2023, consistent with its $R^2$ of 0.926. The 95% confidence interval widens progressively toward the end of the test period, reflecting the growing uncertainty of autoregressive forecasts over longer horizons, but the observed price stays within the band for almost the entire period. MLR fails visibly, with forecasts oscillating erratically and producing large directional errors, which explains its $R^2$ of 0.276. Among the ML models, XGBoost and Random Forest both track the upward trajectory but underestimate the pace of the acceleration from mid-2023 onward. SVM follows the general trend without any particularly notable pattern in its deviations. The ANN remains the most unstable, with visible spikes at several points, though the regularisation has reduced their severity compared to the baseline specification.

#### Forecast Residuals

The residual plots below zoom in on the forecast errors for each model, making it easier to spot any systematic bias or unusual episodes that the trajectory plots might obscure. Within each variety, the y-axis scale is fixed across all panels to allow direct comparison of residual amplitude between models.

*This chunk plots the forecast residuals (predicted minus actual) for each model over the test period. A residual series hovering around zero with no systematic pattern indicates an unbiased model; persistent positive or negative deviations reveal directional bias, while increasing variance over time suggests heteroskedasticity in the forecast errors.*

```{r residuals_plots, fig.width=12, fig.height=5}

df_residuals <- bind_rows(
  df_forecasts_ara %>%
    mutate(residual = predicted - actual,
           series   = "Arabica"),
  df_forecasts_rob %>%
    mutate(residual = predicted - actual,
           series   = "Robusta")
)

  df_residuals %>% filter(series == "Arabica"),

  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed",
             color = "grey40", linewidth = 0.5) +

                  ymax = ifelse(residual > 0, residual, 0)),

  geom_line(color = "#8B4513", linewidth = 0.6) +
  facet_wrap(~ model, ncol = 3, scales = "fixed") +

  theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
  theme(
    strip.text       = element_text(face = "bold", size = 10),
    strip.background = element_rect(fill = "#f5ece6", color = NA),
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "#fafafa", color = NA),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    axis.text.x      = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)
  ) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "1 year", date_labels = "%Y")


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# PLOT 2 — ROBUSTA RESIDUALS
# Fixed y-axis scale across all panels to allow direct
# comparison of residual amplitude between models.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

p_res_rob <- ggplot(
  df_residuals %>% filter(series == "Robusta"),
  aes(x = date, y = residual)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed",
             color = "grey40", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = ifelse(residual > 0, 0, residual),
                  ymax = ifelse(residual > 0, residual, 0)),
              fill = "#2E8B57", alpha = 0.15) +
  geom_line(color = "#2E8B57", linewidth = 0.6) +
  facet_wrap(~ model, ncol = 3, scales = "fixed") +

  theme(
    strip.text       = element_text(face = "bold", size = 10),
    strip.background = element_rect(fill = "#e8f5ec", color = NA),
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "#fafafa", color = NA),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    axis.text.x      = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)
  ) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "1 year", date_labels = "%Y")

p_res_ara
p_res_rob
```

**For Arabica** : Almost all models show a pronounced negative spike just before 2022, reflecting a common failure to anticipate the sharp price peak at that point in the cycle. MLR and ANN overestimate the most at the start of the test period, while other models also show some positive bias early on but to a lesser degree. From late 2022 onward, XGBoost and Random Forest stand out with larger positive residuals than the other models, suggesting they were slow to incorporate the price decline and continued to forecast higher prices than what was actually observed. Beyond these episodes, residuals oscillate reasonably around zero for the remaining models.

**For Robusta** : ARIMAX produces the most well-behaved residuals, oscillating around zero without any persistent directional bias. Random Forest shows two distinct negative episodes: one from mid-2021 to early 2022, and another from late 2022 through 2023. MLR follows a similar pattern but concentrated mostly in 2023, with the largest negative residuals of all models during that period. XGBoost mirrors this pattern but in a less pronounced way, with residuals that dip negative but partially recover more quickly. SVM deviates significantly at times but tends to correct itself faster than the other models when it diverges. The ANN is the most unstable, with residuals that lean predominantly negative and swing sharply in both directions throughout the test period.


For the two econometric models, adjustment quality also extends to the calibration of their 95% prediction intervals.

*This chunk checks what share of actual test-set observations fall inside the 95% prediction intervals already computed above for ARIMAX (`df_ci_ara`, `df_ci_rob`) and MLR (`df_ci_mlr_ara`, `df_ci_mlr_rob`). No new model fitting takes place here.*

```{r prediction_interval_coverage, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

# ----------------------------------------------------------
# EMPIRICAL COVERAGE OF THE 95% PREDICTION INTERVALS
# Uses the lower/upper bounds already computed above for
# ARIMAX (df_ci_ara, df_ci_rob) and MLR (df_ci_mlr_ara,
# df_ci_mlr_rob) to check what share of actual test-set
# observations fall inside each interval. No new model
# fitting takes place in this chunk.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

coverage_arimax_ara <- mean(actual_ara >= df_ci_ara$lower & actual_ara <= df_ci_ara$upper) * 100
coverage_arimax_rob <- mean(actual_rob >= df_ci_rob$lower & actual_rob <= df_ci_rob$upper) * 100
coverage_mlr_ara     <- mean(actual_ara >= df_ci_mlr_ara$lower & actual_ara <= df_ci_mlr_ara$upper) * 100
coverage_mlr_rob     <- mean(actual_rob >= df_ci_mlr_rob$lower & actual_rob <= df_ci_mlr_rob$upper) * 100

cat("95% prediction interval coverage:\n",
    "MLR    - Arabica:", round(coverage_mlr_ara, 1),    "% | Robusta:", round(coverage_mlr_rob, 1),    "%\n",
    "ARIMAX - Arabica:", round(coverage_arimax_ara, 1), "% | Robusta:", round(coverage_arimax_rob, 1), "%\n")
```

Empirical coverage is close to nominal for MLR-Arabica (97.7%) but falls short elsewhere (81.4%-84.6%), a pattern linked to the non-stationarity limitation discussed later in this document.

## Model Interpretation

This section turns from aggregate accuracy to what each model says about the predictors themselves. Econometric Models reads the coefficients of MLR and ARIMAX directly, since both admit a direct economic interpretation, before Variable Importance and Partial Dependence Plots turns to the two techniques used to interpret the four machine learning models instead.

### Econometric Models

Linear Regression and ARIMAX are treated together in this section because their coefficients admit a direct economic reading, unlike the four machine learning models discussed next. The tables below report the MLR and ARIMAX coefficients for the 14 predictors side by side, estimated on the full initial training window for each variety, with statistical significance indicated by conventional significance stars.

*This chunk does not re-estimate anything: it re-extracts the same coefficients already displayed separately for MLR and ARIMAX earlier in this chapter, using the same underlying logic (`tidy()` for MLR, `coef()`/`vcov()` for ARIMAX), and joins the two into a single table per variety so the two sets of estimates can be read side by side, matching the layout used in the written thesis. The original per-model tables above are left untouched.*

```{r econometric_coefficients_merged, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

# ----------------------------------------------------------
# TABLES 4.3/4.4 -- MLR AND ARIMAX COEFFICIENTS SIDE BY SIDE
# Re-extracts the MLR and ARIMAX coefficients using the same
# logic as the extraire_coefs_mlr()/extraire_coefs_arimax()
# functions defined earlier in this chapter, then joins the
# two data frames by Variable so they can be displayed side
# by side in a single table per variety. No re-estimation
# takes place: this is purely a display-layer chunk.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

extraire_df_mlr <- function(df_levels, var_dep, n_train) {
  modele_lm <- lm(
    as.formula(paste(var_dep, "~ .")),
    data = df_levels[1:n_train, c(var_dep, vars_exo)]
  )
  tidy(modele_lm) %>%
    filter(term != "(Intercept)") %>%
    transmute(
      Variable = labels_mlr[term],
      MLR_Est  = round(estimate, 4),
      MLR_p    = round(p.value, 4),
      MLR_Sig  = case_when(
        p.value < 0.001 ~ "***",
        p.value < 0.01  ~ "**",
        p.value < 0.05  ~ "*",
        p.value < 0.1   ~ ".",
        TRUE            ~ ""
      )
    )
}

extraire_df_arimax <- function(model) {
  co    <- coef(model)
  se    <- sqrt(diag(vcov(model)))
  tstat <- co / se
  pval  <- 2 * pnorm(abs(tstat), lower.tail = FALSE)

  data.frame(term = names(co), estimate = co, p.value = pval,
             stringsAsFactors = FALSE) %>%
    filter(!grepl("^ar|^ma|^intercept|drift", term, ignore.case = TRUE)) %>%
    transmute(
      Variable   = labels_mlr[term],
      ARIMAX_Est = round(estimate, 4),
      ARIMAX_p   = round(p.value, 4),
      ARIMAX_Sig = case_when(
        p.value < 0.001 ~ "***",
        p.value < 0.01  ~ "**",
        p.value < 0.05  ~ "*",
        p.value < 0.1   ~ ".",
        TRUE            ~ ""
      )
    )
}

construire_table_econometrique <- function(df_levels, var_dep, n_train,
                                            model, couleur_header, caption_text) {
  df_mlr    <- extraire_df_mlr(df_levels, var_dep, n_train)
  df_arimax <- extraire_df_arimax(model)

  df_mlr %>%
    left_join(df_arimax, by = "Variable") %>%
    kable(caption   = caption_text,
          booktabs  = TRUE, row.names = FALSE,
          col.names = c("Variable", "Estimate", "p-value", "Sig.",
                        "Estimate", "p-value", "Sig.")) %>%
    kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"),
                  font_size = 11, full_width = TRUE) %>%
    add_header_above(c(" " = 1, "MLR" = 3, "ARIMAX" = 3)) %>%
    row_spec(0, bold = TRUE, background = couleur_header, color = "white")
}

construire_table_econometrique(
  df_levels      = df_arabica_levels,
  var_dep        = "arabica_price",
  n_train        = n_train_ara_lev,
  model          = res_arimax_ara$model,
  couleur_header = "#8B4513",
  caption_text   = "MLR and ARIMAX regression coefficients — Arabica"
)

construire_table_econometrique(
  df_levels      = df_robusta_levels,
  var_dep        = "robusta_price",
  n_train        = n_train_rob_lev,
  model          = res_arimax_rob$model,
  couleur_header = "#2E8B57",
  caption_text   = "MLR and ARIMAX regression coefficients — Robusta"
)
```

For Arabica, the two models agree on COT net Managed Money and WTI as significant, positively signed predictors, consistent with the expectation that bullish speculative positioning and rising energy costs align with rising coffee prices, and on Sugar, also significant and positively signed under both specifications. Beyond this common ground, the two models diverge: MLR additionally finds Ending stocks significant and negative, consistent with inventory theory, while ARIMAX instead finds the Federal Funds Rate significant and negative. Four of the 14 predictors reach conventional significance under each model, though not entirely the same four. Under MLR, two coefficients carry the wrong sign relative to economic theory, CPI and Production, and both are statistically insignificant.

For Robusta, both models again agree on WTI and COT net Managed Money as significant, positively signed predictors. MLR additionally finds Sugar and Consumption significant with the expected sign, but four further coefficients, CPI, DXY, Cocoa and Ending stocks, are significant with the wrong sign. Under ARIMAX, CPI is significant as well but with the theoretically consistent positive sign, DXY approaches significance at the 10% level with the expected negative sign, and Cocoa and Ending stocks are not significant. This pattern, where several of MLR's wrong-signed Robusta coefficients turn correctly signed or insignificant under ARIMAX, is consistent with ARIMAX's autoregressive component absorbing part of the shared trend among the predictors, reducing the burden placed on the exogenous coefficients relative to MLR's purely cross-sectional specification.


### Variable Importance and Partial Dependence Plots

#### Variable Importance

The comparative performance metrics reported above indicate how well each model forecasts coffee prices out of sample, but they say nothing about which variables are driving those forecasts. This section addresses that question by computing permutation importance for all six models and both coffee varieties, using a model-agnostic approach that is directly comparable across model families.

*This chunk computes permutation importance for all six models and both coffee varieties. For each model, a single instance is first fitted on the full initial training window. Each of the 14 predictors is then permuted independently on the test set while all other variables remain unchanged, and the resulting increase in MSE relative to the walk-forward baseline is recorded as the importance score. For ARIMAX, only the exogenous regressors are permuted, with the autoregressive component held fixed. A positive score indicates that shuffling the variable degrades forecast accuracy, and therefore that the model relies on that variable; a score close to zero or negative indicates that the variable contributes little to the forecasts.*

```{r importance_permutation_all, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, cache=TRUE}

# ----------------------------------------------------------
# PERMUTATION IMPORTANCE — ALL SIX MODELS
# For each model, a single instance is fitted on the full
# initial training window. Each predictor is then permuted
# independently on the test set, predictions are regenerated,
# and the increase in MSE relative to the baseline is used
# as the importance score. A larger increase means the model
# relies more heavily on that variable.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

library(randomForest)
library(xgboost)
library(e1071)
library(nnet)
library(forecast)

labels_vi <- labels_mlr

# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 1 — PREPARE SCALED DATASETS AND TEST SETS
# Both training and test sets are Min-Max scaled using the
# full sample min/max, consistent with the walk-forward
# estimation procedure used throughout the document.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

# Arabica
vars_exo_ara  <- intersect(vars_exo, colnames(df_arabica_levels))
df_ara_modele <- df_arabica_levels[, c("arabica_price", vars_exo_ara)]
df_ara_scaled <- as.data.frame(sapply(df_ara_modele, minmax_scale))
train_ara     <- df_ara_scaled[1:n_train_ara_lev, ]
test_ara      <- df_ara_scaled[(n_train_ara_lev + 1):nrow(df_ara_scaled), ]
actual_ara    <- test_ara[["arabica_price"]]

# Robusta
vars_exo_rob  <- intersect(vars_exo, colnames(df_robusta_levels))
df_rob_modele <- df_robusta_levels[, c("robusta_price", vars_exo_rob)]
df_rob_scaled <- as.data.frame(sapply(df_rob_modele, minmax_scale))
train_rob     <- df_rob_scaled[1:n_train_rob_lev, ]
test_rob      <- df_rob_scaled[(n_train_rob_lev + 1):nrow(df_rob_scaled), ]
actual_rob    <- test_rob[["robusta_price"]]


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 2 — FIT ALL MODELS ON THE FULL TRAINING WINDOW
# Each model is fitted once on the initial training set.
# These training-set models are used exclusively for the
# permutation importance computation — they do not replace
# the walk-forward models used for performance evaluation.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

# MLR
modele_mlr_ara <- lm(arabica_price ~ ., data = train_ara)
modele_mlr_rob <- lm(robusta_price ~ ., data = train_rob)

# ARIMAX — reuse the fixed-order reference model already fitted in
# the main ARIMAX chunk (res_arimax_ara$model, res_arimax_rob$model),
# rather than re-fitting with auto.arima() here. auto.arima() with
# narrow search bounds would produce a different order than the one
# actually used for the walk-forward results reported elsewhere in
# this document, so reusing the reference model keeps the
# permutation importance scores consistent with those results.
xreg_train_ara <- as.matrix(train_ara[, vars_exo_ara])
xreg_test_ara  <- as.matrix(test_ara[,  vars_exo_ara])
xreg_train_rob <- as.matrix(train_rob[, vars_exo_rob])
xreg_test_rob  <- as.matrix(test_rob[,  vars_exo_rob])

modele_arimax_ara <- res_arimax_ara$model
modele_arimax_rob <- res_arimax_rob$model

# Random Forest
set.seed(42)
modele_rf_ara <- randomForest(arabica_price ~ ., data = train_ara,
                               ntree = 500)
set.seed(42)
modele_rf_rob <- randomForest(robusta_price ~ ., data = train_rob,
                               ntree = 500)

# XGBoost
X_train_ara   <- as.matrix(train_ara[, vars_exo_ara])
y_train_ara   <- train_ara[["arabica_price"]]
X_test_ara    <- as.matrix(test_ara[, vars_exo_ara])

X_train_rob   <- as.matrix(train_rob[, vars_exo_rob])
y_train_rob   <- train_rob[["robusta_price"]]
X_test_rob    <- as.matrix(test_rob[, vars_exo_rob])

set.seed(42)
modele_xgb_ara <- xgboost(
  data      = X_train_ara, label = y_train_ara,
  nrounds   = tuning_xgb_ara$nrounds,
  max_depth = tuning_xgb_ara$max_depth,
  eta       = tuning_xgb_ara$eta,
  subsample = tuning_xgb_ara$subsample,
  verbose = 0, objective = "reg:squarederror"
)

set.seed(42)
modele_xgb_rob <- xgboost(
  data      = X_train_rob, label = y_train_rob,
  nrounds   = tuning_xgb_rob$nrounds,
  max_depth = tuning_xgb_rob$max_depth,
  eta       = tuning_xgb_rob$eta,
  subsample = tuning_xgb_rob$subsample,
  verbose = 0, objective = "reg:squarederror"
)

# SVM
modele_svm_ara <- svm(arabica_price ~ ., data = train_ara,
                       kernel = "radial",
                       cost   = tuning_svm_ara$cost,
                       gamma  = tuning_svm_ara$gamma)
modele_svm_rob <- svm(robusta_price ~ ., data = train_rob,
                       kernel = "radial",
                       cost   = tuning_svm_rob$cost,
                       gamma  = tuning_svm_rob$gamma)

# ANN
set.seed(42)
modele_ann_ara <- nnet(arabica_price ~ ., data = train_ara,
                        size   = tuning_ann_ara$size,
                        decay  = tuning_ann_ara$decay,
                        linout = TRUE, maxit = 500, trace = FALSE)
set.seed(42)
modele_ann_rob <- nnet(robusta_price ~ ., data = train_rob,
                        size   = tuning_ann_rob$size,
                        decay  = tuning_ann_rob$decay,
                        linout = TRUE, maxit = 500, trace = FALSE)


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 3 — BASELINE MSE FOR EACH MODEL
# The baseline MSE is computed from the walk-forward
# predictions already stored in the result objects, not
# from the training-set models fitted above. This ensures
# that the importance scores reflect the actual forecasting
# performance reported in the comparative table.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

mse_base <- list(
  mlr_ara   = mean((actual_ara - as.numeric(res_mlr_ara$predicted))^2),
  mlr_rob   = mean((actual_rob - as.numeric(res_mlr_rob$predicted))^2),
  arimax_ara = mean((res_arimax_ara$actual - res_arimax_ara$predicted)^2,
                    na.rm = TRUE),
  arimax_rob = mean((res_arimax_rob$actual - res_arimax_rob$predicted)^2,
                    na.rm = TRUE),
  rf_ara    = mean((actual_ara - as.numeric(res_rf_ara$predicted))^2),
  rf_rob    = mean((actual_rob - as.numeric(res_rf_rob$predicted))^2),
  xgb_ara   = mean((actual_ara - as.numeric(res_xgb_ara$predicted))^2),
  xgb_rob   = mean((actual_rob - as.numeric(res_xgb_rob$predicted))^2),
  svm_ara   = mean((actual_ara - as.numeric(res_svm_ara$predicted))^2),
  svm_rob   = mean((actual_rob - as.numeric(res_svm_rob$predicted))^2),
  ann_ara   = mean((actual_ara - as.numeric(res_ann_ara$predicted))^2),
  ann_rob   = mean((actual_rob - as.numeric(res_ann_rob$predicted))^2)
)


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 4 — PERMUTATION IMPORTANCE FUNCTION
# For each predictor, the column is shuffled in the test
# set, predictions are regenerated using the training-set
# model, and the increase in MSE relative to baseline is
# recorded. The procedure is wrapped in a function that
# accepts any predict-compatible model object.
#
# Arguments:
#   test_set    : scaled test set data frame
#   var_dep     : name of the dependent variable column
#   vars_exo_v  : vector of predictor names
#   predict_fun : function(model, newdata) -> numeric vector
#   modele      : fitted model object
#   mse_base    : baseline MSE from walk-forward predictions
# ----------------------------------------------------------

permutation_importance <- function(test_set, var_dep, vars_exo_v,
                                    predict_fun, modele, mse_base_val) {
  set.seed(42)
  resultats <- lapply(vars_exo_v, function(var) {
    test_perm        <- test_set
    test_perm[[var]] <- sample(test_perm[[var]])
    preds            <- predict_fun(modele, test_perm)
    actual           <- test_set[[var_dep]]
    mse_perm         <- mean((actual - preds)^2)
    data.frame(
      Variable   = labels_vi[var],
      Importance = mse_perm - mse_base_val
    )
  })
  do.call(rbind, resultats) %>%
    filter(!is.na(Variable)) %>%
    arrange(desc(Importance))
}


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 5 — COMPUTE PERMUTATION IMPORTANCE FOR ALL MODELS
# Each model uses its own predict function wrapper to
# ensure consistent output format across model families.
# ARIMAX uses forecast() with the permuted xreg matrix;
# XGBoost requires a matrix input rather than a data frame.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

# MLR
imp_perm_mlr_ara <- permutation_importance(
  test_ara, "arabica_price", vars_exo_ara,
  function(m, d) predict(m, newdata = d),
  modele_mlr_ara, mse_base$mlr_ara)

imp_perm_mlr_rob <- permutation_importance(
  test_rob, "robusta_price", vars_exo_rob,
  function(m, d) predict(m, newdata = d),
  modele_mlr_rob, mse_base$mlr_rob)

# ARIMAX — permutation applied to xreg only
# The AR component is kept fixed; only the contribution of
# each exogenous regressor is evaluated.
imp_perm_arimax_ara <- do.call(rbind, lapply(vars_exo_ara, function(var) {
  set.seed(42)
  xreg_perm        <- xreg_test_ara
  xreg_perm[, var] <- sample(xreg_perm[, var])
  fc <- forecast(modele_arimax_ara,
                 h    = nrow(xreg_perm),
                 xreg = xreg_perm)
  preds    <- as.numeric(fc$mean)
  mse_perm <- mean((res_arimax_ara$actual - preds)^2, na.rm = TRUE)
  data.frame(Variable   = labels_vi[var],
             Importance = mse_perm - mse_base$arimax_ara)
})) %>% filter(!is.na(Variable)) %>% arrange(desc(Importance))

imp_perm_arimax_rob <- do.call(rbind, lapply(vars_exo_rob, function(var) {
  set.seed(42)
  xreg_perm        <- xreg_test_rob
  xreg_perm[, var] <- sample(xreg_perm[, var])
  fc <- forecast(modele_arimax_rob,
                 h    = nrow(xreg_perm),
                 xreg = xreg_perm)
  preds    <- as.numeric(fc$mean)
  mse_perm <- mean((res_arimax_rob$actual - preds)^2, na.rm = TRUE)
  data.frame(Variable   = labels_vi[var],
             Importance = mse_perm - mse_base$arimax_rob)
})) %>% filter(!is.na(Variable)) %>% arrange(desc(Importance))

# Random Forest
imp_perm_rf_ara <- permutation_importance(
  test_ara, "arabica_price", vars_exo_ara,
  function(m, d) as.numeric(predict(m, newdata = d)),
  modele_rf_ara, mse_base$rf_ara)

imp_perm_rf_rob <- permutation_importance(
  test_rob, "robusta_price", vars_exo_rob,
  function(m, d) as.numeric(predict(m, newdata = d)),
  modele_rf_rob, mse_base$rf_rob)

# XGBoost — requires matrix input
imp_perm_xgb_ara <- do.call(rbind, lapply(vars_exo_ara, function(var) {
  set.seed(42)
  X_perm        <- X_test_ara
  X_perm[, var] <- sample(X_perm[, var])
  preds         <- predict(modele_xgb_ara, newdata = X_perm)
  mse_perm      <- mean((actual_ara - preds)^2)
  data.frame(Variable   = labels_vi[var],
             Importance = mse_perm - mse_base$xgb_ara)
})) %>% filter(!is.na(Variable)) %>% arrange(desc(Importance))

imp_perm_xgb_rob <- do.call(rbind, lapply(vars_exo_rob, function(var) {
  set.seed(42)
  X_perm        <- X_test_rob
  X_perm[, var] <- sample(X_perm[, var])
  preds         <- predict(modele_xgb_rob, newdata = X_perm)
  mse_perm      <- mean((actual_rob - preds)^2)
  data.frame(Variable   = labels_vi[var],
             Importance = mse_perm - mse_base$xgb_rob)
})) %>% filter(!is.na(Variable)) %>% arrange(desc(Importance))

# SVM
imp_perm_svm_ara <- permutation_importance(
  test_ara, "arabica_price", vars_exo_ara,
  function(m, d) as.numeric(predict(m, newdata = d)),
  modele_svm_ara, mse_base$svm_ara)

imp_perm_svm_rob <- permutation_importance(
  test_rob, "robusta_price", vars_exo_rob,
  function(m, d) as.numeric(predict(m, newdata = d)),
  modele_svm_rob, mse_base$svm_rob)

# ANN
imp_perm_ann_ara <- permutation_importance(
  test_ara, "arabica_price", vars_exo_ara,
  function(m, d) as.numeric(predict(m, newdata = d)),
  modele_ann_ara, mse_base$ann_ara)

imp_perm_ann_rob <- permutation_importance(
  test_rob, "robusta_price", vars_exo_rob,
  function(m, d) as.numeric(predict(m, newdata = d)),
  modele_ann_rob, mse_base$ann_rob)

cat("Permutation importance computed for all 6 models.\n")
```

The permutation importance scores are now available for all six models and both varieties. The plots below summarise the top three variables per model for each coffee variety across the four ML models, allowing direct comparison of predictor hierarchies. MLR and ARIMAX are excluded from this comparison for reasons discussed in the code. The full rankings for all 14 variables are reported in the Appendices.

*This chunk produces the top-3 comparative importance plots for the main text. For each ML model and each variety, the three variables with the highest permutation importance scores are extracted and displayed side by side using `facet_wrap()`. MLR is excluded because severe multicollinearity causes all its permutation scores to be negative. ARIMAX is excluded because it predicts in original price units rather than the Min-Max scaled range, making its importance scores not directly comparable to those of the ML models. The y-axis scale varies freely across panels to accommodate differences in the magnitude of importance scores between models.*

```{r importance_comparative_plots, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.width=11, fig.height=5}

# ----------------------------------------------------------
# COMPARATIVE IMPORTANCE PLOTS (MAIN TEXT)
# Only the four ML models are included in the comparative
# chart, as they share the same Min-Max scaled prediction
# space and produce directly comparable importance scores.
# MLR is excluded because severe multicollinearity causes
# all permutation scores to be negative, making the chart
# uninformative. ARIMAX is excluded because it predicts in
# original price units rather than the [0,1] scaled range,
# making its importance scores several orders of magnitude
# larger than those of the ML models and not directly
# comparable.
# Negative importance scores are set to zero and excluded
# from the ranking before the top 3 are selected.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

construire_top3 <- function(imp_list, noms_modeles) {
  do.call(rbind, mapply(function(imp_df, nom) {
    imp_df %>%
      filter(Importance > 0) %>%
      slice_max(Importance, n = 3) %>%
      mutate(Model = nom)
  }, imp_list, noms_modeles, SIMPLIFY = FALSE)) %>%
    mutate(
      Model          = factor(Model,
                              levels = c("Random Forest", "XGBoost",
                                         "SVM", "ANN")),
      Variable_Model = paste(Variable, Model, sep = "__"),
      Variable_Model = reorder(Variable_Model, Importance)
    )
}

top3_ara <- construire_top3(
  list(imp_perm_rf_ara, imp_perm_xgb_ara,
       imp_perm_svm_ara, imp_perm_ann_ara),
  c("Random Forest", "XGBoost", "SVM", "ANN")
)

top3_rob <- construire_top3(
  list(imp_perm_rf_rob, imp_perm_xgb_rob,
       imp_perm_svm_rob, imp_perm_ann_rob),
  c("Random Forest", "XGBoost", "SVM", "ANN")
)


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# PLOT FUNCTION
# ncol = 4 places all four models on a single row.
# panel.spacing gives enough room between panels.
# scales = "free" allows each panel to use its own axis
# range since importance magnitudes differ across models.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

plot_top3 <- function(top3_df, color, bg_color, title, r2_labels) {
  top3_df <- top3_df %>%
    mutate(Model = factor(Model,
                          levels = names(r2_labels),
                          labels = paste0(names(r2_labels),
                                          "\n(R² = ", r2_labels, ")")))
  ggplot(top3_df,
         aes(x = Variable_Model, y = Importance)) +
    geom_bar(stat = "identity", fill = color, alpha = 0.85, width = 0.55) +
    geom_text(aes(label = round(Importance, 4)),
              hjust = -0.15, size = 3, color = "grey40") +
    coord_flip() +
    facet_wrap(~ Model, scales = "free", ncol = 4) +
    scale_x_discrete(labels = function(x) gsub("__.*", "", x)) +
    scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.40))) +
    labs(title    = title,
         subtitle = "Top 3 variables by permutation importance (ΔMSE). Negative scores excluded.",
         x = NULL, y = "ΔMSE") +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
    theme(
      panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
      panel.grid.minor   = element_blank(),
      strip.text         = element_text(face = "bold", size = 10),
      strip.background   = element_rect(fill = bg_color, color = NA),
      plot.title         = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12),
      plot.subtitle      = element_text(size = 9, color = "grey40"),
      axis.text.y        = element_text(size = 10, color = "grey20"),
      axis.text.x        = element_text(size = 8, color = "grey40"),
      panel.spacing      = unit(2, "lines")
    )
}

plot_top3(top3_ara, "#8B4513", "#f5ece6",
          "Top 3 variable importance by model — Arabica futures",
          r2_labels = c("Random Forest" = "0.815", "XGBoost" = "0.812",
                        "SVM" = "0.813", "ANN" = "0.728"))
ggsave("importance_arabica.png", width = 11, height = 5, dpi = 300, bg = "white")

plot_top3(top3_rob, "#2E8B57", "#e8f5ec",
          "Top 3 variable importance by model — Robusta futures",
          r2_labels = c("Random Forest" = "0.676", "XGBoost" = "0.797",
                        "SVM" = "0.761", "ANN" = "0.456"))
ggsave("importance_robusta.png", width = 11, height = 5, dpi = 300, bg = "white")
```

Across the four ML models, the results for Arabica are fairly consistent. Ending stocks consistently ranks among the top three predictors across all four ML models, confirming inventory levels as a reliable short-run driver of Arabica prices. COT net MM and WTI also feature prominently, appearing in the top three for most models, which points to speculative positioning and energy costs as secondary but recurring drivers. WTI ranks third for XGBoost and ANN, while Fed Funds Rate and Sugar also feature across Random Forest and ANN. The broad agreement on Ending stocks and COT net MM across four structurally different model families is reassuring, confirming that their predictive contribution is real and not just a coincidence of one particular model's structure.

For Robusta, macroeconomic variables dominate. WTI ranks first for Random Forest, SVM and ANN, while Fed Funds Rate appears in the top three of all four models, making it the most consistently important predictor for this variety. Sugar also features in two of the four models. The ANN Robusta scores are substantially larger in magnitude than those of the other models, which is a direct consequence of its lower baseline accuracy: a less precise model is simply more sensitive to any perturbation of the input variables, amplifying the permutation importance scores relative to better-performing models.

#### Partial Dependence Plots

Partial dependence plots complement the permutation importance results by showing not just how much a variable matters to each model, but in which direction and through what kind of relationship. For a given predictor, the procedure fixes that variable at a sequence of values spanning its observed range, holds every other predictor at its actual value for each training observation, generates predictions at each step, and averages them across the training set. The resulting curve traces how the model's expected output moves as the variable changes, once the influence of the other thirteen predictors has been averaged out.

Computing this for all fourteen variables and all four ML models would produce far more panels than the main text can reasonably hold, so the comparison here is restricted to the variables that came out as consensus drivers in the permutation importance analysis for each variety: Ending stocks, COT net MM and WTI for Arabica, and Fed Funds Rate and WTI for Robusta. These are shown faceted across the four ML models so the shape of each relationship can be compared side by side. The full set of plots, covering each model's own top three variables individually, is reported in the Appendices.

*The chunk below sets up the machinery needed to compute a partial dependence curve for any combination of model and predictor, then applies it to the consensus variables identified for each coffee variety. The four ML models are not re-estimated here: they are the same objects already fitted on the full initial training window in the variable importance chunk. The grid of values tested for each variable is built over the range actually observed in the training set on the scaled axis, rather than the full [0,1] interval, so the model is never asked to predict outside the range of data it was trained on.*

```{r pdp_main_compute, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# ----------------------------------------------------------
# PARTIAL DEPENDENCE PLOTS — GENERIC FUNCTIONS
# A PDP measures a model's average marginal dependence on a single
# variable: for a grid of values of that variable, the value is held
# fixed across every observation in the training set, predictions are
# recomputed, and then averaged. The four ML models reuse the objects
# already fitted on the full initial training window in the
# importance_permutation_all chunk, with no re-estimation here.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

# STEP 1 — Bounds in original units for each predictor and for each
# dependent variable.
# All ML models are trained on data scaled to [0,1] by minmax_scale().
# The PDP grid and the resulting predictions therefore both need to be
# converted back to original units (USD/lb, USD/tonne, %, etc.) to be
# interpretable in the plots. calculer_bornes() just pulls the min and
# max of each variable from the unscaled dataset, which serve as the
# reference points for this linear back-transformation.
calculer_bornes <- function(df, variables) {
  bornes <- lapply(variables, function(v)
    c(min = min(df[[v]], na.rm = TRUE), max = max(df[[v]], na.rm = TRUE)))
  names(bornes) <- variables
  bornes
}

# Bounds for the 14 predictors, by variety (used to convert the x-axis
# of each PDP back from the [0,1] scale)
bornes_ara <- calculer_bornes(df_ara_modele, vars_exo_ara)
bornes_rob <- calculer_bornes(df_rob_modele, vars_exo_rob)

# Bounds for the dependent variable (price), by variety (used to
# convert the y-axis, i.e. the averaged prediction, back from [0,1] to
# USD/lb or USD/tonne)
bornes_prix_ara <- c(min = min(df_ara_modele$arabica_price),
                     max = max(df_ara_modele$arabica_price))
bornes_prix_rob <- c(min = min(df_rob_modele$robusta_price),
                     max = max(df_rob_modele$robusta_price))


# STEP 2 — Predictor-only data, required by XGBoost.
# Unlike lm(), randomForest(), svm() and nnet(), which all accept a
# full data frame (the dependent variable column included, simply
# ignored by predict()), predict.xgb.Booster() requires a numeric
# matrix containing only the predictor columns. These two objects are
# built once here and reused for every PDP call involving XGBoost,
# instead of being rebuilt for each variable tested.
train_ara_xgb <- train_ara[, vars_exo_ara]
train_rob_xgb <- train_rob[, vars_exo_rob]


# STEP 3 — Named lists of the four already-fitted ML models, by variety.
# These objects (modele_rf_ara, modele_xgb_ara, etc.) were trained once
# on the full training window in the importance_permutation_all chunk
# and are reused here as-is, with no retraining. Grouping them into a
# named list allows looping over the four models with lapply() in the
# steps below, instead of duplicating the same block four times.
modeles_ara <- list("Random Forest" = modele_rf_ara, "XGBoost" = modele_xgb_ara,
                    "SVM" = modele_svm_ara, "ANN" = modele_ann_ara)
modeles_rob <- list("Random Forest" = modele_rf_rob, "XGBoost" = modele_xgb_rob,
                    "SVM" = modele_svm_rob, "ANN" = modele_ann_rob)


# STEP 4 — Select the right input dataset depending on the model.
# This function captures the only structural difference between
# XGBoost and the other three models: XGBoost needs the predictor-only
# matrix (donnees_predicteurs), while Random Forest, SVM and ANN accept
# the full data frame (donnees_full), which includes the dependent
# variable column without that causing any issue for predict().
obtenir_donnees_pdp <- function(nom_modele, donnees_full, donnees_predicteurs) {
  if (nom_modele == "XGBoost") donnees_predicteurs else donnees_full
}


# STEP 5 — Prediction wrapper, needed because XGBoost expects a matrix
# rather than a data frame.
# predict.xgb.Booster() explicitly requires a matrix or xgb.DMatrix
# object as input and fails if passed a data frame. as.matrix() is
# therefore only applied in the XGBoost branch; the other three models
# call predict() directly on the data frame, consistent with the rest
# of the document.
predire_pdp <- function(nom_modele, modele, donnees) {
  if (nom_modele == "XGBoost") {
    as.numeric(predict(modele, newdata = as.matrix(donnees)))
  } else {
    as.numeric(predict(modele, newdata = donnees))
  }
}


# STEP 6 — Compute the PDP for one model and one variable.
# What happens at each point of the grid:
#   (a) take a fresh copy of the full training set
#   (b) overwrite the column of the variable of interest with a SINGLE
#       fixed value across ALL observations (the other 13 predictors
#       stay at their real, observation-specific values)
#   (c) generate a prediction for each of these modified observations
#   (d) average these predictions across the whole training set
# The result of that average, for each grid value, is one point on the
# PDP curve. The grid itself is built over the range actually observed
# in the training set on the [0,1] scale, rather than the full [0,1]
# interval, to avoid extrapolating the model beyond values it actually
# saw during training.
calculer_pdp <- function(nom_modele, modele, donnees_train, variable,
                          bornes_var, bornes_cible, n_points = 20) {

  # (a) Grid of n_points equally spaced values, on the [0,1] scale,
  # spanning the range actually observed for this variable in the
  # training set
  grille_scaled <- seq(min(donnees_train[[variable]]),
                       max(donnees_train[[variable]]),
                       length.out = n_points)

  # (b)-(d) For each grid value: copy the data, overwrite the column of
  # the tested variable with that fixed value on every row, predict,
  # then average the predictions obtained across the training set
  predictions_moyennes <- sapply(grille_scaled, function(val) {
    donnees_modifiees <- donnees_train
    donnees_modifiees[[variable]] <- val
    mean(predire_pdp(nom_modele, modele, donnees_modifiees))
  })

  # Convert both axes, x (variable value) and y (averaged prediction),
  # back from the [0,1] scale to original units, using the bounds
  # computed in Step 1
  data.frame(
    Model = nom_modele,
    x     = bornes_var["min"] + grille_scaled * (bornes_var["max"] - bornes_var["min"]),
    y     = bornes_cible["min"] + predictions_moyennes * (bornes_cible["max"] - bornes_cible["min"])
  )
}


# STEP 7 — PDP for the consensus variables shown in the main text:
# Ending stocks, COT net MM and WTI for Arabica, Fed Funds Rate and WTI
# for Robusta, computed for all four ML models.
# generer_pdp_variable() loops over the four models of one variety
# (via lapply() on names(modeles)) and stacks (rbind) the four
# resulting curves for ONE variable, tagging each row with that
# variable's readable label.
generer_pdp_variable <- function(modeles, donnees_full, donnees_predicteurs,
                                  variable, label_variable,
                                  bornes_vars, bornes_cible) {
  resultat <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(modeles), function(nom) {
    calculer_pdp(nom, modeles[[nom]],
                obtenir_donnees_pdp(nom, donnees_full, donnees_predicteurs),
                variable, bornes_vars[[variable]], bornes_cible)
  }))
  resultat$Variable <- label_variable
  resultat
}

# Arabica: three calls (one per consensus variable), stacked into a
# single data frame of 4 models x 3 variables x 20 points = 240 rows
df_pdp_ara <- rbind(
  generer_pdp_variable(modeles_ara, train_ara, train_ara_xgb,
                       "ending_stocks", "Ending stocks",
                       bornes_ara, bornes_prix_ara),
  generer_pdp_variable(modeles_ara, train_ara, train_ara_xgb,
                       "cot_net_mm", "COT net MM",
                       bornes_ara, bornes_prix_ara),
  generer_pdp_variable(modeles_ara, train_ara, train_ara_xgb,
                       "wti", "WTI",
                       bornes_ara, bornes_prix_ara)
)
# Convert to factors with a fixed level order, so facet_grid() displays
# models and variables in the intended order rather than alphabetically
df_pdp_ara$Model    <- factor(df_pdp_ara$Model,
                              levels = c("Random Forest", "XGBoost", "SVM", "ANN"),
                              labels = c("Random Forest\n(R² = 0.815)", "XGBoost\n(R² = 0.812)",
                                         "SVM\n(R² = 0.813)", "ANN\n(R² = 0.728)"))
df_pdp_ara$Variable <- factor(df_pdp_ara$Variable,
                              levels = c("Ending stocks", "COT net MM", "WTI"))

# Robusta: same logic, with the two consensus variables specific to
# this variety
df_pdp_rob <- rbind(
  generer_pdp_variable(modeles_rob, train_rob, train_rob_xgb,
                       "fed_funds_rate", "Fed Funds Rate",
                       bornes_rob, bornes_prix_rob),
  generer_pdp_variable(modeles_rob, train_rob, train_rob_xgb,
                       "wti", "WTI",
                       bornes_rob, bornes_prix_rob)
)
df_pdp_rob$Model    <- factor(df_pdp_rob$Model,
                              levels = c("Random Forest", "XGBoost", "SVM", "ANN"),
                              labels = c("Random Forest\n(R² = 0.676)", "XGBoost\n(R² = 0.797)",
                                         "SVM\n(R² = 0.761)", "ANN\n(R² = 0.456)"))
df_pdp_rob$Variable <- factor(df_pdp_rob$Variable,
                              levels = c("Fed Funds Rate", "WTI"))
```

*This chunk renders the main-text PDP figure for Arabica, with the three consensus variables as rows and the four ML models as columns.*

```{r pdp_main_plots_arabica, fig.width=9, fig.height=5.5, out.width="100%"}

# ----------------------------------------------------------
# PDP PLOT — ARABICA (MAIN TEXT)
# Separated into its own chunk so fig.height can be set specifically
# for this plot's 3 rows of panels (Ending stocks, COT net MM, WTI),
# rather than sharing a single height with the Robusta plot below,
# which only has 2 rows. facet_grid2() with independent = "x" frees
# the x-axis per panel rather than per column (see note in the
# pdp_main_compute chunk for why this matters given the very
# different units and ranges of the variables shown). out.width =
# "100%" caps the rendered width to the page's text width; fig.height
# is set directly here since out.width alone does not constrain the
# rendered height, which otherwise follows the fig.width:fig.height
# ratio set below.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

library(ggh4x)

ggplot(df_pdp_ara, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_line(color = "#8B4513", linewidth = 0.9) +
  facet_grid2(Variable ~ Model, scales = "free_x", independent = "x") +
  labs(title    = "Partial dependence plots — Arabica futures",
       subtitle = "Predicted price (USD/lb), other predictors held at their observed values",
       x = NULL, y = "Predicted price (USD/lb)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9) +
  theme(
    strip.text       = element_text(face = "bold", size = 8),
    strip.background = element_rect(fill = "#f5ece6", color = NA),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "#fafafa", color = NA),
    axis.text.x      = element_text(size = 6)
  )

ggsave("pdp_arabica.png", width = 9, height = 5.5, dpi = 300, bg = "white")
```

The Arabica results line up reasonably well across the three consensus variables, though the shape of each relationship varies a fair amount depending on the model. Ending stocks pulls prices down for all four models, which matches what inventory theory would predict, but Random Forest and XGBoost get there in a very different way than SVM and ANN. The two tree-based models show a sharp drop right at the bottom of the observed range and then go essentially flat for the rest of it, while SVM and ANN trace something closer to a straight downward slope across the whole range. This is not really a disagreement about the underlying effect so much as a difference in how each model family is built: trees split the data into a handful of regions and predict a constant value within each one, which mechanically produces these step-like jumps, whereas SVM and ANN are smooth functions and will always look smoother as a result. COT net MM is the cleanest result of the three. It rises for every single model, which fits the financialisation argument made earlier in this section about speculative positioning, and SVM in particular shows a fairly pronounced curve while ANN comes closest to a straight line. WTI follows the same step-versus-smooth split as Ending stocks, with the tree-based models again concentrating most of the increase in a narrow band before flattening out, but all four models agree on the direction: higher oil prices push the Arabica forecast up, consistent with the energy cost channel.

*This chunk computes the mean and standard deviation of the Federal Funds Rate before and after the 2022 tightening cycle, supporting the discussion of its partial dependence shape below.*

```{r pdp_fed_funds_regimes, message=FALSE}
# ----------------------------------------------------------
# FED FUNDS RATE — TWO MONETARY REGIMES
# Quick summary statistics supporting the PDP interpretation below:
# the Federal Funds Rate behaves very differently before and after
# the 2022 tightening cycle, which is relevant context for reading
# the flat/mildly positive PDP shape observed for this variable.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

stats_pre_2022 <- dataset_mensuel %>%
  filter(date >= "2008-01" & date <= "2021-12") %>%
  summarise(moyenne = mean(fed_funds_rate, na.rm = TRUE),
            ecart_type = sd(fed_funds_rate, na.rm = TRUE))

stats_post_2022 <- dataset_mensuel %>%
  filter(date >= "2022-01") %>%
  summarise(moyenne = mean(fed_funds_rate, na.rm = TRUE),
            ecart_type = sd(fed_funds_rate, na.rm = TRUE))

cat("2008-2021 — mean:", round(stats_pre_2022$moyenne, 2),
    "| sd:", round(stats_pre_2022$ecart_type, 2), "\n")
cat("2022-2023 — mean:", round(stats_post_2022$moyenne, 2),
    "| sd:", round(stats_post_2022$ecart_type, 2), "\n")
```

Robusta tells a more mixed story. WTI is unambiguous again, rising across all four models, with the same step pattern showing up for Random Forest and XGBoost and a smoother climb for SVM and ANN. Fed Funds Rate is a messier case. Random Forest and XGBoost barely move at all across the observed range, SVM rises and then turns down slightly toward the top, and ANN rises throughout but without much curvature. None of the four models actually reproduces the negative relationship that basic monetary policy reasoning would suggest. This is worth noting because the usual culprit, multicollinearity, does not really apply here: the Federal Funds Rate carries a low VIF in the Robusta ARIMAX specification reported earlier, in contrast to CPI and DXY, whose sign reversals in the MLR results were plausibly attributed to exactly that problem. 

A more likely explanation is that the relationship between policy rates and Robusta prices is not linear over the full sample. The Federal Funds Rate averaged just 0.62% with limited variation between 2008 and 2021, save for a brief hike cycle around 2018–2019, before climbing to an average of 3.35% from 2022 onward as the Federal Reserve tightened policy sharply. A PDP averaged across the whole training period cannot really distinguish a genuinely weak effect from two very different monetary regimes blending together.

## Discussion

### Overall Model Performance

The out-of-sample results present a consistent and interpretable picture of predictive performance across the six model families. Two broad conclusions emerge. First, ARIMAX's explicit autoregressive structure gives it a clear edge over every other model for both varieties, confirming that the persistence of prices around their own past values is a primary source of short-run predictability that none of the five remaining models, all of which rely solely on contemporaneous exogenous predictors, can fully replicate. Second, the performance gap between the strongest and weakest models is substantially wider for Robusta than for Arabica, reflecting the shorter estimation sample, the more pronounced multicollinearity among Robusta predictors, and the sharp late-sample price acceleration discussed further below.

For Arabica, ARIMAX stands clearly apart from the rest of the field once its order is fixed on the initial training window and applied as-is throughout the walk-forward loop, reaching an out-of-sample 
$R^2$ of 0.955. XGBoost, Random Forest and SVM form a second tier close together at 0.812, 0.815 and 0.813 respectively, suggesting the three pick up much of the same signal from the predictor set rather than exploiting genuinely different information. MLR achieves $R^2 = 0.784$, a result that reflects the strong trending co-movement between Arabica prices and the macroeconomic variables in levels rather than genuine structural predictive power. The ANN trails at 0.728, an instability the Conclusion returns to.

For Robusta, ARIMAX again delivers the strongest result at $R^2=0.926$, though the margin over the second tier is narrower than for Arabica: XGBoost follows at $R^2=0.797$, while SVM and Random Forest achieve 0.761 and 0.676 respectively. The most striking result is the collapse of MLR to $R^2 =0.276$, with forecast trajectories that oscillate erratically around the observed series and produce large directional errors. This failure reflects the well-known sensitivity of OLS to multicollinearity in short samples. With only 153 training observations and 14 highly collinear predictors, as documented in the correlation and VIF analyses, individual coefficient estimates carry high variance and are poorly identified. Under the walk-forward protocol, where the model is re-estimated from scratch at every step as the training window expands by one observation, this instability translates directly into forecasting behaviour: small changes in the training sample can shift the fitted coefficients substantially from one step to the next, producing the erratic, oscillating forecasts visible in the Robusta residual plots rather than a smooth or systematically biased error pattern. The regularisation exercise conducted as a robustness check on MLR supports this reading directly: Ridge regression, which shrinks and stabilises every coefficient without removing any predictor, nearly doubles Robusta's $R^2$ to 0.464, while the same penalty applied to Arabica's already better-behaved coefficients makes performance worse rather than better. This asymmetry is exactly what a multicollinearity-driven explanation predicts, and it confirms that Robusta's weak MLR result is a symptom of collinearity and sample size rather than a failure of the predictor set itself.

The coefficient tables from the ARIMAX training-set estimation further illuminate the challenge of identifying interpretable linear relationships in this predictor space. For both varieties, only a small number of regressors reach conventional significance thresholds: Sugar, WTI, the Federal Funds Rate and COT net MM for Arabica, and CPI, WTI and COT net MM for Robusta, with DXY approaching significance at the 10% level. This outcome is not a failure of specification but a further manifestation of the same multicollinearity problem discussed above: Production, Consumption and Exports move almost in lockstep over the sample, as the correlation matrix shows pairwise coefficients between them ranging from 0.73 to 0.94, and CPI trends closely alongside all three for the same reason. As with the MLR case, this leaves the OLS component of ARIMAX unable to isolate the individual contribution of any one of these variables, inflating standard errors and suppressing t-statistics even when the group's collective predictive content is substantial. This observation provides a retrospective justification for the machine learning approach adopted in this study: Random Forest and XGBoost are specifically designed to exploit the predictive information contained in groups of correlated variables through non-linear combinations and variable selection mechanisms that are unavailable to the linear regression component of ARIMAX.

The overall level of predictive accuracy achieved, with $R^2$ values generally above 0.75 across the best-performing models for both varieties, is worth noting in context. These results are obtained on series in levels, and the co-trending of prices with macroeconomic variables may inflate $R^2$ beyond what would be achievable on stationary first-differenced series. This point is taken up fully in the Conclusion.

This overall pattern, where ARIMAX outperforms every machine learning model for both varieties, sits in some tension with the wider literature, though not with all of it. Kohzadi et al. (1996), discussed in the Literature Review, found a neural network outperforming an ARIMA benchmark for wheat and live cattle prices, and Deina et al. (2022) found non-linear methods outperforming linear benchmarks consistently across both coffee varieties and all forecast horizons tested. Here, the reverse holds for every machine learning model, including the ANN, a pattern Masini et al. (2023), also reviewed earlier, observe in their own empirical illustration, where a penalised linear regression outperforms random forest. ARIMAX's advantage here is therefore consistent with part of the wider evidence base, not simply an anomaly specific to this thesis, even if it diverges from Kohzadi's and Deina's coffee- and commodity-specific results. The richer exogenous predictor set built into ARIMAX throughout this thesis, compared to a purely autoregressive benchmark, is one plausible difference from Kohzadi's and Deina's comparisons specifically, though this thesis does not test that distinction directly. Nayak et al. (2024) offer indirect support for this reading: comparing an almost identical model set, ARIMAX, MLR, ANN, SVR and Random Forest, for vegetable price forecasting in India, they find that an ARIMAX specification built with only two exogenous weather variables achieves a lower RMSE than all four alternatives for two of the three crops studied, tomato and potato, though the ordering reverses for the third, onion. This is not a direct test of a fourteen-variable specification, but it suggests that even a modest exogenous predictor set can be enough to close the gap reported in univariate comparisons such as Kohzadi's and Deina's.

### The Role of Financial and Speculative Variables

The permutation importance analysis, computed across all four machine learning models rather than any single one, provides the clearest picture of which predictors drive out-of-sample accuracy, and the consistency of the ranking across four structurally different model families is what makes it informative rather than an artefact of one particular architecture. For Arabica, Ending stocks ranks among the top three predictors for all four ML models (contributing a ΔMSE of 0.045 for Random Forest alone, by some margin its largest single predictor), the single most consistent finding in the comparison. COT net Managed Money follows closely, ranking top three for three of the four models, and WTI for three of the four as well, though not always the same three. The dominance of speculative positioning is consistent with the progressive financialisation of commodity futures markets more broadly: the net position of Managed Money participants captures market-wide expectations about future price direction that are not yet reflected in contemporaneous fundamentals. The strong predictive power of COT net MM at the one-month-ahead horizon suggests that this sentiment signal is not fully incorporated into current prices, creating a forecasting opportunity that the tree-based and kernel models exploit through their non-linear variable interactions. Sugar No.1 prices feature prominently for the ANN in particular, consistent with the strong co-movement between the two series already documented in the correlation analysis (0.71, the highest pairwise price correlation observed in this study) and with the direct supply-side link between coffee and sugar cultivation in Brazil, the world's largest producer of both crops. A plausible interpretation is that shifts in the relative profitability of the two crops are anticipated by market participants and reflected in coffee futures prices before they appear in realised production data, though this study does not test this mechanism directly and the finding is limited to the observed correlation and the variable's contribution to forecast accuracy.

The mechanics of the COT signal also point to a feedback structure worth making explicit. A positive net Managed Money position reflects funds that have already taken long positions in anticipation of rising prices. If that buying pressure itself contributes to the price increase, as the positive and significant COT coefficient in both the MLR and ARIMAX specifications suggests, the resulting price rise could in principle reinforce the original bullish positioning rather than simply confirming it. This self-reinforcing dynamic would be consistent with what the permutation importance results show, namely that COT net MM contributes meaningfully to several of the ML models' one-month-ahead forecasts. However, the present analysis cannot speak to this mechanism directly: walk-forward forecasting accuracy and a positive coefficient sign are compatible with a self-reinforcing dynamic, but neither result is designed to test for one, and no claim of this kind is made here beyond noting that the observed coefficient sign and forecasting contribution do not rule it out. The lagged-COT robustness check conducted later in this study, which adds COT net MM at one, two and three months back to the baseline predictor set, offers a further piece of evidence here: the lagged values do not meaningfully improve one-month-ahead forecasts for most models, suggesting that whatever information the lags carry is already implicitly absorbed by the contemporaneous COT variable, which is a more parsimonious result than a genuine multi-period feedback loop would imply, though it does not settle the question either way.

For Robusta, the importance hierarchy differs from Arabica in its upper ranks. The Federal Funds Rate is the standout result here: it ranks in the top three for all four ML models, the strongest consensus finding for this variety, and WTI ranks first specifically for three of the four models. The stronger role of energy costs is consistent with the production geography of Robusta: cultivation is concentrated in a small number of countries, chiefly Vietnam and Indonesia, compared to the twelve countries that contribute to the Arabica indices in this study, so country-specific shocks to production and logistics costs plausibly translate more directly into aggregate price movements. The consistency of the Federal Funds Rate is worth reading alongside the partial dependence results discussed earlier in this study: the rate sat close to zero with limited variation for most of the 2008–2021 period before climbing sharply from 2022 onward, and this later regime coincides closely with the test period used to evaluate the models. A predictor whose behaviour shifts so markedly within the window being forecast is well placed to carry genuine one-month-ahead signal, even where the partial dependence shape itself is not always the smooth, monotonic relationship that a simple monetary policy channel would predict.

Two patterns stand out across both varieties. First, the two most consistently important predictors identified across all four ML models, Ending stocks for Arabica and the Federal Funds Rate for Robusta, both belong to categories, USDA fundamentals and monetary policy respectively, that are not obviously "financial positioning" in the narrow sense, suggesting that the informative variables differ by variety rather than falling into one single dominant category. Second, climate variables sit consistently in the lower half of the ranking for both varieties, averaging 9.1 and 9.6 of 14 respectively across the eight model-variety combinations. Rather than a disappointing result, this echoes Bastianin et al. (2018), discussed in the Literature Review, who find that ENSO shocks account for a modest share of the variance in Colombian coffee prices, with the much larger remainder attributed to broader world coffee market shocks, a category this thesis's macroeconomic and financial predictors are well placed to capture. This finding carries a practical implication: short-run price signals for coffee are not reliably captured by any single category of predictor, but the specific variables that matter, inventory levels for Arabica, energy and interest rate conditions for Robusta, are worth monitoring directly rather than assuming climate or supply data alone will suffice at monthly frequency.

### Arabica vs Robusta: Structural Differences

The contrast between Arabica and Robusta results across models reveals structural differences between the two markets that go beyond the shorter sample available for Robusta, though the ARIMAX result in particular now needs to be read carefully in light of the order-fixing exercise conducted in this study.

Under the fixed-order specification, ARIMAX now performs better for Arabica ($R^2 = 0.955$, ARIMA(2,0,1)) than for Robusta ($R^2= 0.926$, ARIMA(1,0,3)), the reverse of the ranking obtained when the order was re-selected at every walk-forward step. This reversal is informative in its own right. Fixing the order via a single, thorough search on the full initial training window removed a source of noise that appears to have disproportionately affected Arabica under the earlier, re-adaptive specification, plausibly because that specification occasionally selected an unstable or under-specified order on the smaller training windows encountered early in the walk-forward loop. Robusta's result, by contrast, barely moved between the two specifications, suggesting its autoregressive structure was already being captured reasonably well even without fixing the order. Both series still carry meaningful short-run autocorrelation, as reflected in the richer moving-average component retained for Robusta (an MA(3) term) against the two autoregressive terms retained for Arabica, but the practical gain from the methodological change discussed in this study accrued mostly to Arabica rather than to Robusta.

The failure of MLR on Robusta but not Arabica is partly a sample size effect, with 153 versus 168 training observations, but also reflects the more pronounced multicollinearity among Robusta predictors already documented in the VIF diagnostics, where Production, Consumption, Exports and CPI all trend upward together over the shorter 2008–2023 window available for this variety. With fewer training observations to begin with, this shared trend leaves OLS even less able to separate the individual contribution of each predictor than it is for Arabica, where the same trending variables are estimated over a longer 2006–2023 window. The regularisation results reported above sharpen this contrast further: Ridge nearly doubles Robusta's $R^2$ while making Arabica's worse, which is difficult to explain by sample size alone and points instead to a genuine difference in how entangled the two varieties' predictors are with one another.

The relatively weaker performance of tree-based models on Robusta, with Random Forest at $R^2 = 0.676$ and XGBoost at 0.797 compared to their Arabica counterparts of 0.815 and 0.812, reflects the extrapolation limitation of ensemble methods. Random Forest and XGBoost average over training observations and cannot produce predictions that substantially exceed the range of target values seen during training. The sharp upward acceleration in Robusta prices from mid-2023 onward moves beyond the price range of the training set, causing both models to produce forecasts that flatten while the observed series continues rising. This limitation is clearly visible in the forecast trajectory and residual plots, where a persistent negative bias emerges for both tree-based models from late 2022 onward.

This divide between the two varieties is not one the existing literature anticipates. The Literature Review explains why Arabica and Robusta diverge through climate, different agronomic zones and opposite ENSO exposure, but the results here point to a macro-financial divide instead: Robusta's sensitivity to WTI and the Federal Funds Rate has no established explanation in the literature reviewed for this thesis. Maurice and Davis (2012), cited earlier, find that oil price movements affect both varieties, but say nothing about why one might be more exposed than the other. The asymmetry is reported here as an empirical finding rather than a sourced mechanism.

# Conclusion

This study estimated six forecasting models, two econometric benchmarks in the form of ARIMAX and Multiple Linear Regression and four machine learning algorithms comprising Random Forest, XGBoost, Support Vector Machine and Artificial Neural Network, applied to monthly Arabica and Robusta coffee futures prices over the 2000–2023 period. Using a walk-forward expanding window validation protocol with an 80/20 train/test split, all models were evaluated on three out-of-sample metrics across a rich predictor set spanning macroeconomic, fundamental, climatic and speculative variables.

The principal empirical finding is that ARIMAX, with its $(p,d,q)$ order fixed on the initial training window and applied unchanged throughout the walk-forward loop, emerges as the strongest model for both coffee varieties, achieving out-of-sample $R^2$ values of 0.955 for Arabica and 0.926 for Robusta. XGBoost forms the strongest of the remaining models, at 0.812 for Arabica and 0.797 for Robusta, demonstrating that gradient boosting can identify non-linear relationships among predictors that the linear regression component of ARIMAX cannot accommodate, even as ARIMAX's own autoregressive structure captures the persistence in prices that a cross-sectional model like MLR cannot. The Multiple Linear Regression benchmark performs reasonably well for Arabica but collapses for Robusta at $R^2=0.276$, and the regularisation exercise conducted alongside it confirms that this collapse is driven by multicollinearity among a short sample of predictors rather than by a lack of genuine information in the predictor set: Ridge regression nearly doubles Robusta's $R^2$ while leaving Arabica's essentially unchanged or slightly worse.

The variable importance analysis, computed consistently across all four machine learning models, shows that the most informative predictors differ by variety rather than falling into one single dominant category. For Arabica, Ending stocks, COT net Managed Money and WTI are the most consistently important predictors, reflecting inventory dynamics, the financialisation of the coffee futures market, and the energy cost channel respectively. For Robusta, WTI and the Federal Funds Rate lead, plausibly linked to Robusta's more concentrated production geography and to the sharp shift in the interest rate regime that coincides with the test period used to evaluate the models. Climate variables contribute relatively little predictive power at the one-month-ahead forecasting horizon, a finding consistent with the lag, typically six to nine months, between a climate shock during flowering or fruit development and its eventual effect on realised production and, in turn, prices. This is not evidence that climate is irrelevant to coffee prices, but rather that a contemporaneous monthly model is not designed to capture this delayed transmission.

The four robustness checks and the model-specific tuning extensions conducted in this study yield several findings of independent interest. The disaggregated climate check confirms that the production-weighted aggregation of climate indices is the appropriate specification, since replacing the two global indices with 28 individual national series systematically worsens performance across all ML models. The variety-specific check reveals an important asymmetry: restricting climate and supply variables to the six Robusta-producing countries improves performance for four of the six models, with XGBoost reaching its strongest result at $R^2=0.849$, while the same restriction uniformly deteriorates Arabica performance because the global indices are already dominated by Arabica-producing countries. The GDP growth check provides no support for including this variable as a predictor, and the lagged COT check provides little support for the idea that recent speculative positioning history improves one-month-ahead forecasts beyond what the contemporaneous position already captures. Separately, the Random Forest pruning exercise confirms that cost-complexity pruning is technically compatible with an ensemble of trees, contrary to what the absence of a cp argument in R's `randomForest` might suggest, but that applying it is nonetheless harmful, since it removes the diversity across trees that the ensemble's averaging step relies on.

Several limitations constrain the interpretation of these results. Estimating ML models on non-stationary price levels raises the risk of spurious correlations driven by common trends. The ANN exhibits instability that persists across random initialisation, network depth, activation function and the specific package and optimiser used to fit it, as documented in the Appendix. The hyperparameter tuning procedure for SVM and ANN relies on a limited number of validation splits rather than a fully nested walk-forward search, which can leave small architectural differences reflecting a particular training run rather than a stable ranking. The national climate averages do not account for the distribution of coffee cultivation within each country. Data availability further restricts each variety to a shorter estimation sample than the full 2000-2023 period covered by the exploratory analysis, since the CFTC Disaggregated COT report only begins in June 2006 and Robusta futures prices only from January 2008. And all six models assume static predictor relationships over a 24-year period that witnessed substantial structural change in the coffee market.

These limitations suggest a few directions worth pursuing. Lagged climate variables at three, six and twelve months could capture the delayed weather-to-price channel that a contemporaneous specification cannot, though the lagged COT check in this study is a reminder that such extensions need to be tested, not assumed to help. A more systematic setup for the ANN, for example averaging results across several random initialisations, could address its instability more directly than any single fix tried here. And a rolling-window or regime-switching specification could let predictor relationships evolve over time, closer to how the coffee market actually behaved across the sample each model was estimated on.

From a practical standpoint, the results point toward inventory levels, speculative positioning, energy prices and, for Robusta specifically, the interest rate environment, as the more useful short-run signals for coffee, monitored together rather than any one in isolation; climate conditions at monthly frequency are the clearer exception, given the lag between a weather shock and its eventual effect on prices. For Robusta specifically, the variety-specific results suggest tracking supply conditions in its own producing countries, chiefly Vietnam and Brazil, the two largest Robusta producers worldwide, followed by Indonesia, India, Uganda and Côte d'Ivoire, rather than global aggregates that dilute the signal relevant to this variety. Taken together, these results point to a practical takeaway as much as a modelling one: which signals matter, and how they matter, differs enough between Arabica and Robusta that treating them as a single coffee market would miss real structure in the data.
